topics.t: Why chemistry matters and what matter is
topics.h: The paracetamol in your bag, the urea on a Punjab wheat field and the fuel that lifts an ISRO rocket all began as a chemist's question: what is this made of and how can it change?
p: Chemistry is the branch of science that studies the composition, structure and properties of matter and the changes matter undergoes.

Chemistry feeds and heals us: fertilisers and pesticides raise crop yields, and life-saving drugs are made in labs, e.g. cisplatin and taxol for cancer therapy and AZT (azidothymidine) for AIDS patients.
Industry runs on chemistry: acids, alkalis, dyes, polymers, metals, superconducting ceramics and conducting polymers all come from chemical processes.

Chemistry also repairs damage: safer substitutes for ozone-depleting CFCs in refrigerators, and green chemistry, which designs processes that cut waste and hazardous chemicals for sustainable development.
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Air, water, a pencil and your own body are matter; light, heat and a thought are not.

ex.q: Classify as matter or not matter: steam, a sound wave, a grain of rice, sunlight.
st: Test each one: does it have mass and take up space?
Steam (water vapour) has mass and fills its container, so it is matter.
A grain of rice clearly has mass and volume, so it is matter.
A sound wave and sunlight are forms of energy; they have no mass of their own and occupy no space.
ex.a: Matter: steam, rice grain. Not matter: sound wave, sunlight.

topics.rl: India is one of the world's largest makers of generic medicines, and plants in Hyderabad and Ahmedabad synthesise drug molecules in tonnes. The greener their reactions, the less effluent reaches rivers like the Musi and Sabarmati.

topics.t: States of matter and mixtures versus pure substances
topics.h: The same water is a glacier on the Himalayas, the Ganga in the plains and a monsoon cloud overhead: one substance, three states.
p: Solids: particles packed tightly in order, little freedom to move, so they have definite shape and volume. Liquids: particles close but able to move past each other, so definite volume but no definite shape. Gases: particles far apart and moving fast, so neither definite shape nor definite volume.
Changing temperature and pressure interconverts the states: solid ⇌ liquid ⇌ gas on heating or cooling (or on changing pressure).

A mixture has two or more substances in any ratio. Homogeneous mixtures have uniform composition throughout (sugar solution, air); heterogeneous mixtures do not (a mixture of salt and sugar crystals, grains and pulses with stones).

Pure substances have fixed composition. Elements contain only one kind of atom (Na, Cu, or molecules like H₂, O₂). Compounds contain atoms of different elements in a fixed ratio (H₂O, CO₂, sugar); their properties differ from their elements, and they can be broken down only by chemical methods.
Components of a mixture keep their own properties and can be separated by physical methods: hand-picking, filtration, crystallisation, distillation and so on.

ex.q: Classify: (i) brass, (ii) a mix of sand and iron filings, (iii) glucose, (iv) ozone.
st: Brass is a uniform alloy of copper and zinc in variable proportion, so a homogeneous mixture.
Sand and iron filings are visibly separate, so a heterogeneous mixture.
Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, has C, H and O in a fixed ratio, so a compound.
Ozone, O₃, contains only oxygen atoms, so an element (in molecular form).
ex.a: Homogeneous mixture; heterogeneous mixture; compound; element

topics.rl: At salt pans in the Rann of Kutch, seawater (a homogeneous mixture) is left to evaporate in the sun until common salt crystallises out, a physical separation on a giant scale.

topics.t: Properties of matter and the SI system
topics.h: In 1999 NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one team used pound-force and another used newtons. Units are not a formality; they can make or break a mission.
p: Physical properties can be measured without changing the identity of a substance: colour, odour, melting point, boiling point, density. Chemical properties need a chemical change to observe: acidity, basicity, combustibility, reactivity.
A physical quantity = a number × a unit, e.g. 5.0 kg. A number with no unit is meaningless. Earlier, the English system (foot, pound) and the metric system (based on powers of ten) were both used.

The International System of Units (SI, Système International d'Unités, 1960) has seven base quantities: length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time (second, s), electric current (ampere, A), thermodynamic temperature (kelvin, K), amount of substance (mole, mol), luminous intensity (candela, cd).

Since 2019 the base units are defined by fixing exact values of constants: the metre by the speed of light, the kilogram by the Planck constant h = 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the second by the caesium-133 transition frequency, the kelvin by the Boltzmann constant, the ampere by the elementary charge, the candela by luminous efficacy.
The mole is defined as exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities; this number is the Avogadro constant expressed in mol⁻¹.

ex.q: Sort into physical or chemical properties of iron: (i) melts at 1538 °C, (ii) rusts in moist air, (iii) is grey and lustrous, (iv) reacts with dilute HCl giving H₂.
st: Ask: can I observe it without making a new substance?
Melting point and colour/lustre are observed while iron stays iron, so physical.
Rusting forms hydrated iron oxide, and reaction with acid forms FeCl₂ and H₂: new substances, so chemical.

topics.rl: The National Physical Laboratory (CSIR-NPL) in New Delhi keeps India's national measurement standards and supplies Indian Standard Time; its atomic clocks realise the SI second using caesium.

topics.t: Prefixes, mass, volume, density and the unit factor method
topics.h: A COVID vaccine dose is 0.5 mL, an ISRO cryogenic tank holds tens of cubic metres. Prefixes and unit factors let a chemist move between these worlds without a single slip.
p: SI prefixes: pico (p) 10⁻¹², nano (n) 10⁻⁹, micro (μ) 10⁻⁶, milli (m) 10⁻³, centi (c) 10⁻², deci (d) 10⁻¹, kilo (k) 10³, mega (M) 10⁶, giga (G) 10⁹, tera (T) 10¹².
Mass is the amount of matter in a body and is constant everywhere; weight is the force of gravity on it and changes with place. Mass is measured accurately with an analytical balance.
Volume: 1 L = 1 dm³ = 1000 mL = 1000 cm³, and 1 m³ = 1000 dm³ = 1000 L. In the lab: burette and pipette deliver measured volumes; measuring cylinder and volumetric flask hold known volumes.
Density = mass ÷ volume. SI unit kg m⁻³; commonly g cm⁻³. 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³.
Unit factor method (dimensional analysis): multiply by a ratio equal to 1, such as (2.54 cm / 1 in), so the unwanted unit cancels and the wanted unit remains.

ex.q: Convert 2 days into seconds using unit factors.

topics.rl: Hospital pharmacists convert doses between mg and μg every day. Misreading 'μg' as 'mg' means a thousand-fold error, which is why many hospitals prefer writing 'mcg' or the full word 'microgram'.

topics.t: Temperature scales and scientific notation
topics.h: A doctor says 98.6, a weather app says 37 and a chemist writes 310.15: all three describe the same healthy human body.
p: Three common scales: Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F) and Kelvin (K). Water freezes at 0 °C = 32 °F = 273.15 K and boils at 100 °C = 212 °F = 373.15 K.
Conversions: °F = (9/5)(°C) + 32 and K = °C + 273.15. Kelvin has no negative values; 0 K is the lowest possible temperature.
Scientific notation writes any number as N × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ N < 10 and n is an integer: 232.508 = 2.32508 × 10², 0.00016 = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴.
Multiplying or dividing: handle the N parts normally and add (or subtract) the exponents: (5.6 × 10⁵) × (6.9 × 10⁸) = 38.64 × 10¹³ = 3.864 × 10¹⁴.
Adding or subtracting: first rewrite both numbers with the same exponent, then add the N parts: 6.65 × 10⁴ + 8.95 × 10³ = 6.65 × 10⁴ + 0.895 × 10⁴ = 7.545 × 10⁴.

ex.q: Lucknow records 45 °C on a May afternoon. Express this in °F and in K.

topics.rl: ISRO's cryogenic upper stage stores liquid hydrogen at about 20 K (−253 °C). Engineers work in kelvin because gas laws and thermodynamics use the absolute scale.

topics.t: Precision, accuracy and significant figures
topics.h: A batsman who hits the same spot outside off stump every ball is precise; one who hits the stumps is accurate. Lab readings work exactly the same way.
p: Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value. If the true mass is 2.00 g, readings 1.95 g and 1.93 g are precise but not accurate; 2.01 g and 1.99 g are both precise and accurate.
Significant figures are the meaningful digits in a measurement: all certain digits plus the first uncertain one. All non-zero digits count; zeros between non-zero digits count (2.005 has 4).

Leading zeros never count (0.03 has 1). Trailing zeros count only if there is a decimal point (0.200 has 3; 100 has 1, but 100. has 3 and 100.0 has 4). In scientific notation all digits of N count (4.01 × 10² has 3). Exact (counted or defined) numbers have infinite significant figures.

Addition/subtraction: keep as many decimal places as the number with the fewest decimal places (12.11 + 18.0 + 1.012 = 31.122 → 31.1). Multiplication/division: keep as many significant figures as the least precise number (2.5 × 1.25 = 3.125 → 3.1).

Rounding off: if the digit removed is more than 5, raise the preceding digit by one (1.386 → 1.39); if less than 5, leave it (4.334 → 4.33); if exactly 5, leave the preceding digit if it is even and raise it if it is odd (6.35 → 6.4, 6.25 → 6.2).

ex.q: A student measures 4.123 cm and 2.0 cm and multiplies them. Report the area correctly.
st: The answer must have 2 significant figures (the fewer).
Round 8.246 to 2 figures: the digit after 8.2 is 4 (less than 5), so it stays 8.2.

topics.rl: In a cricket bowling speed gun, the display shows 145.3 km/h, not 145.2817... because the radar can only measure to about 0.1 km/h. Writing extra digits would claim precision the instrument does not have.

topics.t: Conservation of mass, definite and multiple proportions
topics.h: Burn a candle on a sealed balance and the reading never changes. That simple fact, carefully measured by Lavoisier, launched modern chemistry.
p: Law of conservation of mass (Antoine Lavoisier, 1789): matter can neither be created nor destroyed. In any reaction, total mass of reactants = total mass of products.

Law of definite proportions (Joseph Proust): a given compound always contains exactly the same elements in the same proportion by mass, whatever its source. Natural and lab-made cupric carbonate both contain about 51.35% Cu, 9.74% C and 38.91% O.
Law of multiple proportions (John Dalton, 1803): if two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio.
Example of multiple proportions: 2 g of hydrogen combines with 16 g of oxygen in water and with 32 g of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide; 16 : 32 = 1 : 2.

To verify a law from data, fix the mass of one element (e.g. 1 g), find the mass of the other in each sample, and compare: equal values support definite proportions; simple whole-number ratios support multiple proportions.

ex.q: Carbon forms two oxides. In oxide A, 12 g C combines with 16 g O; in oxide B, 12 g C combines with 32 g O. Which law do these data illustrate?
st: The mass of carbon is fixed at 12 g in both.
Masses of oxygen: 16 g and 32 g.
Ratio 16 : 32 = 1 : 2, a simple whole-number ratio (CO and CO₂).

topics.rl: Engineers at coal-fired thermal power stations run a mass balance: the coal and air going in must equal the ash, flue gases and water vapour coming out. If the totals do not match, a measurement is wrong, because mass is never lost.

topics.t: Gaseous volumes, Avogadro's law and Dalton's atomic theory
topics.h: Two balloons of hydrogen plus one of oxygen give two balloons of steam, not three. Explaining that missing balloon forced chemists to invent the molecule.
p: Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes (1808): when gases combine or are produced in a reaction, they do so in a simple whole-number ratio by volume, provided all gases are at the same temperature and pressure. 100 mL H₂ + 50 mL O₂ → 100 mL water vapour (2 : 1 : 2).

Avogadro's law (1811): equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. Avogadro distinguished atoms from molecules, which explained Gay-Lussac's ratios.

Dalton's atomic theory (1808): matter consists of indivisible atoms; all atoms of an element have identical properties, including mass, and atoms of different elements differ in mass; compounds form when atoms of different elements combine in a fixed ratio; reactions only reorganise atoms, which are neither created nor destroyed.
Dalton's theory explains conservation of mass, definite proportions and multiple proportions.

It could not explain the law of gaseous volumes, because it did not distinguish between atoms and molecules (2 volumes of H₂ + 1 volume of O₂ giving 2 volumes of water vapour needs O₂ molecules to split).

ex.q: What volume of oxygen at the same T and P is needed to burn 30 mL of methane completely? CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)
st: By Gay-Lussac's law, gas volumes are in the ratio of coefficients: CH₄ : O₂ = 1 : 2.

topics.rl: CNG kits on Delhi autos meter fuel and air by volume. The ideal air-to-gas volume ratio comes straight from the combustion equation and Gay-Lussac's law.

topics.t: Atomic, molecular and formula mass
topics.h: A single carbon atom weighs about 2 × 10⁻²³ g, far too little for any balance. So chemists invented a tiny new ruler: the atomic mass unit.
p: One atomic mass unit (amu, now written u, the unified mass) is exactly 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom; 1 u = 1.66056 × 10⁻²⁴ g. On this scale ¹²C = 12 u exactly and ¹H = 1.0078 u.

Most elements are mixtures of isotopes, so we use the average atomic mass = Σ (fractional abundance × isotopic mass). Chlorine (75.77% ³⁵Cl, 24.23% ³⁷Cl) averages 35.45 u; natural carbon averages 12.011 u.
Molecular mass = sum of atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule: CH₄ = 12.011 + 4(1.008) = 16.043 u; H₂O = 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.02 u.
Ionic solids such as NaCl have no discrete molecules; they form a 3-D lattice of ions. For them we use formula mass: NaCl = 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5 u.
Multiply each atomic mass by how many times that atom appears, then add; brackets multiply everything inside (Ca(OH)₂ has 2 O and 2 H).

ex.q: Calculate the molecular mass of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ (C = 12.011 u, H = 1.008 u, O = 16.00 u).

topics.rl: Mass spectrometers at India's forensic labs and at BARC separate isotopes by mass, which is how they measure the exact isotope mix behind an element's average atomic mass.

topics.t: The mole, molar mass and molar volume
topics.h: A 'dozen' bananas means 12; a 'mole' of anything means 6.022 × 10²³. Counting atoms by the mole is how chemists weigh out particles they cannot see.
p: The mole is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions). This number is the Avogadro constant, N_A ≈ 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Molar mass = mass of one mole of a substance in grams; it is numerically equal to the atomic, molecular or formula mass in u. H₂O: 18.02 g mol⁻¹; NaCl: 58.5 g mol⁻¹.
Moles n = mass ÷ molar mass; number of particles = n × N_A; mass = n × molar mass.
Molar volume of an ideal gas: 22.4 L at STP (273.15 K and 1 atm, the older convention) and 22.7 L at 273.15 K and 1 bar (the current standard). Moles of gas = volume ÷ molar volume.
Always ask 'one mole of what?': 1 mol of O₂ has 6.022 × 10²³ molecules but 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ oxygen atoms.

ex.q: How many moles and how many molecules are present in 36 g of water (H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)?

topics.rl: An Indian Railways tank wagon carrying about 50 tonnes of liquid ammonia (17 g mol⁻¹) holds nearly 3 million moles, roughly 1.8 × 10³⁰ molecules, all tracked by mass at weighbridges.

topics.t: Percentage composition, empirical and molecular formulas
topics.h: A forensic lab gets an unknown white powder. Burn it, weigh the pieces, and the numbers alone reveal its formula. That is the power of percentage composition.
p: Mass percent of an element = (mass of that element in 1 mol of compound ÷ molar mass of compound) × 100. Comparing a sample's measured percentage with the theoretical value checks its purity.
Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms (CH₂O for glucose). Molecular formula: the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆).

Empirical formula from percentages: (1) take a 100 g sample so percentages become grams, (2) divide each by its atomic mass to get moles, (3) divide all by the smallest number of moles, (4) multiply by a small integer if needed to make whole numbers.
Molecular formula = n × empirical formula, where n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass.
For ethanol, C₂H₅OH (molar mass 46.068 g mol⁻¹): C 52.14%, H 13.13%, O 34.73%. The three percentages always add to 100.

ex.q: A compound contains 40.0% C, 6.67% H and 53.33% O. Its molar mass is 180 g mol⁻¹. Find its empirical and molecular formulas (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16).
st: Divide by 3.33: C = 1, H = 2, O = 1, so the empirical formula is CH₂O.
ex.a: Empirical formula CH₂O; molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆

topics.rl: FSSAI labs test honey and ghee by elemental and compositional analysis; a percentage that does not match the expected value flags adulteration before the product reaches a kirana shelf.

topics.t: Stoichiometry and the limiting reagent
topics.h: A dosa stall with 10 cups of batter but only 4 spoons of oil can make only as many dosas as the oil allows. In reactions, the 'oil' is called the limiting reagent.
p: Stoichiometry is the calculation of masses (and sometimes volumes) of reactants and products from a balanced equation. Coefficients give mole ratios: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) means 1 mol CH₄ + 2 mol O₂ → 1 mol CO₂ + 2 mol H₂O.
The same equation can be read as masses (16 g CH₄ + 64 g O₂ → 44 g CO₂ + 36 g H₂O) or, for gases at the same T and P, as volumes.

Balance by inspection: write correct formulas, balance atoms that appear in only one reactant and one product first, leave H and O (or elements present as free elements) for last, then re-count every atom. Never change a subscript.
Limiting reagent: the reactant that is used up first; it decides how much product forms. The other reactant is in excess and some of it is left over.

Method: convert each reactant to moles, divide by its coefficient (or compare with what the equation needs), and the smaller value marks the limiting reagent. Calculate product from the limiting reagent only.

ex.q: 28 g of N₂ and 3 g of H₂ react: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). Find the limiting reagent, the mass of NH₃ formed and the mass of excess reactant left (N = 14, H = 1).
st: 1 mol N₂ needs 3 mol H₂, but only 1.5 mol is present, so H₂ is limiting.
N₂ used = 1.5/3 = 0.5 mol; N₂ left = 0.5 mol = 14 g.
ex.a: H₂ is limiting; 17 g NH₃ forms; 14 g N₂ remains

topics.rl: IFFCO's ammonia plants deliberately feed nitrogen and hydrogen close to the 1 : 3 ratio. Excess of either gas would be wasted compression energy, so plant engineers live by limiting-reagent arithmetic.

topics.t: Concentration: mass percent, mole fraction and molarity
topics.h: ORS packets, saline drips at AIIMS and the acid in a car battery all depend on one question: how much solute is in how much solution?
p: A solution = solute (smaller component) + solvent (larger component). Concentration can be expressed as mass percent, mole fraction, molarity or molality.
Mass percent (w/w) = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100, where mass of solution = solute + solvent.
Mole fraction of A: x_A = n_A ÷ (n_A + n_B). It has no unit, and the mole fractions of all components add up to 1.
Molarity M = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in litres (mol L⁻¹). Note: volume of solution, not of solvent.
Dilution keeps the moles of solute the same: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.

ex.q: 4 g of NaOH is dissolved in water to make 250 mL of solution. Find the molarity (NaOH = 40 g mol⁻¹).

topics.rl: WHO-recommended ORS dissolves a sachet in 1 litre of clean water to give fixed molar concentrations of sodium, potassium and glucose. The ASHA workers who distribute it across India are, in effect, delivering molarity.

topics.t: Molality and converting between concentration terms
topics.h: A solution labelled 1.00 M in a cool Shimla lab becomes slightly less than 1.00 M in a hot Chennai lab. Molality never plays that trick.
p: Molality m = moles of solute ÷ mass of solvent in kilograms (mol kg⁻¹). Note: kilograms of solvent, not of solution.
Molality does not change with temperature, because mass does not change on heating; molarity does, because volume expands or contracts with temperature.
To prepare a solution of given molarity: moles needed = M × V(L); mass = moles × molar mass; dissolve in a little solvent in a volumetric flask and make up to the mark.
To convert molarity to molality you need the density of the solution: mass of 1 L solution = density × 1000 mL; subtract the mass of solute to get mass of solvent; then m = moles ÷ kg of solvent.
Lab safety: wear goggles and gloves when handling NaOH pellets or concentrated acids; NaOH is corrosive and its dissolution releases heat.

ex.q: A 2.0 M NaOH solution has density 1.08 g mL⁻¹. Find its molality (NaOH = 40 g mol⁻¹).
st: Take 1 L of solution: mass = 1.08 × 1000 = 1080 g.

topics.rl: When you study boiling- and freezing-point changes of solutions in Class 12, concentrations are given as molality, because molality does not drift when the solution is heated or cooled.

topics.t: Discovery of the electron: cathode rays, e/m and Millikan
topics.h: The old fat CRT TVs in Indian homes worked by firing a beam of electrons at a glowing screen. That beam is a direct descendant of the cathode ray tube that revealed the electron.
p: Cathode ray discharge tube: a glass tube with two electrodes, gas at very low pressure and a very high voltage. A stream of particles moves from the cathode (−) to the anode (+). The rays are invisible but make a fluorescent coating such as zinc sulphide glow.

Properties of cathode rays: they travel in straight lines without fields, they consist of negatively charged particles called electrons, and their behaviour does not depend on the electrode material or the gas in the tube. So electrons are a basic constituent of all atoms.

J. J. Thomson (1897) bent cathode rays with electric and magnetic fields and measured the charge-to-mass ratio: e/mₑ = 1.758820 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹. Deflection is larger when the charge is larger, the mass smaller or the field stronger.
R. A. Millikan's oil drop experiment (1906–1914) found the charge of the electron: −1.602176 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (taken as −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). Combining with e/m gives mₑ = 9.1094 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
Summary table: electron charge −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg (about 0.00054 u); proton +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1.67262 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (1.00727 u); neutron 0, 1.67493 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (1.00867 u).

ex.q: Use e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and e/mₑ = 1.758820 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹ to find the mass of an electron.

topics.rl: Electron-beam welding in ISRO's workshops joins rocket-engine parts by steering an electron beam with magnetic fields, the same physics Thomson used to measure e/m.

topics.t: Protons, neutrons and the first atomic models
topics.h: Rutherford said firing alpha particles at gold foil and seeing some bounce back was like firing a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and having it come back to hit you.
p: Canal (anode) rays: in a discharge tube with a perforated cathode, positively charged particles travel opposite to cathode rays. Their charge-to-mass ratio depends on the gas, some carry multiple units of positive charge, and they bend opposite to electrons in fields. The lightest such particle, from hydrogen, is the proton.
Chadwick (1932) bombarded a thin sheet of beryllium with α-particles and detected electrically neutral particles slightly heavier than protons: neutrons.

Thomson's model (1898): an atom is a uniform sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it, like seeds in a watermelon (also called the plum pudding model). It explained neutrality but not later experiments.

Rutherford's α-scattering experiment: a beam of α-particles was aimed at a very thin gold foil (about 100 nm) and a zinc sulphide screen recorded flashes. Most passed straight through, a small fraction were deflected by small angles, and very few (about 1 in 20,000) bounced back nearly 180°.

Rutherford's nuclear model: almost all the mass and all the positive charge sit in a tiny nucleus (radius about 10⁻¹⁵ m versus about 10⁻¹⁰ m for the atom). Most of the atom is empty space, and electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular paths held by electrostatic attraction.

ex.q: Link each observation of the gold foil experiment to its conclusion.
st: Most α-particles passed undeflected → most of the atom is empty space.
A few were deflected through small angles → positive charge is concentrated in a small region that repels α-particles passing close by.
Very few bounced back → the nucleus is extremely small, very dense and holds almost all the mass.
ex.a: Empty space; concentrated positive charge; tiny, dense, massive nucleus

topics.rl: If an atom were the size of Kolkata's Eden Gardens cricket ground, its nucleus would be roughly a mustard seed (a couple of millimetres across) at the centre, with electrons out in the far stands.

topics.t: Atomic number, mass number, isotopes and isobars
topics.h: Heavy water from India's plants at Kota and Tuticorin is just water made with a heavier isotope of hydrogen, yet it keeps nuclear reactors running.
p: Atomic number Z = number of protons (= number of electrons in a neutral atom). Mass number A = protons + neutrons; protons and neutrons together are called nucleons. Number of neutrons = A − Z.
Notation: ᴬ_Z X, e.g. ³⁵₁₇Cl has 17 protons, 18 neutrons, 17 electrons. For ions adjust electrons only: Cl⁻ has 18 electrons, Na⁺ has 10.

Isotopes: atoms with the same Z but different A (different numbers of neutrons). Hydrogen: protium ¹H (0 neutrons, 99.985%), deuterium ²H or D (1 neutron, 0.015%), tritium ³H or T (2 neutrons, trace, radioactive).
Isotopes have almost identical chemical properties because chemistry is controlled by electrons, which are the same. Isobars: same A, different Z, e.g. ¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N.

Drawbacks of Rutherford's model: by classical electromagnetic theory, a revolving (accelerating) electron should radiate energy, spiral inwards and fall into the nucleus, so the atom would be unstable. It also says nothing about how electrons are distributed or their energies.

ex.q: Find protons, neutrons and electrons in ⁵⁶₂₆Fe³⁺.
st: Electrons = 26 − 3 = 23 (a 3+ ion has lost three electrons)

topics.rl: Doctors at Tata Memorial use radioactive iodine-131 to treat thyroid cancer. It behaves chemically like ordinary iodine-127, so the thyroid absorbs it, but it emits radiation that destroys diseased tissue.

topics.t: Electromagnetic waves and Planck's quantum
topics.h: All India Radio's Vividh Bharati, the X-ray at your dentist and the sunlight on your face are the same thing: electromagnetic waves of different wavelengths.
p: Maxwell (1870) showed that light is an electromagnetic wave: oscillating electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel. No medium is needed; in vacuum all such waves travel at c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

Wave characteristics: wavelength λ (distance between two successive crests), frequency ν (waves passing a point per second, unit hertz, Hz = s⁻¹), amplitude, and wavenumber ν̄ = 1/λ (waves per unit length, m⁻¹ or cm⁻¹). Key relation: c = νλ.

Electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing wavelength (decreasing frequency): gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Visible light runs from violet (about 400 nm) to red (about 750 nm).
Black body radiation could not be explained by the wave theory. Max Planck (1900) proposed that atoms emit or absorb energy only in discrete packets called quanta (photons for light).
Energy of one quantum: E = hν = hc/λ, where Planck's constant h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Higher frequency (shorter wavelength) means more energetic photons.

ex.q: A medium-wave AIR station broadcasts on 819 kHz. Find the wavelength of its radio waves.

topics.rl: Steelworkers, for example at Bhilai, have long judged furnace temperature by colour: red-hot iron is cooler than yellow-white iron. That colour shift with temperature is black body radiation, the puzzle that led Planck to quanta.

topics.t: Photoelectric effect and the dual nature of radiation
topics.h: The solar panels on Rajasthan's rooftops work because light can knock electrons free. Einstein explained this with photons in his theory of the photoelectric effect, the work that won him his Nobel Prize.
p: Photoelectric effect (H. Hertz, 1887): when light of suitable frequency falls on a metal surface such as potassium, rubidium or caesium, electrons (photoelectrons) are ejected.

Observations: electrons are ejected the instant light strikes (no time lag); the number of electrons ejected is proportional to the intensity of light; for each metal there is a threshold frequency ν₀ below which no electrons are ejected, however bright the light; above ν₀, the kinetic energy of the electrons increases with frequency but not with intensity.

Einstein (1905): light is a stream of photons. A photon of energy hν gives all its energy to one electron: hν = hν₀ + ½mₑv². Here W₀ = hν₀ is the work function (minimum energy to remove the electron).
So KE = h(ν − ν₀). Brighter light means more photons and more electrons, but not faster electrons.
Dual behaviour: radiation shows wave nature in interference and diffraction, and particle nature in black body radiation and the photoelectric effect.

ex.q: Light of frequency 1.0 × 10¹⁵ Hz falls on a metal with threshold frequency 7.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find the kinetic energy of the ejected electrons (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).

topics.rl: India's National Solar Mission counts on photovoltaic cells in which photons release electrons in silicon. The physics that limits a solar cell's efficiency starts with Einstein's equation.

topics.t: Atomic spectra and the hydrogen spectrum
topics.h: Astronomers identified helium in the Sun's spectrum in 1868 before anyone found it on Earth. Every element signs its name in light.
p: White light through a prism gives a continuous spectrum: all colours from violet to red merging into each other.

Atoms in the gas phase give line spectra. An emission spectrum shows bright lines on a dark background (energy given out by excited atoms); an absorption spectrum shows dark lines on a bright background at exactly the same wavelengths (energy absorbed). These lines are a fingerprint of each element, and line spectra show that electron energy is quantised.
Hydrogen's emission lines fall into series: Lyman (n₁ = 1, ultraviolet), Balmer (n₁ = 2, visible), Paschen (n₁ = 3, infrared), Brackett (n₁ = 4, infrared), Pfund (n₁ = 5, infrared).
Rydberg formula: ν̄ = 109 677 (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) cm⁻¹, where n₁ = 1, 2, 3, ... and n₂ = n₁ + 1, n₁ + 2, ... The constant 109 677 cm⁻¹ is the Rydberg constant for hydrogen.
Elements such as rubidium, caesium, thallium, indium, gallium and scandium were discovered by studying spectra.

ex.q: Calculate the wavenumber of the first line of the Lyman series (n₂ = 2 → n₁ = 1).

topics.rl: ISRO's Aditya-L1 solar observatory carries spectrographs that read the Sun's spectral lines to measure the temperature and composition of the solar atmosphere.

topics.t: Bohr's model: postulates, radius and energy
topics.h: In 1913 Niels Bohr took Rutherford's collapsing atom and added one bold rule: electrons may only live in certain orbits. The atom stopped collapsing, and hydrogen's spectrum made sense.
p: Postulates: (1) the electron moves round the nucleus in circular orbits of fixed radius and energy (stationary states or energy levels), numbered n = 1, 2, 3, ...; (2) energy does not change while the electron stays in an orbit; (3) energy is absorbed or emitted only when the electron jumps between orbits, with ν = ΔE/h (Bohr frequency rule); (4) angular momentum is quantised: mₑvr = nh/2π.
Radius of the nth orbit of hydrogen: rₙ = 52.9 n² pm (n = 1 gives the Bohr radius a₀ = 52.9 pm). For hydrogen-like ions: rₙ = 52.9 (n²/Z) pm.
Energy of the nth level: Eₙ = −R_H (1/n²) with R_H = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J. For hydrogen-like ions (He⁺, Li²⁺, Be³⁺): Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ (Z²/n²) J.

Negative energy means the electron is bound: a free electron at rest, infinitely far from the nucleus (n = ∞), has zero energy. As n decreases the energy becomes more negative and the electron is more strongly bound; n = 1 is the most stable (ground) state.
Higher Z pulls electrons closer (smaller r) and binds them more tightly (more negative E).

ex.q: Find the radius and the energy of the first orbit of He⁺ (Z = 2).

topics.rl: Bohr's model is how neon signs on Mumbai's Marine Drive are explained in class: electrons jump up when current passes, then fall back and emit light of specific colours.

topics.t: Bohr's explanation of the hydrogen spectrum and its limits
topics.h: Bohr's formula predicted hydrogen's lines to several decimal places, a stunning success. Yet put a second electron in the atom and the model falls apart.
p: Energy gap between levels: ΔE = Ef − Ei = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ (1/nᵢ² − 1/nf²) J. ΔE is negative for emission (nf < nᵢ) and positive for absorption (nf > nᵢ).
Frequency of the line: ν = |ΔE|/h = 3.29 × 10¹⁵ (1/nf² − 1/nᵢ²) Hz for emission; wavelength λ = c/ν; wavenumber ν̄ = 1.09677 × 10⁷ (1/nf² − 1/nᵢ²) m⁻¹.
Ionisation energy of hydrogen from the ground state = energy to move the electron from n = 1 to n = ∞ = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per atom (about 1312 kJ mol⁻¹).

Limitations: Bohr's model cannot explain the fine structure (doublets) of hydrogen lines, the spectra of multi-electron atoms such as helium, the splitting of lines in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect) or in an electric field (Stark effect), or why atoms form molecules with definite shapes.
Its deeper flaw, shown later by de Broglie and Heisenberg, is that an electron cannot have a precisely defined orbit.

ex.q: Calculate the energy released when an electron in hydrogen falls from n = 5 to n = 2.
st: ν = 4.578 × 10⁻¹⁹/6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ = 6.91 × 10¹⁴ Hz; λ = c/ν ≈ 434 nm (violet Balmer line)

topics.rl: Sodium-vapour street lamps on Indian highways glow yellow-orange because of a doublet of very close lines near 589 nm. That pair of lines is exactly the kind of fine structure Bohr's model could not explain.

topics.t: Dual nature of matter and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
topics.h: If light can behave like particles, can particles behave like waves? A young Louis de Broglie said yes in 1924, and electron microscopes now image viruses because he was right.
p: de Broglie (1924): every moving particle has a wavelength λ = h/mv = h/p, where p = mv is momentum. Heavier or faster particles have shorter wavelengths.
Evidence: a beam of electrons undergoes diffraction just like X-rays, a wave property. The electron microscope uses the wave nature of electrons and magnifies about 15 million times.
For everyday objects λ is far too small to detect: a 0.1 kg cricket ball at 10 m s⁻¹ has λ = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ m. Wave effects matter only for tiny masses like electrons.
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle (1927): it is impossible to know exactly and simultaneously both the position and the momentum (or velocity) of an electron. Δx × Δp ≥ h/4π, or Δx × Δv ≥ h/4πm.
The more precisely we fix position (small Δx), the larger the uncertainty in momentum (large Δp), and vice versa.

ex.q: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moving at 1.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
ex.a: About 0.73 nm, comparable to X-ray wavelengths

topics.rl: IISc Bengaluru and AIIMS run cryo-electron microscopes that use electron waves to reveal the 3-D shapes of proteins and viruses, something no light microscope could resolve.

topics.t: Uncertainty in action and the Schrödinger equation
topics.h: Heisenberg's principle quietly destroyed Bohr's neat circular orbits. In their place Schrödinger wrote one equation that still underlies every chemistry simulation run on India's PARAM supercomputers.
p: Significance: an exact orbit means knowing an electron's position and velocity together, which the uncertainty principle forbids. So we can only speak of the probability of finding an electron at a point. For large objects the uncertainty is negligible.

Calculation: Δv ≥ h/(4π m Δx). For an electron located within 0.1 Å (10⁻¹¹ m), Δv ≈ 5.79 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, huge compared with its speed. For a 40 g golf ball the uncertainty in position is about 10⁻³³ m, utterly negligible.
Bohr's model fails because it ignores the dual (wave) nature of the electron and contradicts the uncertainty principle by assuming fixed orbits.

Quantum mechanics (Heisenberg and Schrödinger, 1926) treats the electron as a wave. Schrödinger's equation is Ĥψ = Eψ, where Ĥ is the Hamiltonian operator, ψ the wave function and E the total energy. Solving it gives the allowed energy levels and the corresponding wave functions.
For the hydrogen atom the equation gives energy levels and wave functions labelled by quantum numbers. An atomic orbital is the wave function ψ of one electron in an atom.

ex.q: An electron is located within Δx = 0.1 Å = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Estimate the minimum uncertainty in its velocity (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, π = 3.1416).
ex.a: About 5.79 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, so the electron's path cannot be pinned down

topics.rl: Drug-design start-ups in Bengaluru solve approximate Schrödinger equations on computers to predict how a molecule will bind to a protein before anyone synthesises it.

topics.t: Orbitals and the four quantum numbers
topics.h: Every seat in a stadium has a stand, row, seat number and direction it faces. Every electron in an atom has a similar four-part address: its quantum numbers.
p: Features of the quantum mechanical model: electron energy is quantised; exact position and momentum cannot be known together; ψ itself has no physical meaning, but ψ² (|ψ|²) gives the probability density of finding the electron at a point.

Principal quantum number n = 1, 2, 3, ... gives the shell (K, L, M, N), size and, for hydrogen, the energy. Azimuthal quantum number l = 0 to n − 1 gives the subshell and shape: l = 0, 1, 2, 3 are s, p, d, f.
Magnetic quantum number mₗ = −l, ..., 0, ..., +l gives the orientation; a subshell has (2l + 1) orbitals and a shell has n² orbitals.
Spin quantum number mₛ = +½ or −½ (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925): the electron spins clockwise or anticlockwise. An orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin, so a shell holds at most 2n².

Orbit versus orbital: an orbit is Bohr's definite circular path (planar, can hold up to 2n² electrons, contradicts the uncertainty principle); an orbital is a 3-D region of high probability described by ψ (holds at most 2 electrons, consistent with quantum mechanics).

ex.q: List all subshells and the number of orbitals and electrons possible for n = 3.

topics.rl: MRI scanners at AIIMS work by flipping the spins of hydrogen nuclei in a magnetic field, the same kind of 'up or down' spin idea that the spin quantum number gives electrons.

topics.t: Valid quantum numbers, orbital shapes and nodes
topics.h: A p orbital looks like a dumbbell, but the electron is never found exactly at the nucleus between the lobes. Places with zero probability are called nodes, and you can count them with simple formulas.
p: Checking a set (n, l, mₗ, mₛ): l must be 0 to n − 1, mₗ must be between −l and +l, mₛ must be +½ or −½. (3, 2, −2, +½) is valid; (2, 2, 0, +½) is not (l cannot equal n); (3, 1, −2, −½) is not (|mₗ| > l).
Orbital shapes are shown by probability density plots or by boundary surface diagrams, which enclose a region where the probability of finding the electron is high (about 90%).

s orbitals are spherical, and their size grows with n (1s < 2s < 3s). p orbitals (from n = 2) are dumbbell-shaped with two lobes; the three p orbitals px, py, pz point along the x, y and z axes and are equal in energy and shape.

d orbitals (from n = 3) are five in number: dxy, dyz, dxz (lobes between the axes), dx²−y² (lobes along the x and y axes) and dz² (two lobes along z with a doughnut-shaped ring around the middle). In an isolated atom all five have equal energy.
Nodes: radial nodes = n − l − 1; angular nodes (nodal planes) = l; total nodes = n − 1. Example: 3p has 1 radial node and 1 angular node.

ex.q: Find radial, angular and total nodes for 4d.

topics.rl: The colour of a ruby or of Rajasthan's blue pottery glaze comes from electrons jumping between d orbitals of chromium or cobalt ions, which only makes sense once you know how d orbitals are shaped and oriented.

topics.t: Orbital energies, the (n + l) rule, Aufbau and Pauli
topics.h: Why does potassium put its 19th electron in 4s instead of 3d? The answer is a tug-of-war between nuclear attraction and shielding by inner electrons.
p: In hydrogen, orbital energy depends only on n: 1s < 2s = 2p < 3s = 3p = 3d < 4s = 4p = 4d = 4f. Orbitals of equal energy are called degenerate.

In multi-electron atoms, inner electrons shield (screen) outer ones, so an outer electron feels an effective nuclear charge Z_eff less than Z. Orbitals that penetrate closer to the nucleus feel more Z_eff; penetration order s > p > d > f, so energy now depends on both n and l: 2s < 2p, 3s < 3p < 3d.

(n + l) rule: the lower the value of (n + l), the lower the energy. If two orbitals have the same (n + l), the one with lower n has lower energy. Order: 1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p < 5s < 4d < 5p < 6s < 4f < 5d < 6p < 7s.
Aufbau principle: in the ground state, orbitals are filled in order of increasing energy.
Pauli exclusion principle (1926): no two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers the same. So an orbital holds at most 2 electrons, with opposite spins, and a shell holds at most 2n².

ex.q: Use the (n + l) rule to decide which fills first: 4p or 5s; 4f or 5d.
st: 4p: 4 + 1 = 5; 5s: 5 + 0 = 5. Equal, so lower n (4p) fills first.
4f: 4 + 3 = 7; 5d: 5 + 2 = 7. Equal, so lower n (4f) fills first.

topics.rl: Seating at a crowded Mumbai local works like Aufbau: people fill the most convenient seats first and, like Pauli's rule, only two can squeeze onto a single seat facing opposite ways.

topics.t: Hund's rule, electronic configurations and extra stability
topics.h: Chromium 'should' be 3d⁴4s², yet it is 3d⁵4s¹. Electrons will happily break the expected pattern for the comfort of a half-filled set.
p: Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity: in degenerate orbitals (p, d, f), electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before any pairing begins. Pairing in p starts with the 4th electron, in d with the 6th, in f with the 8th.
Electronic configuration is written in spdf notation (N: 1s² 2s² 2p³) or with orbital boxes. Noble gas core notation shortens it: Na = [Ne] 3s¹, Fe = [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s².
Core electrons fill the inner, completed shells; valence electrons in the outermost shell take part in bonding. For first-30 elements: K [Ar]4s¹, Ca [Ar]4s², Sc [Ar]3d¹4s², ... Zn [Ar]3d¹⁰4s².

Exceptions: Cr = [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Half-filled and completely filled subshells are extra stable because of their symmetrical distribution of electrons and their larger exchange energy (more pairs of parallel-spin electrons can exchange positions).
For cations, remove electrons from the outermost shell first: Fe²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁶ (4s electrons leave first), Fe³⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵. Count unpaired electrons using Hund's rule.

ex.q: Write the configuration of Mn (Z = 25) and Mn²⁺ and count unpaired electrons in each.
st: Mn: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²; the five 3d electrons sit singly in five orbitals → 5 unpaired.
3d⁵ again has 5 unpaired electrons, all with parallel spins (a stable half-filled set).

topics.rl: The blue of copper sulphate solution in a school lab and the green of nickel salts both come from partly filled d subshells: Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹ and Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸. Colourless zinc salts (Zn²⁺, 3d¹⁰) show what a completely filled d subshell does.

topics.ch: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
topics.t: Why classify? Triads, octaves and early tables
topics.h: By 1865 chemists knew 63 elements and had no map. Every attempt to organise them was like sorting a cricket team by jersey colour until someone found the real pattern.
p: Classification lets us study elements systematically: instead of memorising each one, we learn trends and families. Only 31 elements were known in 1800; 63 by 1865; 118 today.

Johann Döbereiner (1829) found triads: groups of three similar elements in which the middle element's atomic weight is about the mean of the other two. Li (7), Na (23), K (39): (7 + 39)/2 = 23. Others: Ca–Sr–Ba and Cl–Br–I. The idea worked only for a few elements.
A. E. B. de Chancourtois (1862), a French geologist, arranged elements by atomic weight on a cylinder (the telluric helix), showing periodic recurrence of properties. His work drew little attention.

John Newlands (1865) proposed the law of octaves: when elements are arranged by increasing atomic weight, every eighth element has properties like the first, like musical notes. It held only up to calcium. He was later awarded the Davy Medal (1887).
Lothar Meyer (1869) plotted physical properties such as atomic volume, melting point and boiling point against atomic weight and obtained a periodically repeating pattern.

ex.q: Check whether Ca (40), Sr (88) and Ba (137) form a Döbereiner triad.

topics.rl: Online grocery apps group products into categories so you can find anything quickly. Classification of elements does the same for 118 elements.

topics.ch: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
topics.t: Mendeleev's periodic law and his bold predictions
topics.h: Mendeleev described elements nobody had seen, giving their densities and formulas of their oxides. Years later gallium and germanium turned up almost exactly as he predicted.
p: Mendeleev's periodic law (1869): the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic weights.

He arranged elements in horizontal rows and vertical columns in order of increasing atomic weight so that elements with similar properties fell in the same column, and he gave more weight to similarity of properties (such as formulas of oxides and hydrides) than to strict order of weight.

Boldness: he left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties. Eka-aluminium became gallium (predicted atomic weight 68, density 5.9 g cm⁻³, oxide E₂O₃; actual Ga: 70, 5.94 g cm⁻³, Ga₂O₃). Eka-silicon became germanium (predicted 72, oxide EO₂, chloride ECl₄; actual Ge: 72.6, GeO₂, GeCl₄).
He also corrected some atomic weights that did not fit, trusting the periodic pattern over doubtful measurements.

Anomalies: some elements had to be placed out of atomic-weight order (iodine, 127, after tellurium, 128, so that iodine sat with the halogens); isotopes, having different atomic weights, should have needed different places; and hydrogen had no fixed position.

ex.q: Why did Mendeleev place iodine (127) after tellurium (128), breaking his own atomic-weight order?
st: Iodine's properties resemble chlorine and bromine (halogens).
Tellurium's properties resemble sulphur and selenium.
Keeping similar elements in the same group mattered more to him than strict weight order.
ex.a: To keep iodine in the halogen group and tellurium with sulphur and selenium

topics.rl: A good IPL scout leaves a slot open for a player type the team lacks and describes exactly what kind of player should fill it. Mendeleev did that for gallium and germanium.

topics.ch: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
topics.t: Moseley, the modern periodic law and the long form table
topics.h: A 26-year-old Henry Moseley fired electrons at metals and measured the X-rays. One straight-line graph fixed the inverted pairs that had bothered Mendeleev for 40 years.
p: Moseley (1913) found that the square root of the frequency of X-rays emitted by an element (√ν) gives a straight line when plotted against atomic number Z, but not against atomic mass. So atomic number is the more fundamental property.
Modern periodic law: the physical and chemical properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
Arranged by atomic number, the inverted pairs (Te 52 before I 53; Ar 18 before K 19; Co 27 before Ni 28) fall in the correct order naturally.

The long form of the periodic table has 7 horizontal periods and 18 vertical groups, numbered 1 to 18 as recommended by IUPAC. Period numbers equal the highest principal quantum number of the elements.
The 14 lanthanoids (Ce to Lu, Z = 58–71) and 14 actinoids (Th to Lr, Z = 90–103) are placed in separate rows at the bottom to keep the table compact.

ex.q: Explain how the modern periodic law resolves the position of argon (Ar, 39.9) before potassium (K, 39.1).
st: By atomic weight, K (39.1) should come before Ar (39.9).
By atomic number, Ar has Z = 18 and K has Z = 19.
Ordering by Z places Ar with the noble gases and K with the alkali metals, matching their properties.

topics.rl: Just as Aadhaar replaced name-based records with a unique number for every person, the atomic number became each element's unique ID, ending confusion caused by atomic weights.

topics.ch: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
topics.t: IUPAC names for elements with Z above 100
topics.h: When element 118 was first made, nobody could agree on who discovered it, so it needed a neutral placeholder name. IUPAC's answer: 'ununoctium', built from numbers alone.
p: For newly made elements with Z > 100, IUPAC gives a temporary systematic name built from numerical roots of the digits of Z, followed by the ending -ium.
Roots: 0 = nil (n), 1 = un (u), 2 = bi (b), 3 = tri (t), 4 = quad (q), 5 = pent (p), 6 = hex (h), 7 = sept (s), 8 = oct (o), 9 = enn (e).
The symbol is made from the first letters of the roots (three letters). Examples: 101 unnilunium (Unu), 104 unnilquadium (Unq), 118 ununoctium (Uuo), 120 unbinilium (Ubn).
Spelling tweaks: the final 'i' of bi and tri is dropped before -ium (bium, trium); the final 'n' of enn is dropped before nil (ennil).
After discovery is confirmed, IUPAC approves an official name and symbol: 101 is mendelevium (Md), 104 rutherfordium (Rf), 118 oganesson (Og).

ex.q: Write the IUPAC temporary name and symbol for Z = 113.
st: Add -ium; 'tri' loses its 'i': un + un + trium
Name: ununtrium; symbol from first letters: U, u, t

topics.rl: Element 113, nihonium, honours Japan, where it was made. New superheavy elements are created only in large accelerators, a field Indian scientists contribute to through international collaborations.

topics.ch: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
topics.t: Electronic configuration, periods and groups
topics.h: Give any element's atomic number and you can find its exact seat in the periodic table, the way an IRCTC PNR leads you to coach and berth.
p: The period number equals the principal quantum number (n) of the outermost (valence) shell. Each new period begins a new shell: period 1 fills 1s, period 2 fills 2s and 2p, and so on.

Number of elements in each period = number of electrons that can be placed in the orbitals being filled: 2 (1s), 8 (2s, 2p), 8 (3s, 3p), 18 (4s, 3d, 4p), 18 (5s, 4d, 5p), 32 (6s, 4f, 5d, 6p) and 32 in period 7 (7s, 5f, 6d, 7p).
Elements in a group have the same valence-shell configuration, which is why they show similar chemistry: all group 1 elements end in ns¹, all halogens in ns² np⁵.

Finding the position: block = last subshell to receive an electron; period = highest n; group = number of ns electrons (s-block), number of (n−1)d + ns electrons (d-block), or 10 + number of ns + np electrons (p-block).
Example rules at work: Z = 17 is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵ → p-block, period 3, group 10 + 7 = 17 (chlorine).

ex.q: Locate the element with Z = 26 in the periodic table.

topics.rl: In the electronics industry around Noida, engineers dope silicon (group 14) with phosphorus (group 15) or boron (group 13). Knowing group numbers tells them instantly which adds extra electrons and which creates holes.

topics.ch: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
topics.t: s, p, d and f blocks; metals, non-metals and metalloids
topics.h: Sodium in your salt, chlorine in tap water disinfection, iron in the Delhi Metro tracks and neodymium in phone speakers: four blocks of the periodic table in one day.
p: s-block (groups 1 and 2): ns¹ (alkali metals) and ns² (alkaline earth metals). Reactive metals with low ionisation enthalpies; they lose electrons readily to form 1+ and 2+ ions. Their compounds are mostly ionic, except those of lithium and beryllium. Metallic character and reactivity increase down the group.

p-block (groups 13–18): ns² np¹ to ns² np⁶. Together, s- and p-block elements are the representative or main group elements. Group 18 (noble gases, ns² np⁶; He 1s²) have closed shells and very low reactivity. Group 16 elements are the chalcogens and group 17 the halogens; non-metallic character increases across a period and decreases down a group.

d-block (groups 3–12): (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns⁰⁻² (e.g. Pd is 4d¹⁰ 5s⁰). Transition elements: all metals, mostly form coloured ions, show variable valence (oxidation states), paramagnetism and catalytic activity. Zn, Cd and Hg ((n−1)d¹⁰ ns²) lack most transition properties.

f-block (inner transition elements): lanthanoids (Ce, Z = 58 to Lu, Z = 71) and actinoids (Th, Z = 90 to Lr, Z = 103), filling (n−2)f orbitals. Actinoids are radioactive; elements after uranium (Z = 92) are transuranium elements, mostly made artificially in tiny amounts.
Metals (more than 78% of known elements) lie on the left; non-metals at the top right. Metalloids such as Si, Ge, As, Sb and Te lie along the zig-zag border and show properties of both.

ex.q: Classify by block and type: Mg, Cl, Ti, Si, U.

topics.rl: Kerala's monazite beach sands are a major source of thorium and rare-earth (lanthanoid) elements, which India processes through IREL for magnets, phosphors and future nuclear fuel.

topics.ch: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
topics.t: Atomic and ionic radii, and isoelectronic species
topics.h: Lose an electron and you shrink a lot: a sodium atom has a radius of 186 pm, but Na⁺ has only 95 pm. Size explains half of the periodic table's behaviour.
p: Properties vary periodically because valence-shell configurations repeat at regular intervals of atomic number.

Atomic radius is measured as covalent radius (half the distance between two bonded atoms in a molecule: Cl₂ bond 198 pm → r(Cl) = 99 pm) or metallic radius (half the distance between neighbouring nuclei in a metal crystal: Cu–Cu 256 pm → 128 pm).

Across a period atomic radius decreases: electrons enter the same shell while nuclear charge increases, pulling them closer. Down a group it increases: a new shell is added each time and inner electrons shield the outer ones.

A cation is smaller than its atom (fewer electrons, same nuclear charge, often a lost shell): Na 186 pm, Na⁺ 95 pm. An anion is larger than its atom (extra electrons repel and Z_eff per electron falls): F 64 pm, F⁻ 136 pm.
Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons. Among them, the higher the nuclear charge, the smaller the radius: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺ (all 10 electrons).

ex.q: Arrange in decreasing radius: Mg²⁺, O²⁻, Na⁺, F⁻, N³⁻.
st: Nuclear charges: N 7, O 8, F 9, Na 11, Mg 12.
Smaller Z means weaker pull on the same 10 electrons, so a larger ion.

topics.rl: Water filters that soften hard water in Indian homes swap Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ for Na⁺ on ion-exchange resins; the size and charge of these ions decide how strongly the resin holds them.

topics.ch: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
topics.t: Ionisation enthalpy: trends and anomalies
topics.h: It takes 2372 kJ to pull one electron off each atom in a mole of helium, but only 376 kJ for caesium. That six-fold gap explains why caesium explodes in water and helium does nothing at all.
p: Ionisation enthalpy (ΔᵢH) is the energy needed to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻. Unit: kJ mol⁻¹. It is always positive (energy is absorbed).

Successive ionisation enthalpies always increase (ΔᵢH₂ > ΔᵢH₁), because removing an electron from a positive ion is harder. A very large jump appears when an electron is removed from a noble-gas core.
Trend across a period: generally increases (higher effective nuclear charge, smaller size). Noble gases have the highest values in each period and alkali metals the lowest.
Trend down a group: decreases, because atomic size increases and inner electrons shield the outer electron from the nucleus.

Anomalies: Be (899) > B (801) because B's 2p electron is less penetrating and better shielded than Be's 2s electron; N (1402) > O (1314) because N has a stable half-filled 2p³, while in O one 2p orbital holds a pair whose mutual repulsion makes one electron easier to remove.

ex.q: Explain why the first ionisation enthalpy of Mg (738 kJ mol⁻¹) is higher than that of Al (577 kJ mol⁻¹).
st: Mg: [Ne] 3s². The electron removed is a 3s electron.
Al: [Ne] 3s² 3p¹. The electron removed is a 3p electron.
A 3p electron penetrates less and is shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is held less tightly and is easier to remove.
ex.a: Al loses a less penetrating, better shielded 3p electron, so its ΔᵢH₁ is lower

topics.rl: Caesium's very low ionisation enthalpy is why it is used in photoelectric cells: even visible light carries enough energy to knock out its loosely held outer electron.

topics.ch: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
topics.t: Electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity
topics.h: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, yet chlorine, not fluorine, releases the most energy when it gains an electron. Small size has a hidden cost.
p: Electron gain enthalpy (Δ_egH) is the enthalpy change when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g). If energy is released, Δ_egH is negative (exothermic). Halogens have large negative values; noble gases have large positive values because the electron must enter a new, higher shell.
Trends: Δ_egH generally becomes more negative across a period (higher effective nuclear charge, smaller size) and less negative down a group (larger size).

Anomaly: O (−141) and F (−328) have less negative values than S (−200) and Cl (−349). In the small n = 2 shell, the incoming electron suffers strong repulsion from the electrons already there. So Cl has the most negative electron gain enthalpy of all elements.

Electronegativity is a qualitative measure of the ability of an atom in a chemical compound to attract shared electrons to itself. It is not directly measurable; Linus Pauling's scale gives fluorine the highest value, 4.0.
Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group. High electronegativity goes with non-metallic character; low electronegativity with metallic character.

ex.q: Arrange F, Cl, Br, I in order of (a) electronegativity and (b) negative electron gain enthalpy.
st: (a) Electronegativity falls smoothly down the group: F > Cl > Br > I.
(b) Δ_egH values: F −328, Cl −349, Br −325, I −295 kJ mol⁻¹.
Most negative first: Cl > F > Br > I (fluorine is pushed below chlorine by repulsion in its small 2p subshell).
ex.a: (a) F > Cl > Br > I; (b) Cl > F > Br > I

topics.rl: Fluoride toothpastes and the Teflon on non-stick tawas both rely on fluorine's very high electronegativity, which makes the C–F bond one of the strongest and least reactive in chemistry.

topics.ch: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
topics.t: Valence, anomalous second-period elements and nature of oxides
topics.h: Lithium behaves more like magnesium than like sodium, and aluminium oxide can neutralise both acids and bases. The periodic table has diagonal shortcuts and double agents.
p: Valence (oxidation state) is periodic: for s- and p-block elements it equals the number of valence electrons or 8 minus that number. Group 1 shows +1, group 2 +2, group 13 +3; group 15 −3 in hydrides; group 17 −1. Oxygen shows −2 in Na₂O but +2 in OF₂, because F is more electronegative.

Second-period elements (Li to F) differ from the rest of their groups because of very small size, high charge/radius ratio, high electronegativity and absence of d orbitals. Their maximum covalency is 4 (B in [BF₄]⁻), while Al can reach 6 ([AlF₆]³⁻). They also form strong pπ–pπ multiple bonds (C=C, C≡C, N≡N, C=O).
Diagonal relationship: Li resembles Mg, Be resembles Al and B resembles Si, because size and charge effects balance along the diagonal.
Reactivity is highest at the two extremes of a period: alkali metals (lose electrons easily, strong reducing agents) and halogens (gain electrons readily, strong oxidising agents).
Oxides change from basic on the left to acidic on the right: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH (basic); Cl₂O₇ + H₂O → 2HClO₄ (acidic). Middle oxides are amphoteric (Al₂O₃, As₂O₃) or neutral (CO, NO, N₂O).

ex.q: Classify the period 3 oxides Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇.
st: Metals on the left give basic oxides: Na₂O (strongly basic), MgO (basic).
Al₂O₃ reacts with both acids and bases: amphoteric.
Non-metals on the right give acidic oxides: SiO₂ (weakly acidic), P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇ (strongly acidic).
ex.a: Basic → amphoteric → acidic across the period

topics.rl: Farmers in Kerala add lime (CaO, a basic oxide) to acidic soils, while sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from factories (acidic oxides) cause acid rain that damages the marble of the Taj Mahal.

topics.t: Lewis symbols, the octet rule and covalent bonds
topics.h: Noble gases sit alone like toppers who need no study group. Every other atom bonds to imitate their full outer shell.
p: Atoms combine to reach a more stable, lower-energy arrangement. Only valence (outer-shell) electrons take part. A Lewis symbol shows them as dots round the element symbol: Na•, •C• with four dots, :Cl• with seven. The number of dots usually gives the group valence, or 8 minus it.

Kössel: highly electropositive metals lose electrons and highly electronegative non-metals gain electrons, forming ions with noble-gas configurations (Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻). The electrostatic attraction between ions is an electrovalent (ionic) bond; electrovalence = number of unit charges on the ion.
Octet rule (Kössel and Lewis, 1916): atoms combine by transferring or sharing valence electrons so that each attains eight electrons in its valence shell (two for H, a duplet).

Langmuir (1919) refined Lewis's ideas and coined 'covalent bond': a bond formed by mutual sharing of electron pairs. One shared pair = single bond (Cl–Cl), two pairs = double bond (O=C=O), three pairs = triple bond (N≡N, H–C≡C–H).

ex.q: Show the formation of CO₂ using the octet rule.
st: C has 4 valence electrons; each O has 6.
C shares two pairs with each O.
Each O now has 4 shared + 4 lone electrons = 8; C has 8 shared electrons.
Structure: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each oxygen.
ex.a: O=C=O, two double bonds, every atom with an octet

topics.rl: LPG (propane and butane) burns in Indian kitchens because its C–H and C–C covalent bonds rearrange with O₂ into the stronger C=O and O–H bonds of CO₂ and water, releasing energy.

topics.t: Drawing Lewis structures, formal charge and octet limits
topics.h: Ozone protects us from UV rays, yet its Lewis structure seems to give one oxygen a positive charge. Formal charge is the bookkeeping that settles which structure is best.
p: Method: (1) add valence electrons of all atoms (add one per negative charge, subtract one per positive charge); (2) place the least electronegative atom in the centre (H and F are always terminal); (3) draw single bonds; (4) complete octets on outer atoms with lone pairs; (5) if the central atom lacks an octet, convert lone pairs into multiple bonds.

Formal charge (FC) of an atom = (valence electrons) − (non-bonding electrons) − ½(bonding electrons). The sum of formal charges equals the charge on the species. The best structure has the smallest formal charges, with negative charges on more electronegative atoms.
In O₃ (central O with one double and one single bond): central O = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1; doubly bonded O = 6 − 4 − 2 = 0; singly bonded O = 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.

Limitations of the octet rule: incomplete octet (BeH₂ and BeCl₂ have 4 electrons round Be; BCl₃ and AlCl₃ have 6); odd-electron molecules (NO, NO₂); expanded octet with d orbitals for period 3 and beyond (PF₅ has 10 electrons round P, SF₆ has 12, and S in H₂SO₄ has 12).
Other drawbacks: noble gases do form compounds (XeF₂, KrF₂, XeOF₂); the octet theory says nothing about shapes of molecules or the energy and relative stability of molecules.

ex.q: Draw the Lewis structure of the nitrite ion, NO₂⁻, and find the formal charges.
st: N in centre, single bonds to both O (4 electrons used); complete O octets (12 more, 16 used); put the last 2 on N.
N has only 6, so make one N=O double bond: O=N–O⁻ with one lone pair on N.
ex.a: [O=N–O]⁻ with one lone pair on N, two on the double-bonded O, three on the single-bonded O (FC −1)

topics.rl: Sulphuric acid, the most-produced chemical in India's fertiliser plants, has sulphur with 12 electrons around it, a classic case where the octet rule simply does not hold.

topics.t: Ionic bonding, lattice enthalpy and Fajans' rules
topics.h: Making Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from atoms actually costs energy. Salt exists only because the ions then crowd into a crystal and release a huge lattice enthalpy.
p: An ionic bond forms easily when: the metal has a low ionisation enthalpy (forms a cation easily), the non-metal has a high negative electron gain enthalpy (forms an anion easily), and the resulting crystal has a high lattice enthalpy.
Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻ needs 495.8 kJ mol⁻¹; Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) releases only 348.7 kJ mol⁻¹. The sum is endothermic, so ion formation alone does not explain stability.

Lattice enthalpy: the energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous ions. For NaCl it is 788 kJ mol⁻¹. This large energy released when the lattice forms is what stabilises ionic solids.

No bond is 100% ionic. Fajans' rules: covalent character of an ionic bond increases when the cation is small, the anion is large, and the charges are high, because a small, highly charged cation polarises (distorts) the electron cloud of the anion.

A cation with an (n−1)dⁿ ns⁰ configuration (typical of transition metals) is more polarising than one of the same size and charge with a noble-gas configuration (ns² np⁶), because d electrons shield the nucleus poorly.

ex.q: Arrange LiCl, NaCl and KCl in order of increasing covalent character.
st: Anion is the same (Cl⁻); compare cations: Li⁺ < Na⁺ < K⁺ in size.
A smaller cation is more polarising.
So covalent character: KCl < NaCl < LiCl.

topics.rl: Rock salt mined at Mandi in Himachal and sea salt from Tuticorin are both NaCl lattices. Its high lattice enthalpy is why salt melts only at about 801 °C, far hotter than any kitchen.

topics.t: Bond length, bond angle, bond enthalpy and bond order
topics.h: The N≡N triple bond needs 946 kJ mol⁻¹ to break. That is why air is 78% nitrogen that plants cannot use directly and why fixing nitrogen into urea takes so much energy.
p: Bond length: the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms, measured by spectroscopy or X-ray diffraction. Covalent radius = half the distance between two identical bonded atoms; van der Waals radius = half the distance between two identical non-bonded atoms in neighbouring molecules (for Cl: 99 pm and 180 pm).
Bond angle: the angle between the orbitals holding bonding electron pairs around the central atom, measured by spectroscopy. H–O–H in water is 104.5°.
Bond enthalpy: energy needed to break one mole of bonds of a type in gaseous molecules into separated gaseous atoms. H–H = 435.8, O=O = 498, N≡N = 946.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
In polyatomic molecules successive bonds break with different energies (H₂O: 502 then 427 kJ mol⁻¹), so we use the average (mean) bond enthalpy: (502 + 427)/2 = 464.5 kJ mol⁻¹ for O–H.

Bond order (Lewis) = number of bonds between two atoms: H₂ 1, O₂ 2, N₂ 3. Isoelectronic species have the same bond order (N₂, CO, NO⁺ all 3). As bond order increases, bond enthalpy increases and bond length decreases.

ex.q: Arrange the C–C bonds in ethane, ethene and ethyne by length and by enthalpy.
st: Higher bond order pulls atoms closer: lengths about 154, 134 and 120 pm.
Higher bond order needs more energy to break.
ex.a: Length: ethane > ethene > ethyne; enthalpy: ethyne > ethene > ethane

topics.rl: Gas welders in Indian workshops use oxy-acetylene torches. Burning ethyne releases a lot of energy partly because its weak π bonds are replaced by very strong C=O and O–H bonds.

topics.t: Resonance: canonical forms and the hybrid
topics.h: A rhinoceros is not half dragon and half unicorn switching back and forth; it is one real animal that no single imaginary picture describes. Resonance hybrids work the same way.
p: When a single Lewis structure cannot explain a molecule's properties, it is represented by two or more structures called canonical (resonance) structures; the real molecule is the resonance hybrid, shown with ↔ between the forms.
Ozone: two canonical forms (O=O–O and O–O=O). Both O–O bonds in O₃ are actually equal, 128 pm, between a single O–O (148 pm) and a double O=O (121 pm).

Carbonate ion CO₃²⁻: three equivalent canonical forms; all three C–O bonds are identical. CO₂ is a hybrid of O=C=O, ⁻O–C≡O⁺ and ⁺O≡C–O⁻; its C–O length (115 pm) lies between C=O (121 pm) and C≡O (110 pm).
Resonance stabilises a molecule: the hybrid has lower energy than any single canonical form. The difference is the resonance energy.
Canonical forms have no real existence; the molecule does not flip between them, and there is no equilibrium among them. Only electron positions differ between canonical forms; atoms stay in place.

ex.q: Why are all three C–O bonds in CO₃²⁻ the same length?
st: Draw three canonical forms, each with one C=O and two C–O⁻ bonds, the double bond in a different position each time.
The real ion is a hybrid of all three.
Each C–O bond has partial double-bond character (bond order 1⅓), so all are identical.
ex.a: The double bond is delocalised over all three C–O bonds

topics.rl: Limestone and marble (CaCO₃), used from the Taj Mahal to Rajasthan's Makrana quarries, owe the symmetry of their carbonate ions to resonance.

topics.t: Polar bonds, dipole moment and molecular shape
topics.h: Rub a comb on dry hair and bring it near a thin stream of tap water: the stream bends. Water molecules are tiny dipoles, and their shape is the reason.
p: Between identical atoms (H₂, Cl₂) the shared pair is equally shared: a non-polar covalent bond. Between atoms of different electronegativity, the pair shifts towards the more electronegative atom, creating partial charges δ⁺ and δ⁻: a polar covalent bond (H^δ⁺–F^δ⁻).

Dipole moment μ = charge (Q) × distance of separation (r). Unit: debye (D); 1 D = 3.33564 × 10⁻³⁰ C m. It is a vector, drawn as a crossed arrow (⟼) with the cross at the positive end, pointing towards the negative end.

In polyatomic molecules the net dipole moment is the vector sum of bond dipoles (and lone-pair contributions). Symmetrical shapes cancel bond dipoles: BeF₂ and CO₂ (linear), BF₃ (trigonal planar), CH₄ and CCl₄ (tetrahedral) all have μ = 0.
Bent H₂O (μ = 1.85 D) and pyramidal NH₃ have non-zero dipole moments, so a measured μ ≠ 0 rules out a linear or planar symmetrical shape.
NH₃ (1.47 D) has a larger μ than NF₃ (0.23 D): in NH₃ the lone-pair moment points the same way as the resultant N–H bond moments, but in NF₃ it opposes the N–F bond moments.

ex.q: CO₂ and H₂O are both triatomic and both contain polar bonds. Why is μ(CO₂) = 0 but μ(H₂O) = 1.85 D?
st: CO₂ is linear: the two C=O bond dipoles are equal and point in opposite directions, so they cancel.
H₂O is bent (104.5°): the two O–H bond dipoles add to give a resultant along the angle bisector.
Shape, not just bond polarity, decides the net dipole moment.
ex.a: Linear CO₂ cancels its bond dipoles; bent H₂O does not

topics.rl: Microwave ovens heat food because polar water molecules keep rotating to follow the oscillating electric field; non-polar oils on their own warm far more slowly.

topics.t: VSEPR theory and molecular shapes
topics.h: Electron pairs around an atom behave like people in a crowded Mumbai local: they spread out as far as they possibly can, and the bulky ones (lone pairs) push hardest.
p: VSEPR theory (Sidgwick and Powell, 1940; developed by Nyholm and Gillespie, 1957): the shape of a molecule depends on the number of valence-shell electron pairs (bonded and lone) around the central atom. Pairs repel and arrange themselves as far apart as possible. A multiple bond counts as a single super pair.
Repulsion order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair, because lone pairs are held by only one nucleus and spread out more.
No lone pairs: 2 pairs linear 180° (BeCl₂); 3 trigonal planar 120° (BF₃); 4 tetrahedral 109.5° (CH₄, NH₄⁺); 5 trigonal bipyramidal 90° and 120° (PCl₅); 6 octahedral 90° (SF₆).

With lone pairs: AB₂E bent (SO₂, O₃); AB₃E trigonal pyramidal (NH₃, 107°); AB₂E₂ bent (H₂O, 104.5°); AB₄E see-saw (SF₄); AB₃E₂ T-shaped (ClF₃); AB₅E square pyramidal (BrF₅); AB₄E₂ square planar (XeF₄).

Method: count valence electrons of the central atom, add one per bonded monovalent atom (and adjust for charge), halve to get total pairs; subtract bond pairs to get lone pairs; pick the arrangement, then describe the shape by the atoms only.

ex.q: Predict the shape of ClF₃.
st: Cl has 7 valence electrons; 3 F atoms contribute 3 → 10 electrons = 5 pairs.
3 bond pairs, 2 lone pairs → trigonal bipyramidal arrangement.
Lone pairs take equatorial positions (more room, fewer 90° repulsions).
The three F atoms form a T.

topics.rl: The bent shape of water, predicted by VSEPR, gives it the polarity that lets it dissolve salts and sugars, which is why your ORS dissolves and why life is water-based.

topics.t: Valence bond theory and orbital overlap
topics.h: Two hydrogen atoms drifting together feel a pull, then a push. At exactly 74 pm the forces balance and a bond is born, releasing 435.8 kJ for every mole.
p: Formation of H₂: as two H atoms approach, new attractive forces (each nucleus attracts both electrons) and repulsive forces (nucleus–nucleus, electron–electron) arise. Attraction dominates at first, so potential energy falls. At 74 pm energy is minimum (the bond length) and 435.8 kJ mol⁻¹ is released; closer than this, repulsion rises steeply.
Orbital overlap concept: a covalent bond forms when half-filled valence orbitals of two atoms overlap and the two electrons pair with opposite spins. Greater overlap gives a stronger bond.
Simple overlap of pure s and p orbitals cannot explain the directional bonds in CH₄ (four identical bonds at 109.5°), NH₃ or H₂O; p orbitals are at 90°. This is why hybridisation is needed.
Overlap can be positive (same phase or sign, leads to bonding), negative (opposite phase, no bond) or zero (orbitals at right angles or with cancelling regions, no bond).

Sigma (σ) bond: head-on (axial) overlap along the internuclear axis: s–s, s–p or p–p. Pi (π) bond: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, with electron density above and below the internuclear axis.

ex.q: Identify the type of overlap in H₂, HCl and Cl₂.
st: H₂: 1s of one H with 1s of the other: s–s, σ bond.
HCl: 1s of H with 3p of Cl, head-on: s–p, σ bond.
Cl₂: 3p of one Cl with 3p of the other, head-on: p–p, σ bond.
ex.a: s–s σ, s–p σ, p–p σ

topics.rl: Hydrogen fuel-cell buses trialled in Indian cities release energy by breaking H–H and O=O bonds and forming stronger O–H bonds. The 435.8 kJ mol⁻¹ H–H bond enthalpy is a key number in their design.

topics.t: Strength of σ and π bonds; introducing hybridisation
topics.h: In ethyne, H–C≡C–H, five bonds hold four atoms. Counting σ and π bonds is one of the most common one-mark questions in boards and JEE.
p: A σ bond is stronger than a π bond, because head-on overlap is larger than sideways overlap. A single bond is one σ; a double bond is 1σ + 1π; a triple bond is 1σ + 2π. A π bond always forms in addition to a σ bond.
Counting: every single bond = 1σ; add 1π for each double bond and 2π for each triple bond. Ethene C₂H₄: 5σ, 1π. Ethyne C₂H₂: 3σ, 2π. CO₂: 2σ, 2π. Benzene C₆H₆: 12σ, 3π.
Hybridisation (Pauling): intermixing of atomic orbitals of slightly different energies on the same atom to form an equal number of new, equivalent hybrid orbitals of identical energy and shape.

Features: the number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed; hybrid orbitals are directed to keep apart as far as possible (minimum repulsion); they overlap more effectively and form stronger bonds than pure orbitals.
Conditions: only valence-shell orbitals hybridise; the orbitals must have almost equal energy; promotion of an electron is not essential, and filled as well as half-filled orbitals can take part.

ex.q: Count σ and π bonds in HCN (H–C≡N).

topics.rl: Acrylonitrile (CH₂=CH–C≡N), made in Gujarat's petrochemical plants for acrylic fibres in sweaters, has 6σ and 3π bonds; its reactive π bonds are where polymerisation happens.

topics.t: sp, sp², sp³ and d-orbital hybridisation
topics.h: The same carbon atom becomes a tetrahedron in methane, a flat triangle in ethene and a straight line in ethyne. Hybridisation is carbon's shape-shifting trick.
p: sp: one s + one p → two sp orbitals at 180° (linear), 50% s character. BeCl₂ (Be: 2s² → 2s¹2p¹, then sp). Carbon in C₂H₂ is sp; the two unhybridised p orbitals form two π bonds (C≡C 120 pm).
sp²: one s + two p → three sp² orbitals at 120° (trigonal planar), 33.3% s character. BCl₃; carbon in C₂H₄ (the unhybridised p forms the π bond; C=C 134 pm).
sp³: one s + three p → four sp³ orbitals at 109.5° (tetrahedral), 25% s character. CH₄; also NH₃ (one lone pair in an sp³ orbital, 107°) and H₂O (two lone pairs, 104.5°).

sp³d: five orbitals → trigonal bipyramidal, as in PCl₅. Three equatorial P–Cl bonds lie in a plane at 120°; two axial bonds lie at 90° to that plane. Axial bonds suffer more repulsion and are slightly longer, which makes PCl₅ reactive. sp³d²: six orbitals → octahedral, as in SF₆. dsp²: square planar, as in [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻.
To predict: count σ bond pairs + lone pairs on the central atom (steric number): 2 → sp, 3 → sp², 4 → sp³, 5 → sp³d, 6 → sp³d².

ex.q: Predict the hybridisation and geometry of the central atom in PCl₅ and in NH₃.
st: PCl₅: P has 5 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → steric number 5 → sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal.
NH₃: N has 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair → steric number 4 → sp³.
With one lone pair, NH₃'s shape is trigonal pyramidal (107°).
ex.a: PCl₅: sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal; NH₃: sp³, trigonal pyramidal

topics.rl: SF₆, an sp³d² octahedral molecule, is so stable and non-reactive that power grids, including India's high-voltage substations, use it as an insulating gas in switchgear.
