p: C and H: heat the compound with copper(II) oxide. Carbon becomes CO₂, which turns lime water milky (C + 2CuO → 2Cu + CO₂); hydrogen becomes water, which turns anhydrous copper sulphate blue (2H + CuO → Cu + H₂O).

Lassaigne's test: fuse the compound with sodium metal so N, S and halogens become ionic: NaCN, Na₂S and NaX. The fused mass is boiled with water to make the sodium fusion extract. Safety: sodium reacts violently with water; use tiny pieces, a fusion tube and a safety screen.
Nitrogen: boil the extract with FeSO₄, then acidify with concentrated H₂SO₄. A Prussian blue colour (iron(III) hexacyanidoferrate(II), Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃) shows nitrogen.
Sulphur: lead acetate gives a black precipitate of PbS; sodium nitroprusside gives a violet colour. If N and S are both present, NaSCN forms and gives a blood-red colour with Fe³⁺ ([Fe(SCN)]²⁺).

Halogens: acidify the extract with HNO₃ and boil off any CN⁻ and S²⁻ (they would interfere), then add AgNO₃: white AgCl (soluble in NH₃), pale yellow AgBr (sparingly soluble in NH₃), yellow AgI (insoluble in NH₃). Phosphorus: oxidise with Na₂O₂ to phosphate, boil with HNO₃ and add ammonium molybdate; a yellow precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate shows P.

ex.q: A sodium fusion extract gives a blood-red colour with FeCl₃ but no Prussian blue with FeSO₄. What does it show?
st: Blood-red colour with Fe³⁺ comes from SCN⁻.
SCN⁻ forms when both N and S are present (NaSCN).
With excess sodium, NaSCN would instead split into NaCN and Na₂S, giving separate tests.
ex.a: Both nitrogen and sulphur are present

topics.rl: State forensic science labs in India use such element tests as quick screening steps before instrumental analysis of seized substances.

topics.ch: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
topics.t: Estimating carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen
topics.h: The protein value printed on your milk packet is often worked out by Kjeldahl's method: measure the nitrogen, multiply by a factor, and you have protein.
p: Liebig's method (C and H): a known mass m of compound is burnt in excess O₂ with CuO. Water is absorbed in anhydrous CaCl₂ and CO₂ in KOH; their mass increases m₁ (H₂O) and m₂ (CO₂) are noted. %C = (12 × m₂ × 100)/(44 × m); %H = (2 × m₁ × 100)/(18 × m).

Dumas method (N): the compound is heated with CuO in CO₂; nitrogen is released as N₂ (oxides of N are reduced over hot copper gauze) and collected over KOH solution, which absorbs CO₂. %N = (28 × V × 100)/(22400 × m), where V is the volume of N₂ in mL at STP.

Kjeldahl's method (N): heat with concentrated H₂SO₄ to convert N into (NH₄)₂SO₄; liberate NH₃ with NaOH and absorb it in a known volume of standard H₂SO₄; titrate the unused acid. From the acid used, find moles of NH₃ = moles of N.
Kjeldahl's method does not work for nitro and azo compounds or for nitrogen in a ring (e.g. pyridine), because this nitrogen is not converted to ammonium sulphate.
Always work through moles: mass of element = moles of element × atomic mass; percentage = (mass of element/mass of sample) × 100.

ex.q: 0.2 g of an organic compound gives 0.44 g CO₂ and 0.18 g H₂O on combustion. Find %C and %H.
st: Remaining 30% may be oxygen (if no other element is present).

topics.rl: Dairy testing labs measure milk protein by Kjeldahl nitrogen analysis. Lab safety: hot concentrated H₂SO₄ in digestion flasks needs fume hoods, goggles and acid-resistant gloves.

topics.ch: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
topics.t: Estimating halogens, sulphur, phosphorus and oxygen
topics.h: A sealed glass Carius tube, a little fuming nitric acid and some silver nitrate turn every chlorine atom in a molecule into weighable silver chloride. Chemists literally weigh atoms by proxy.
p: Carius method (halogens): heat a known mass m of compound with fuming HNO₃ and AgNO₃ in a sealed hard-glass Carius tube in a furnace. The halogen forms AgX, which is filtered, washed, dried and weighed (m₁). %X = (atomic mass of X × m₁ × 100)/(molar mass of AgX × m). For Cl: 35.5/143.5; for Br: 80/188; for I: 127/235.
Sulphur: heat with fuming HNO₃ (or Na₂O₂) in a Carius tube to convert S into H₂SO₄; precipitate it as BaSO₄ with BaCl₂ and weigh (m₁). %S = (32 × m₁ × 100)/(233 × m).

Phosphorus: heat with fuming HNO₃ to convert P into H₃PO₄; precipitate as ammonium phosphomolybdate, (NH₄)₃PO₄·12MoO₃ (M = 1877), or as MgNH₄PO₄, which is ignited to Mg₂P₂O₇ (M = 222). %P = (31 × m₁ × 100)/(1877 × m) or (62 × m₁ × 100)/(222 × m).

Oxygen: usually found by difference: %O = 100 − (sum of all other elements). Directly: the compound is decomposed in N₂, the gases are passed over red-hot coke at 1373 K so all O becomes CO, and CO is passed over I₂O₅ (I₂O₅ + 5CO → I₂ + 5CO₂). %O = (32 × m(CO₂) × 100)/(88 × m).
Safety: Carius tubes are sealed and heated under high pressure; they are opened only after cooling, behind a safety screen.

ex.q: 0.2 g of an organic compound gave 0.287 g of AgCl in a Carius estimation. Find %Cl (Ag = 108, Cl = 35.5).

topics.rl: Pesticide residue labs in Punjab's agricultural universities estimate chlorine content in chlorinated pesticides; classical Carius-type methods underpin the instrumental methods used today.

topics.t: Hydrocarbons as fuels; alkane nomenclature, isomerism and types of carbon
topics.h: CNG in Delhi's autos, LPG in your kitchen, petrol in a bike and the wax of a Diwali candle: all hydrocarbons, compounds of nothing but carbon and hydrogen.
p: Hydrocarbons contain only C and H. They are major fuels: LPG (mainly butane and propane), CNG (mainly methane), petrol, diesel and kerosene come from petroleum and natural gas.
Classification: saturated (only C–C single bonds: alkanes, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, and cycloalkanes), unsaturated (C=C: alkenes, CₙH₂ₙ; C≡C: alkynes, CₙH₂ₙ₋₂) and aromatic (benzene and its derivatives).
Alkanes are named with the IUPAC rules (longest chain, lowest locants, alphabetical order). From C₄ onwards they show chain isomerism: C₄H₁₀ has 2 isomers, C₅H₁₂ has 3, C₆H₁₄ has 5.

Types of carbon: primary (1°) carbon is bonded to one other carbon; secondary (2°) to two; tertiary (3°) to three; quaternary (4°) to four. Hydrogens on 1°, 2° and 3° carbons are called 1°, 2° and 3° hydrogens.
In 2,2,4-trimethylpentane, (CH₃)₃C–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₃: five 1° carbons, one 2°, one 3° and one 4° carbon.

ex.q: Classify each carbon in 2-methylbutane, CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃.
st: C2 (CH) attached to C1, C3 and the methyl branch → 3°.
C3 (CH₂) attached to C2 and C4 → 2°.
C4 (CH₃) and the branch CH₃ → 1° each.

topics.rl: Under the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana, crores of Indian homes switched to LPG. The cleaner flame comes from burning small, simple alkanes completely to CO₂ and water.

topics.t: Preparation of alkanes
topics.h: Vanaspati ghee is made by adding hydrogen to vegetable oils over a nickel catalyst. The same hydrogenation turns ethene into ethane in the lab.
p: From unsaturated hydrocarbons (hydrogenation): alkenes and alkynes add H₂ in the presence of finely divided Pt or Pd at room temperature, or Ni at higher temperature and pressure. CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃–CH₃; CH≡CH + 2H₂ → CH₃–CH₃.
From alkyl halides by reduction (fluorides excepted): zinc and dilute HCl supply hydrogen: CH₃Cl + H₂ → (Zn, H⁺) CH₄ + HCl; C₂H₅Cl + H₂ → C₂H₆ + HCl.

Wurtz reaction: an alkyl halide with sodium in dry ether gives an alkane with double the number of carbons: 2CH₃Br + 2Na → CH₃–CH₃ + 2NaBr. It suits symmetrical alkanes with an even number of carbons; it cannot make methane.
Decarboxylation: heating the sodium salt of a carboxylic acid with soda lime (NaOH + CaO) gives an alkane with one carbon fewer: CH₃COONa + NaOH → (CaO, heat) CH₄ + Na₂CO₃.

Kolbe's electrolysis: electrolysis of an aqueous sodium or potassium salt of a carboxylic acid gives an alkane with an even number of carbons at the anode: 2CH₃COONa + 2H₂O → CH₃–CH₃ + 2CO₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH. Methane cannot be made this way.

ex.q: Which alkane forms in each case: (a) CH₃CH₂COONa + soda lime, heated; (b) Wurtz reaction of CH₃CH₂Br; (c) Kolbe electrolysis of CH₃CH₂COONa?
st: (a) Decarboxylation removes one C: propanoate (3 C) → ethane (2 C).
(b) Wurtz doubles the alkyl group: 2 C₂H₅ → butane (C₄H₁₀).
(c) Kolbe joins two alkyl groups after losing CO₂: 2 C₂H₅ → butane.

topics.rl: Bio-CNG plants in Indore and Pune make methane from food waste; in the lab, methane is made simply by heating sodium acetate with soda lime. Lab safety: heat soda lime mixtures in a hard-glass tube and keep flames away from the collected gas.

topics.t: Properties of alkanes: boiling points, halogenation and other reactions
topics.h: Methane and chlorine can sit together in the dark for ages. Shine sunlight on them and a chain reaction rips through, making chloromethanes in seconds.
p: Physical properties: non-polar, so held by weak van der Waals forces. C₁–C₄ are gases, C₅–C₁₇ liquids, C₁₈ and above solids at 298 K. Boiling point increases with molecular mass; branching lowers it (smaller surface area): pentane 309.1 K > 2-methylbutane 300.9 K > 2,2-dimethylpropane 282.5 K. Alkanes are insoluble in water ('like dissolves like').

Free-radical halogenation: CH₄ + Cl₂ → (hν) CH₃Cl + HCl, then CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄. Reactivity of halogens: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂; fluorination is too violent, iodination is reversible and needs an oxidising agent (HIO₃ or HNO₃). Ease of replacing H: 3° > 2° > 1°.

Mechanism: initiation, Cl₂ → (hν) 2Cl•; propagation, Cl• + CH₄ → •CH₃ + HCl and •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•; termination, Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂, •CH₃ + •CH₃ → CH₃–CH₃, •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl. Termination explains traces of ethane.

Combustion: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (Δ_cH° = −890 kJ mol⁻¹); incomplete combustion gives soot (carbon black). Controlled oxidation: 2CH₄ + O₂ → 2CH₃OH (Cu, 523 K, 100 atm); CH₄ + O₂ → HCHO + H₂O (Mo₂O₃, heat); (CH₃)₃CH → (CH₃)₃COH with KMnO₄.

Isomerisation: n-hexane → 2-methylpentane + 3-methylpentane (anhydrous AlCl₃ + HCl). Aromatisation: n-hexane → benzene (Cr₂O₃/V₂O₅/Mo₂O₃ on alumina, 773 K, 10–20 atm). With steam: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂ (Ni, 1273 K). Pyrolysis (cracking): heating higher alkanes at about 773 K breaks them into smaller alkanes and alkenes.

ex.q: Explain why traces of ethane appear when methane is chlorinated in sunlight.
st: Initiation produces Cl•, which abstracts H from CH₄ to give •CH₃.
ex.a: Ethane forms in a termination step by combination of two methyl radicals

topics.rl: Refineries at Panipat and Jamnagar crack heavy alkanes into smaller ones to make more petrol and LPG, and use isomerisation to raise the octane number of fuel.

topics.t: Conformations of ethane
topics.h: Hold two windmills on one axle and twist one: the blades line up, then sit in the gaps. Ethane's two CH₃ groups do this billions of times a second.
p: Rotation about the C–C σ bond of ethane gives infinitely many spatial arrangements called conformations (conformers or rotamers).

Eclipsed conformation: the hydrogens on the two carbons are directly behind each other (dihedral angle 0°). Staggered conformation: they are as far apart as possible (dihedral angle 60°). Intermediate arrangements are skew conformations.

Sawhorse projection: the C–C bond is drawn as a slanting line, with the front carbon lower left. Newman projection: viewed along the C–C axis; the front carbon is a point (three bonds meet at the centre) and the back carbon is a circle (bonds start from the circle).
The eclipsed form has maximum repulsion between bond electron clouds (torsional strain), so it is least stable; the staggered form has minimum repulsion and is most stable.
The energy difference is only about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹, so rotation is almost free at room temperature, and the conformations cannot be separated.

ex.q: In a Newman projection of staggered ethane, what is the dihedral angle between the nearest C–H bonds on the front and back carbons, and why is it the stable form?
st: In the staggered form, each back C–H lies midway between two front C–H bonds.
Bond pairs are farthest apart → least torsional strain → lowest energy.
ex.a: 60°; minimum torsional strain makes it most stable

topics.rl: Drug designers at Indian biotech firms model the conformations of flexible molecules, because a medicine fits its target protein only in certain shapes, just as staggered and eclipsed ethane differ.

topics.t: Alkenes: the double bond, nomenclature and isomerism
topics.h: Ethene gas released by ripe bananas makes the mangoes in the same basket ripen faster. Its reactive double bond is a molecular trigger.
p: Alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ) contain a C=C double bond made of one strong σ bond (sp²–sp² overlap) and one weaker π bond (sideways overlap of p orbitals). In ethene, C=C is 134 pm (shorter than C–C, 154 pm), all six atoms lie in one plane, and bond angles are about 120°. The C=C bond enthalpy (681 kJ mol⁻¹) is less than twice that of C–C (348 kJ mol⁻¹), showing the π bond is weaker.

Nomenclature: choose the longest chain containing the double bond, number it so the double bond gets the lowest locant, and replace -ane by -ene: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ but-1-ene; CH₃CH=CHCH₃ but-2-ene; (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ 2-methylprop-1-ene.
Structural isomerism: C₄H₈ alkenes include but-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene (chain and position isomers).

Geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism: because the π bond prevents rotation, if each double-bonded carbon carries two different groups, two forms exist. cis: similar groups on the same side; trans: on opposite sides. But-2-ene shows it; but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene do not.

cis isomers are usually polar (non-zero dipole moment) with slightly higher boiling points; trans isomers are less polar or non-polar (trans-but-2-ene has μ = 0) and pack better in crystals, so they usually have higher melting points.

ex.q: Does pent-2-ene show geometrical isomerism? Draw the reasoning.
st: C2 carries H and CH₃ (different); C3 carries H and C₂H₅ (different).
Both double-bond carbons have two different groups, so cis and trans forms exist.

topics.rl: Fruit traders in Azadpur Mandi in Delhi ripen mangoes and bananas in ethylene chambers, a safer alternative to the banned calcium carbide method.

topics.t: Preparation and physical properties of alkenes
topics.h: Hydrogenate an alkyne with a 'poisoned' catalyst and it stops politely at the alkene stage. Use sodium in liquid ammonia instead and you get the opposite geometry.
p: From alkynes: partial reduction with H₂ over Lindlar's catalyst (palladium on charcoal deactivated with sulphur compounds or quinoline) gives cis-alkenes; reduction with sodium in liquid ammonia gives trans-alkenes. CH≡CH + H₂ → (Lindlar) CH₂=CH₂.
From alkyl halides (dehydrohalogenation): heating with alcoholic KOH removes HX from adjacent carbons (β-elimination): CH₃CH₂Br + KOH(alc) → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O.
From vicinal dihalides (dehalogenation): two halogens on adjacent carbons are removed with zinc: CH₂Br–CH₂Br + Zn → CH₂=CH₂ + ZnBr₂.
From alcohols (acidic dehydration): heating with concentrated H₂SO₄ removes water: CH₃CH₂OH → (conc. H₂SO₄, heat) CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O. This is also a β-elimination.

Physical properties: non-polar, insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents. C₂–C₄ are gases, C₅–C₁₇ liquids, higher ones solids. Boiling point rises with size; branched isomers boil lower. Safety: concentrated H₂SO₄ is corrosive, and ethene is flammable; do these preparations in a fume cupboard.

ex.q: Predict the alkene formed in each case: (a) but-2-yne with H₂/Lindlar catalyst, (b) but-2-yne with Na in liquid NH₃.
st: (a) Lindlar adds both H atoms from the same side → cis-but-2-ene.
(b) Na/liquid NH₃ adds H atoms from opposite sides → trans-but-2-ene.

topics.rl: Ethanol from Indian sugarcane molasses can be dehydrated to 'green' ethylene, a renewable route to polythene being explored as part of India's biofuel and bioplastic push.

topics.t: Addition to alkenes: H₂, halogens, HX, Markovnikov and peroxide effect
topics.h: Add HBr to propene and the bromine lands on the middle carbon. Add a pinch of peroxide and it jumps to the end carbon. Same reactants, opposite outcomes, because the mechanism changes.
p: Addition of H₂ (Ni, Pt or Pd) gives alkanes. Addition of Br₂ in CCl₄ gives vicinal dibromides: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → BrCH₂CH₂Br; the reddish-orange colour of bromine disappears, a test for unsaturation.

Addition of HX: reactivity HI > HBr > HCl. With an unsymmetrical alkene, Markovnikov's rule applies: the negative part of the addendum attaches to the double-bonded carbon with fewer hydrogen atoms. CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CHBrCH₃ (2-bromopropane, major).
Markovnikov mechanism (electrophilic addition): H⁺ adds first to give the more stable carbocation; propene gives the 2° cation CH₃CH⁺CH₃ rather than the 1° cation CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺, and Br⁻ then attacks it.

Anti-Markovnikov addition (peroxide or Kharash effect, 1933): in the presence of an organic peroxide such as benzoyl peroxide, HBr adds the opposite way: CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂CH₂Br (1-bromopropane). The mechanism is free-radical: Br• adds to the end carbon to give the more stable 2° radical, which then takes H from HBr.
The peroxide effect is seen only with HBr: the H–Cl bond (430.5 kJ mol⁻¹) is too strong to be split by the radicals, and iodine radicals combine to I₂ instead of adding to the double bond.

ex.q: Predict the major product of HBr with (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ (a) without peroxide, (b) with benzoyl peroxide.
st: (a) H⁺ adds to =CH₂ giving the 3° cation (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH₃; Br⁻ adds there → (CH₃)₃CBr (2-bromo-2-methylpropane).
(b) Br• adds to =CH₂ giving the 3° radical (CH₃)₂C•–CH₂Br; it takes H from HBr → (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br (1-bromo-2-methylpropane).

topics.rl: School labs across India test cooking oils for unsaturation with bromine water: unsaturated oils such as sunflower oil decolourise more bromine than saturated fats like ghee. Handle bromine in a fume hood; it is toxic and corrosive.

topics.t: Hydration, oxidation, ozonolysis and polymerisation of alkenes
topics.h: Every polythene bag in the market began as thousands of ethene molecules linking hands. Alkenes are the building blocks of the plastics industry.
p: Cold concentrated H₂SO₄ adds to alkenes by Markovnikov's rule, giving alkyl hydrogen sulphates: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂SO₄ → CH₃CH₂OSO₃H. Acid-catalysed hydration (dilute acid) adds water by Markovnikov's rule: (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ + H₂O → (H⁺) (CH₃)₃C–OH.
Cold, dilute, aqueous KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent) converts alkenes into vicinal glycols and loses its purple colour, a test for unsaturation: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O + [O] → HOCH₂CH₂OH.
Acidic KMnO₄ or acidic K₂Cr₂O₇ cleaves the double bond, giving ketones and/or acids: CH₃CH=CHCH₃ → 2CH₃COOH; (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ → (CH₃)₂C=O + CO₂ + H₂O.

Ozonolysis: O₃ adds to give an ozonide, which is cleaved by Zn/H₂O into smaller carbonyl compounds. Each C=C becomes two C=O groups. Propene → CH₃CHO + HCHO; 2-methylpropene → CH₃COCH₃ + HCHO. The products reveal the position of the double bond.
Polymerisation: at high temperature and pressure with a catalyst, many ethene molecules join: n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)ₙ– (polythene). Propene gives polypropene, used in ropes, crates and packaging.

ex.q: An alkene on ozonolysis gives propanone (CH₃COCH₃) and ethanal (CH₃CHO). Identify the alkene.
st: Each C=O came from one carbon of the C=C.
Join the carbonyl carbons with a double bond: (CH₃)₂C= from propanone and =CHCH₃ from ethanal.

topics.rl: Polymer plants in Gujarat make lakhs of tonnes of polyethylene and polypropylene a year from ethene and propene. India's single-use plastic rules now push for recycling these polymers.

topics.t: Alkynes: structure, nomenclature, preparation and acidity
topics.h: Old carbide lamps used by miners and village fair vendors dripped water onto calcium carbide; the ethyne released burned with a bright white flame.
p: Alkynes have a C≡C triple bond: general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. Names end in -yne, with the lowest locant for the triple bond: CH≡CCH₂CH₃ but-1-yne; CH₃C≡CCH₃ but-2-yne. C₄H₆ alkynes show position isomerism; C₅H₈ alkynes show position and chain isomerism (pent-1-yne, pent-2-yne, 3-methylbut-1-yne).

Ethyne (HC≡CH): each carbon is sp hybridised; the molecule is linear (180°). The triple bond = 1σ (sp–sp) + 2π (two sets of sideways p overlap, forming a cylindrical π cloud). C≡C is 120 pm long, with bond enthalpy 823 kJ mol⁻¹.
From calcium carbide: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂. CaC₂ itself is made by heating quicklime with coke: CaO + 3C → CaC₂ + CO.
From vicinal dihalides: two successive dehydrohalogenations, with alcoholic KOH and then NaNH₂: CH₂Br–CH₂Br → CH₂=CHBr → HC≡CH.

Hydrogen on a triple-bonded carbon is acidic, because sp carbon (50% s character) is very electronegative. Terminal alkynes react with sodium: HC≡CH + Na → HC≡C⁻Na⁺ + ½H₂ (sodium acetylide). Acidity: HC≡CH > H₂C=CH₂ > CH₃–CH₃. But-2-yne has no acidic H. C₂–C₄ alkynes are gases; alkynes are insoluble in water.

ex.q: Which of these react with sodium metal: ethyne, propyne, but-2-yne? Explain.
st: Acidic H is present only on a carbon of the triple bond (≡C–H).
Ethyne (HC≡CH) and propyne (CH₃C≡CH) have such H atoms → react, releasing H₂.
ex.a: Ethyne and propyne react; but-2-yne does not

topics.rl: Ripening fruit with calcium carbide is banned by FSSAI because commercial carbide carries arsenic and phosphorus impurities. The gas it releases is ethyne, not the ethene that fruit naturally uses.

topics.t: Addition and polymerisation reactions of alkynes
topics.h: Pass ethyne through a red-hot iron tube and three molecules snap together into benzene. One gas becomes the most famous aromatic ring.
p: Addition of H₂: HC≡CH + H₂ → (Pt/Pd/Ni) CH₂=CH₂, then CH₃–CH₃. Alkynes take up two molecules of an addendum because there are two π bonds.
Addition of halogens: HC≡CH + Br₂ → CHBr=CHBr, then CHBr₂–CHBr₂ (1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane). Reddish-orange bromine water is decolourised, a test for unsaturation.
Addition of HX follows Markovnikov's rule in both steps: HC≡CH + HBr → CH₂=CHBr → CH₃CHBr₂ (1,1-dibromoethane, both Br on the same carbon).
Addition of water: with 40% H₂SO₄ and 1% HgSO₄ at 333 K, ethyne gives an unstable enol that changes to ethanal: HC≡CH + H₂O → [CH₂=CHOH] → CH₃CHO. Propyne gives propanone (CH₃COCH₃).

Polymerisation: linear polymerisation of ethyne gives polyacetylene (polyethyne), an electrically conducting polymer. Cyclic polymerisation: three ethyne molecules passed through a red-hot iron tube at 873 K form benzene.

ex.q: Predict the products: (a) propyne + H₂O (Hg²⁺, H⁺, 333 K); (b) ethyne + excess HBr.
st: (a) Markovnikov addition of water gives the enol CH₃C(OH)=CH₂, which tautomerises to propanone.
(b) First HBr gives CH₂=CHBr; second HBr adds by Markovnikov's rule to the same carbon → CH₃CHBr₂.

topics.rl: Polyacetylene's discovery as a conducting plastic won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Flexible electronics research at Indian institutes builds on such conducting polymers.

topics.t: Benzene: structure, aromaticity, preparation and properties
topics.h: Michael Faraday isolated benzene in 1825 from illuminating gas. Forty years later Kekulé proposed its ring, a picture he said came to him in a dream of a snake biting its tail.
p: Benzene, C₆H₆: Kekulé (1865) proposed a hexagonal ring with alternating single and double bonds that oscillate between two forms. Benzene's real structure is a resonance hybrid of the two Kekulé structures; all six C–C bonds are equal (139 pm), between C–C (154 pm) and C=C (133 pm). Despite its 'double bonds', benzene resists addition and is unusually stable.

Orbital picture: all six carbons are sp² hybridised and lie in one plane with all H atoms. Each carbon's unhybridised p orbital overlaps sideways with both neighbours, forming a delocalised π cloud above and below the ring, containing six π electrons.

Aromaticity (Hückel's rule): a compound is aromatic if it is planar, has complete delocalisation of π electrons in the ring, and contains (4n + 2) π electrons (n = 0, 1, 2, ...). Benzene: 6 π electrons (n = 1); naphthalene: 10 (n = 2).

Nomenclature and isomerism: monosubstituted benzenes have one isomer each; disubstituted benzenes have three (ortho 1,2; meta 1,3; para 1,4). C₈H₁₀ aromatic isomers: ethylbenzene and o-, m-, p-xylene.

Preparation: cyclic polymerisation of ethyne (red-hot iron tube, 873 K); decarboxylation of sodium benzoate with soda lime; reduction of phenol vapour over heated zinc dust (C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO). Properties: non-polar, colourless liquids or solids with a characteristic smell, immiscible with water, soluble in organic solvents, burn with a sooty flame.

ex.q: Use Hückel's rule to decide whether the cyclopentadienyl anion (C₅H₅⁻, planar, fully conjugated) is aromatic.
st: Count π electrons: two C=C bonds give 4, and the carbanion lone pair in a p orbital gives 2 → 6 π electrons.
The ion is planar and fully delocalised.

topics.rl: Benzene is a raw material for nylon, dyes and detergents made in Indian chemical hubs like Vapi and Ankleshwar. It is also a carcinogen, so its level in petrol is strictly limited under BS-VI fuel standards.

topics.t: Electrophilic substitution of benzene and its mechanism
topics.h: Benzene's π cloud is an electron-rich carpet. Electrophiles land on it, but benzene always throws out a proton afterwards to keep its precious aromatic ring intact.
p: Nitration: benzene + nitrating mixture (conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄) at 323–333 K → nitrobenzene. Electrophile: nitronium ion, NO₂⁺, formed by HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻.
Halogenation: benzene + Cl₂ with anhydrous FeCl₃ (Lewis acid), in the dark → chlorobenzene. FeCl₃ generates the electrophile Cl⁺: Cl₂ + FeCl₃ → Cl⁺ + [FeCl₄]⁻.
Sulphonation: heating benzene with fuming H₂SO₄ (oleum) gives benzenesulphonic acid, C₆H₅SO₃H; the electrophile is SO₃.

Friedel–Crafts alkylation: benzene + alkyl halide with anhydrous AlCl₃ → alkylbenzene (CH₃Cl gives toluene). Friedel–Crafts acylation: benzene + acyl chloride (or acid anhydride) with anhydrous AlCl₃ → aryl ketone (CH₃COCl gives acetophenone, C₆H₅COCH₃). The electrophiles are R⁺ and RCO⁺.

Mechanism (three steps): (1) generation of the electrophile E⁺; (2) E⁺ attacks the π cloud, forming a carbocation called the arenium ion or σ-complex, in which one carbon becomes sp³ and aromaticity is temporarily lost; (3) a base ([AlCl₄]⁻, HSO₄⁻) removes H⁺ from the sp³ carbon, restoring the aromatic ring.

ex.q: Write the mechanism of nitration of benzene.
st: Step 2: NO₂⁺ attacks the ring; an arenium ion forms (one sp³ carbon carrying H and NO₂; positive charge delocalised over the ring).
Step 3: HSO₄⁻ removes H⁺ from the sp³ carbon; the aromatic ring is restored, giving C₆H₅NO₂.
ex.a: Benzene → nitrobenzene via NO₂⁺ and an arenium ion

topics.rl: Nitrobenzene from benzene is the starting point for aniline, which goes into the indigo dye that colours denim made in Ahmedabad's mills, and into many medicines. Nitrating mixture is highly corrosive and the reaction is exothermic, so it is done with cooling and protective gear.

topics.t: Addition reactions of benzene and directive influence of substituents
topics.h: Put an –OH on benzene and the next group lands at ortho or para; put an –NO₂ and it goes to meta. A substituent acts like a traffic policeman for incoming electrophiles.
p: Under drastic conditions benzene does add: with H₂ over Ni at high temperature and pressure it gives cyclohexane; with Cl₂ in UV light at about 500 K it gives benzene hexachloride (BHC, C₆H₆Cl₆, 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane). Combustion: C₆H₆ + 15/2 O₂ → 6CO₂ + 3H₂O, with a sooty flame.

Ortho- and para-directing groups (activating): –OH, –NH₂, –NHR, –NHCOCH₃, –OCH₃, –CH₃, –C₂H₅. Their +R (or +I and hyperconjugation) effect increases electron density at the ortho and para positions and makes the ring more reactive than benzene.

Meta-directing groups (deactivating): –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COR, –COOH, –COOR, –SO₃H. Their −R and −I effects withdraw electron density, mostly from ortho and para positions, so the meta positions are relatively richer, and the ring is less reactive.

Halogens are special: their strong −I effect deactivates the ring, but their +R effect (lone-pair donation) directs incoming groups to ortho and para positions. So halogens are deactivating but ortho/para directing.
Use: the order of reactions matters. To make m-nitrochlorobenzene, nitrate first (–NO₂ directs meta) then chlorinate; to make p-nitrochlorobenzene, chlorinate first then nitrate.

ex.q: Predict the major products of nitration of (a) toluene and (b) nitrobenzene.
st: (a) –CH₃ is an activating o,p-director → o-nitrotoluene and p-nitrotoluene.
(b) –NO₂ is a deactivating meta-director → m-dinitrobenzene (1,3-dinitrobenzene); the reaction needs harsher conditions.

topics.rl: BHC (gammaxene), once widely sprayed in Indian farms, is made by adding chlorine to benzene in UV light. It has been banned for agricultural use because it persists in soil and food chains.

topics.t: Carcinogenic hydrocarbons and hydrocarbon conversions
topics.h: The black soot on a tandoor chimney or in cigarette smoke contains benzopyrene, a molecule that can bind to DNA. Some hydrocarbons are not just fuels but health hazards.
p: Benzene and polynuclear hydrocarbons with more than two fused benzene rings are toxic and carcinogenic. They form by incomplete combustion of organic materials such as tobacco, coal and petroleum.

Examples include 1,2-benzanthracene, 3-methylcholanthrene, 1,2,5,6-dibenzanthracene and 3,4-benzopyrene (benzo[a]pyrene). Once inside the body they undergo biochemical reactions and damage DNA, which can lead to cancer.

Conversions use the reactions learnt so far, for example: ethyne → benzene (red-hot iron tube); benzene → nitrobenzene (HNO₃/H₂SO₄); ethene → ethanol (H₂O/H⁺); ethanol → ethene (conc. H₂SO₄, heat); propene → 1-bromopropane (HBr, peroxide); sodium ethanoate → methane (soda lime).
Chain-length changes: Wurtz reaction (2RX + 2Na) or Kolbe electrolysis doubles the chain; decarboxylation with soda lime removes one carbon; ozonolysis cuts the chain at a double bond.
Plan a conversion by asking: does the carbon count change, which functional group must appear or disappear, and in what order should the steps go (remember directing effects for benzene)?

ex.q: Convert ethanol into ethyne.
st: 1,2-Dibromoethane + alcoholic KOH → bromoethene; then NaNH₂ → ethyne.

topics.rl: India's ban on smoking in public places and the push from chulhas to LPG under Ujjwala both cut exposure to polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons from incomplete combustion.

qa.q: Which definition best describes chemistry?
qa.a: The study of composition, structure and properties of matter and the changes it undergoes
qa.e: Chemistry deals with what matter is made of, how it is arranged, how it behaves and how it changes into new substances.

qa.q: Which pair of drugs is used in cancer therapy?
qa.a: Cisplatin and taxol
qa.e: Cisplatin (a platinum compound) and taxol are effective anticancer drugs.

qa.q: AZT (azidothymidine) is a drug used for:
qa.a: Treating AIDS patients
qa.e: AZT is an antiviral drug used to help AIDS patients.

qa.q: Which statement about green chemistry is correct?
qa.a: It designs processes that reduce the use and production of hazardous substances
qa.e: Green chemistry aims to make chemical processes cleaner and safer, cutting waste and toxic by-products for sustainable development.

qa.q: Chemists developed substitutes for CFCs mainly because CFCs:
qa.a: Deplete the ozone layer in the stratosphere
qa.e: Chlorofluorocarbons released into the air break down ozone in the stratosphere, so safer refrigerants were needed.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT matter?
qa.a: Light from an LED
qa.e: Light is energy; it has no mass and does not occupy space. The others have mass and volume.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Air is matter. Reason (R): Air has mass and occupies space.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Air has mass (a filled football weighs more than a flat one) and occupies space (it inflates a balloon), which is exactly why it counts as matter.

qa.q: A pharma start-up in Pune redesigns a drug synthesis so that it uses water instead of a toxic solvent and produces less waste. This is an example of:
qa.a: Green chemistry
qa.e: Replacing hazardous solvents and reducing waste is the core idea of green chemistry.

qa.q: Which state of matter has a definite volume but no definite shape?
qa.a: Liquid
qa.e: Liquid particles are close together (fixed volume) but can slide past one another, so a liquid takes the shape of its container.

qa.q: Why does a gas fill any container completely?
qa.a: Its particles are far apart and move freely and fast
qa.e: Gas particles have weak attractions, large spaces between them and rapid random motion, so they spread through all the available space.

qa.q: Which of these is a homogeneous mixture?
qa.a: Sugar dissolved in water
qa.e: Sugar solution has the same composition everywhere; the others have visibly separate parts.

qa.q: Which property is true for a compound but NOT for a mixture?
qa.a: Its constituents are present in a fixed ratio by mass
qa.e: A compound always has its elements in a fixed mass ratio and its properties differ from theirs; mixtures have variable composition.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Water can be broken into hydrogen and oxygen only by chemical methods. Reason (R): Water is a compound.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Constituents of a compound are chemically combined, so physical methods like filtration cannot separate them; electrolysis (a chemical method) is needed.

qa.q: H₂, O₂ and N₂ are best described as:
qa.a: Elements, because each molecule contains only one kind of atom
qa.e: A molecule of an element can have more than one atom, but all of the same kind.

qa.q: What happens when ice at 0 °C is heated at constant pressure until it is steam?
qa.a: Solid → liquid → gas
qa.e: Heating supplies energy that overcomes attractions step by step: ice melts to water, then water boils to steam.

qa.q: A student mixes common salt with sand. Which sequence separates pure salt?
qa.a: Dissolve in water, filter, evaporate the filtrate
qa.e: Salt dissolves and sand does not. Filtering removes sand; evaporating the filtrate gives back salt.

qa.q: How many base quantities does the SI system have?
qa.e: Length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity: seven in all.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of amount of substance?
qa.a: mole
qa.e: Amount of substance is measured in moles (mol).

qa.q: Which is a chemical property of a substance?
qa.a: Combustibility
qa.e: Whether something burns can only be seen by burning it, which forms new substances.

qa.q: In the current SI, the kilogram is defined by fixing the exact numerical value of which constant?
qa.a: Planck constant
qa.e: Since 2019 the kilogram is defined by fixing h = 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J s exactly.

qa.q: Which constant is fixed exactly to define the kelvin?
qa.a: Boltzmann constant
qa.e: The kelvin is defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant k = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

qa.q: The SI second is based on radiation from atoms of:
qa.a: Caesium-133
qa.e: One second is a fixed number (9 192 631 770) of periods of radiation from a transition in the caesium-133 atom.

qa.q: A student records the length of a lab bench as '2.1'. What is wrong?
qa.a: The unit is missing, so the value is meaningless
qa.e: A physical quantity needs both a number and a unit; 2.1 m and 2.1 ft are very different lengths.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The mole is now defined using an exact number of entities. Reason (R): One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The 2019 SI fixes the number of entities in one mole exactly, which is what R states.

qa.q: How many litres are there in 1 m³?
qa.e: 1 m³ = (10 dm)³ = 1000 dm³, and 1 dm³ = 1 L.

qa.q: A metal block of mass 54 g has a volume of 20 cm³. What is its density in g cm⁻³?
qa.e: Density = mass/volume = 54/20 = 2.7 g cm⁻³ (this matches aluminium).

qa.q: The density of water at room temperature is about 1 g cm⁻³. What is it in kg m⁻³?
qa.e: 1 g = 10⁻³ kg and 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³, so 1 g cm⁻³ = 10⁻³/10⁻⁶ = 10³ kg m⁻³.

qa.q: Using 1 inch = 2.54 cm, a 3.0 inch pipette bulb is how many cm long?
qa.e: 3.0 in × (2.54 cm / 1 in) = 7.62 cm; the inch unit cancels.

qa.q: Which glassware is used to deliver a variable, accurately measured volume of liquid during a titration?
qa.a: Burette
qa.e: A burette has fine graduations and a stopcock, so it can deliver any volume precisely during titration.

qa.q: An astronaut takes a 10 kg toolkit from Earth to the Moon. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: Its mass stays 10 kg but its weight decreases
qa.e: Mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on location; weight depends on gravity, which is weaker on the Moon.

qa.q: How many micrometres (μm) are there in 1 mm?
qa.e: 1 mm = 10⁻³ m and 1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m, so 1 mm = 10³ μm.

qa.q: A 500 mL bottle of hand sanitiser has density 0.88 g mL⁻¹. What is the mass of the liquid in grams?
qa.e: Mass = density × volume = 0.88 g mL⁻¹ × 500 mL = 440 g.

qa.q: Normal body temperature is 37 °C. What is it in °F?
At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales show the same number?
Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K. What is this in °C?
A thermometer reads 212 °F. What is the temperature in K?
qa.e: 212 °F is the boiling point of water, 100 °C; add 273.15 to get 373.15 K.

qa.q: Which is 0.0048 written in correct scientific notation?
qa.e: The decimal moves 3 places right to give 4.8 (between 1 and 10), so the exponent is −3.

qa.q: What is (5.6 × 10⁵) × (6.9 × 10⁸) in scientific notation?
qa.e: 5.6 × 6.9 = 38.64 and 10⁵ × 10⁸ = 10¹³. Rewrite 38.64 × 10¹³ as 3.864 × 10¹⁴ so that N is between 1 and 10.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A temperature of −10 K is impossible. Reason (R): 0 K is the lowest temperature on the Kelvin scale.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, so no negative kelvin values exist.

qa.q: How many significant figures are in 0.00340?
qa.e: Leading zeros do not count; 3, 4 and the trailing zero after the decimal point do, giving 3.

qa.q: How many significant figures are in 2.005?
qa.e: Zeros between non-zero digits are significant, so all four digits count.

qa.q: Report 12.11 + 18.0 + 1.012 with the correct number of significant figures.
qa.e: In addition, keep the fewest decimal places among the numbers; 18.0 has one, so 31.122 becomes 31.1.

qa.q: Report 2.5 × 1.25 to the correct number of significant figures.
qa.e: 2.5 has 2 significant figures, so the product 3.125 is rounded to 2 figures: 3.1.

qa.q: Round 6.25 to two significant figures using the rule for a dropped digit of exactly 5.
qa.e: The dropped digit is 5 and the preceding digit 2 is even, so it is left unchanged: 6.2.

qa.q: The true mass of a sample is 3.00 g. Student P reads 2.80 g and 2.81 g; student Q reads 3.01 g and 2.99 g. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: P is precise but not accurate; Q is precise and accurate
qa.e: P's readings agree closely with each other (precise) but are far from 3.00 g (inaccurate). Q's readings agree with each other and with the true value.

qa.q: How many significant figures does the number 100 (written without a decimal point) have?
qa.e: Trailing zeros without a decimal point are not significant, so only the 1 counts. Writing 100. would give 3.

qa.q: Assertion (A): 4.01 × 10² has three significant figures. Reason (R): The power of ten in scientific notation does not affect the number of significant figures.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Only the digits in N (4, 0, 1) are counted; 10² just locates the decimal point.

qa.q: When 12 g of carbon burns completely in 32 g of oxygen, what mass of carbon dioxide forms?
qa.e: By conservation of mass, mass of products = mass of reactants = 12 + 32 = 44 g.

qa.q: Which law states that a compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed proportion by mass?
qa.a: Law of definite proportions
qa.e: Proust's law of definite (constant) proportions says composition by mass is fixed for a given compound.

qa.q: Nitrogen forms N₂O, NO and NO₂. For a fixed 28 g of nitrogen, the oxygen masses are 16 g, 32 g and 64 g. What is the ratio?
qa.e: 16 : 32 : 64 simplifies to 1 : 2 : 4, a simple whole-number ratio as the law of multiple proportions predicts.

qa.q: Two samples of copper oxide were made by different methods. Sample I: 1.60 g gives 1.28 g Cu. Sample II: 4.00 g gives 3.20 g Cu. What percentage of copper do both samples have?
qa.e: 1.28/1.60 × 100 = 80% and 3.20/4.00 × 100 = 80%, the same, which supports the law of definite proportions.

qa.q: Which pair of compounds can illustrate the law of multiple proportions?
qa.a: H₂O and H₂O₂
qa.e: The same two elements (H and O) form both compounds, with oxygen masses 16 g and 32 g per 2 g hydrogen.

qa.q: A student heats 10.0 g of CaCO₃ in an open crucible and finds only 5.6 g of solid left. Why does this NOT break the law of conservation of mass?
qa.a: 4.4 g of CO₂ gas escaped into the air
qa.e: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. The 4.4 g of CO₂ escaped; 5.6 g + 4.4 g = 10.0 g, so total mass is conserved.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The law of definite proportions holds for every compound regardless of its source. Reason (R): A compound can have any ratio of its elements.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: a compound has a fixed ratio; variable ratios belong to mixtures.

qa.q: Who stated the law of conservation of mass after careful experiments on combustion?
qa.a: Antoine Lavoisier
qa.e: Lavoisier's careful weighings of combustion reactions in the late 18th century established conservation of mass.

qa.q: In H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g), 50 mL of hydrogen reacts completely. What volume of HCl forms at the same T and P?
qa.e: Volumes follow the coefficients 1 : 1 : 2, so 50 mL H₂ gives 2 × 50 = 100 mL HCl.

qa.q: Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes applies only when:
qa.a: All gases are measured at the same temperature and pressure
qa.e: Gas volumes depend on T and P, so simple ratios appear only when all volumes are measured under the same conditions.

qa.q: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of:
qa.a: Molecules
qa.e: Avogadro proposed equal numbers of molecules (not atoms or masses) in equal volumes.

qa.q: Which postulate is part of Dalton's atomic theory?
qa.a: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction
qa.e: Dalton said reactions only reorganise atoms. The nucleus, isotopes and orbits came much later.

qa.q: Why could Dalton's atomic theory not explain the law of gaseous volumes?
qa.a: It did not distinguish between atoms and molecules
qa.e: 2 volumes H₂ + 1 volume O₂ → 2 volumes water vapour requires each O₂ molecule to split into two O atoms, an idea Dalton lacked.

qa.q: How many litres of oxygen are needed to burn 10 L of ethene completely at the same T and P? C₂H₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g)
qa.e: C₂H₄ : O₂ = 1 : 3 by volume, so 10 L × 3 = 30 L of O₂.

qa.q: Assertion (A): 2 volumes of H₂ react with 1 volume of O₂ to give 2 volumes of water vapour. Reason (R): Oxygen exists as diatomic molecules that split during the reaction.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Each O₂ molecule supplies one O atom to each of two H₂O molecules; Avogadro's idea of diatomic molecules explains the 2 : 1 : 2 ratio.

qa.q: According to Dalton, all atoms of a given element are identical in:
qa.a: Mass and other properties
qa.e: Dalton held that atoms of one element are identical in mass and all properties; isotopes later showed masses can differ.

qa.q: The atomic mass unit is defined as:
qa.a: 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom
qa.e: Since 1961 the reference standard is carbon-12, assigned exactly 12 u.

qa.q: An element has two isotopes: mass 10 u (20% abundance) and mass 11 u (80% abundance). What is its average atomic mass in u?
Chlorine is 75% ³⁵Cl (mass 35 u) and 25% ³⁷Cl (mass 37 u). Using these rounded values, what is its average atomic mass in u?
What is the molecular mass of CO₂ in u (C = 12.011 u, O = 16.00 u)?
What is the molecular mass of methane, CH₄, in u (C = 12.011 u, H = 1.008 u)?
Why do we speak of the formula mass, not the molecular mass, of sodium chloride?
qa.a: NaCl exists as a 3-D lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, not as discrete molecules
qa.e: In solid NaCl each ion is surrounded by oppositely charged ions; no separate NaCl molecule exists, so we use the formula unit.

qa.q: Find the formula mass of Ca(OH)₂ in u (Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1).
Assertion (A): The atomic mass of natural carbon is 12.011 u, not exactly 12 u. Reason (R): Natural carbon contains small amounts of ¹³C (and traces of ¹⁴C) along with ¹²C.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The average is pulled slightly above 12 by about 1.1% of heavier ¹³C.

qa.q: How many moles of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆, M = 180 g mol⁻¹) are present in 45 g?
How many water molecules are in 9 g of water (H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)? Give the answer in units of 10²³ (use N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹).
qa.e: 9 g is 0.5 mol, and 0.5 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³ molecules.

qa.q: How many oxygen atoms are in 0.5 mol of O₂? Give the answer in units of 10²³.
qa.e: 0.5 mol O₂ contains 0.5 × 2 = 1 mol O atoms = 6.022 × 10²³ atoms.

qa.q: What volume in litres does 0.25 mol of nitrogen occupy at STP, taking molar volume as 22.4 L mol⁻¹?
What is the mass in grams of 2.5 mol of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃ = 100 g mol⁻¹)?
A cylinder holds 45.4 L of methane at 273.15 K and 1 bar. Taking molar volume as 22.7 L mol⁻¹, how many moles of methane does it hold?
Which contains the largest number of atoms? (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23)
qa.a: 1 g of H₂
qa.e: 1 g H₂ = 0.5 mol molecules = 1 mol atoms. 1 g O₂ = 1/16 mol atoms; 1 g Na = 1/23 mol; 1 g CO₂ = 3/44 mol atoms. Hydrogen wins by far.

qa.q: Assertion (A): One mole of H₂O and one mole of CO₂ contain the same number of molecules. Reason (R): Both have the same molar mass.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A mole always contains 6.022 × 10²³ entities, so A is true. R is false: H₂O is 18 g mol⁻¹ and CO₂ is 44 g mol⁻¹.

qa.q: What is the mass percent of oxygen in water (H = 1, O = 16)? Give the answer to two decimal places.
What is the mass percent of carbon in ethanol, C₂H₅OH (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)? Give the answer to two decimal places.
Which statement about empirical and molecular formulas is correct?
qa.a: The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula
qa.e: Molecular formula = n × empirical formula with n = 1, 2, 3...; for water n = 1, so both are H₂O.

qa.q: A hydrocarbon has empirical formula CH₂ and molar mass 56 g mol⁻¹. What is n in (CH₂)ₙ?
qa.e: Empirical formula mass = 14; n = 56/14 = 4, so the molecular formula is C₄H₈.

qa.q: A compound has 2.0 mol C and 5.0 mol H for every 1.0 mol O in a sample. What is its empirical formula?
qa.a: C₂H₅O
qa.e: The ratio 2 : 5 : 1 is already the simplest whole-number ratio, so the empirical formula is C₂H₅O.

qa.q: Moles from a 100 g sample give the ratio C : H = 1 : 1.5. What is the empirical formula?
qa.a: C₂H₃
qa.e: 1 : 1.5 is not whole; multiply by 2 to get 2 : 3, so C₂H₃.

qa.q: A sample of 'pure' NaCl (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5) is found to contain 36.0% sodium by mass. The theoretical value is 39.3%. What does this suggest?
qa.a: The sample is impure
qa.e: Pure NaCl always has 23/58.5 × 100 ≈ 39.3% Na. A lower value means other substances are present.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Benzene (C₆H₆) and ethyne (C₂H₂) have the same empirical formula. Reason (R): Both have C and H in a 1 : 1 atom ratio.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: C₆H₆ and C₂H₂ both reduce to CH because their C : H ratio is 1 : 1.

qa.q: What mass of CO₂ in grams is produced when 32 g of methane burns completely? CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
qa.e: 32 g CH₄ = 2 mol; 1 mol CH₄ gives 1 mol CO₂, so 2 mol CO₂ = 2 × 44 = 88 g.

qa.q: How many grams of water form when 16 g of methane burns completely? CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
qa.e: 1 mol CH₄ gives 2 mol H₂O = 2 × 18 = 36 g.

qa.q: What is the coefficient of O₂ when C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O is balanced with the smallest whole numbers?
qa.e: C₂H₆ + 3.5O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O; doubling to clear the fraction gives 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O.

qa.q: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, a student takes 4 mol H₂ and 3 mol O₂. Which is the limiting reagent?
qa.a: H₂
qa.e: 4 mol H₂ needs only 2 mol O₂; 3 mol O₂ is available, so O₂ is in excess and H₂ runs out first.

qa.q: In the same reaction (4 mol H₂ and 3 mol O₂), how many moles of oxygen are left over?
qa.e: Only 2 mol O₂ reacts with 4 mol H₂, leaving 3 − 2 = 1 mol O₂.

qa.q: 10 g of hydrogen reacts with 64 g of oxygen. What is the maximum mass of water formed in grams? 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (H = 1, O = 16)
qa.e: H₂ = 5 mol, O₂ = 2 mol. 2 mol O₂ needs 4 mol H₂, so O₂ is limiting and gives 4 mol H₂O = 72 g.

qa.q: Which information does a balanced chemical equation NOT give directly?
qa.a: The rate at which the reaction proceeds
qa.e: A balanced equation shows the quantitative relationship of substances but says nothing about speed.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The amount of product formed depends on the limiting reagent. Reason (R): The limiting reagent is the reactant present in the largest mass.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: the limiting reagent is the one that is consumed first, judged by moles and the mole ratio, not by mass.

qa.q: 2 g of a substance is dissolved in 18 g of water. What is the mass percent of the solute?
qa.e: Mass of solution = 2 + 18 = 20 g; mass % = 2/20 × 100 = 10%.

qa.q: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.5 mol of glucose in enough water to make 2.5 L of solution?
A solution contains 1 mol of ethanol and 4 mol of water. What is the mole fraction of ethanol?
How many mL of 5 M H₂SO₄ are needed to prepare 500 mL of 0.5 M H₂SO₄?
qa.e: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ → 5 × V₁ = 0.5 × 500 → V₁ = 50 mL. Safety: always add acid slowly to water, never water to acid, with goggles on.

qa.q: What mass of NaOH in grams is needed to make 500 mL of 0.2 M solution (NaOH = 40 g mol⁻¹)?
In a two-component solution, the mole fraction of the solute is 0.12. What is the mole fraction of the solvent?
qa.e: Mole fractions add up to 1, so x(solvent) = 1 − 0.12 = 0.88.

qa.q: Why is the molarity of a solution defined per litre of solution rather than per litre of solvent?
qa.a: Because the volume we actually measure in a volumetric flask is that of the final solution
qa.e: Adding a solute changes total volume; molarity counts moles in the final measured volume of solution.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mole fraction has no unit. Reason (R): It is a ratio of moles to moles.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Units cancel in a ratio of moles to total moles, so mole fraction is a pure number.

qa.q: What is the molality of a solution containing 0.5 mol of urea in 250 g of water?
qa.e: m = 0.5 mol ÷ 0.250 kg = 2 mol kg⁻¹.

qa.q: 18 g of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in 500 g of water. What is the molality?
Why is molality preferred over molarity for experiments done over a range of temperatures?
qa.a: Molality depends on masses, which do not change with temperature
qa.e: Volume changes with temperature, so molarity drifts; molality uses mass of solvent, which stays fixed.

qa.q: How many grams of KOH (M = 56 g mol⁻¹) are needed to make 200 mL of 0.5 M KOH solution?
A 1.0 M solution of NaCl (M = 58.5 g mol⁻¹) has density 1.0585 g mL⁻¹. What is its molality?
qa.e: 1 L has mass 1058.5 g, of which 58.5 g is NaCl, leaving 1000 g water. m = 1.0/1.000 = 1.0 mol kg⁻¹.

qa.q: A solution contains 3 mol of a solute dissolved in 486 g of water (H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹). What is the mole fraction of the solute?
qa.e: Moles of water = 486/18 = 27 mol; x(solute) = 3/(3 + 27) = 0.1.

qa.q: A 3.0 M solution of a solute (M = 60 g mol⁻¹) has density 1.18 g mL⁻¹. What is its molality?
qa.e: 1 L has mass 1180 g; solute = 3 × 60 = 180 g; water = 1000 g; m = 3.0/1.000 = 3.0 mol kg⁻¹.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Molarity of a solution decreases slightly when it is warmed. Reason (R): The volume of a solution increases on heating while the moles of solute stay the same.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: M = n/V; with n constant and V rising, M falls. That is exactly why molality is temperature-independent and molarity is not.

qa.q: What is the charge on an electron as found by Millikan (to four significant figures)?
qa.e: The electron carries a negative charge of magnitude 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ is its mass in kg, and 1.759 × 10¹¹ is e/m in C kg⁻¹.

qa.q: What did J. J. Thomson measure using electric and magnetic fields on cathode rays?
qa.a: The charge-to-mass ratio of the electron
qa.e: Thomson balanced electric and magnetic deflections to get e/mₑ = 1.758820 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹.

qa.q: Using e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, what is e/mₑ in units of 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹ (to two decimal places)?
Why did scientists conclude that electrons are present in the atoms of all elements?
qa.a: Cathode rays had the same properties whatever the gas or electrode material used
qa.e: Because the particles were identical from every gas and every metal, they had to be a universal constituent of matter.

qa.q: Approximately how many times heavier is a proton than an electron? Give the ratio to two decimal places (mₚ = 1.67262 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, mₑ = 9.10939 × 10⁻³¹ kg).
In Millikan's experiment, charges on oil drops were always whole-number multiples of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What does this show?
qa.a: Electric charge is quantised; it comes in units of the electronic charge
qa.e: The charge on any drop was n × e, so charge exists in discrete packets of e.

qa.q: Which particle has the smallest mass?
qa.a: Electron
qa.e: The electron (9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg) is about 1/1836 the mass of a proton; the neutron is slightly heavier than the proton.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Cathode rays are deflected towards the positive plate in an electric field. Reason (R): Cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Negative particles are attracted to the positive plate, which is exactly why the beam bends that way.

qa.q: Who discovered the neutron and how?
qa.a: Chadwick, by bombarding beryllium with α-particles
qa.e: In 1932 Chadwick found that α-particles striking beryllium released neutral particles with mass slightly greater than a proton.

qa.q: Which property of canal rays differs from cathode rays?
qa.a: Their charge-to-mass ratio depends on the gas in the tube
qa.e: Canal rays are positive ions of the gas, so their e/m changes with the gas used; cathode rays are the same electrons from every gas.

qa.q: In Rutherford's experiment, what fraction of α-particles bounced back by nearly 180°?
qa.a: About 1 in 20,000
qa.e: Only a very tiny fraction rebounded, which showed the nucleus is extremely small.

qa.q: Thomson's model of the atom is also called:
qa.a: Plum pudding or watermelon model
qa.e: Thomson pictured electrons embedded in a uniform positive sphere, like seeds in a watermelon.

qa.q: The radius of a nucleus is about 10⁻¹⁵ m and that of an atom about 10⁻¹⁰ m. How many times larger is the atom's radius?
Why was a very thin gold foil used in Rutherford's experiment?
qa.a: So α-particles would pass through only a few layers of atoms and scattering could be traced to single atoms
qa.e: Gold can be beaten into extremely thin sheets (about 100 nm), so each α-particle meets very few atoms and the results reveal atomic structure.

qa.q: Which observation could Thomson's model NOT explain?
qa.a: A few α-particles bouncing back from gold foil
qa.e: A thinly spread positive charge could never repel a fast α-particle straight back; only a concentrated nucleus could.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Most α-particles passed undeflected through gold foil. Reason (R): Most of the space in an atom is empty.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since the nucleus occupies a tiny volume, most α-particles meet nothing that can deflect them.

qa.q: How many neutrons are in ⁸⁰₃₅Br?
qa.e: Neutrons = A − Z = 80 − 35 = 45.

qa.q: A species has 18 electrons, 16 protons and 16 neutrons. What is it?
qa.a: ³²₁₆S²⁻
qa.e: 16 protons means sulphur; mass number 16 + 16 = 32; two extra electrons give charge 2−.

qa.q: Which pair are isobars?
qa.a: ¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N
qa.e: Isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers; ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N both have A = 14.

qa.q: Why do isotopes of an element show nearly identical chemical properties?
qa.a: They have the same number of electrons and protons
qa.e: Chemical behaviour depends on electrons, which are fixed by Z. Isotopes differ only in neutrons.

qa.q: How many neutrons does deuterium have?
qa.e: Deuterium ²₁H has one proton and one neutron (A = 2).

qa.q: What is the main reason Rutherford's model fails to explain the stability of atoms?
qa.a: A revolving electron should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus
qa.e: Classical electromagnetic theory says an accelerating charge emits radiation; the electron would lose energy and collapse into the nucleus, but real atoms are stable.

qa.q: How many electrons, protons and neutrons are in ²⁴₁₂Mg²⁺?
qa.e: Z = 12 protons; neutrons = 24 − 12 = 12; a 2+ ion has 12 − 2 = 10 electrons.

qa.q: Assertion (A): ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl have different chemical properties. Reason (R): They have different numbers of neutrons.
qa.a: A is false but R is true
qa.e: Both isotopes have 17 electrons, so their chemistry is essentially the same; A is false. R is true: 18 and 20 neutrons.

qa.q: What is the frequency of light of wavelength 500 nm? Give the answer in units of 10¹⁴ Hz (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹).
What is the wavenumber of radiation of wavelength 500 nm, in units of 10⁶ m⁻¹?
What is the energy of one photon of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz? Give it in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
Which region of the electromagnetic spectrum has the highest frequency?
qa.a: Gamma rays
qa.e: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and therefore the highest frequency and photon energy.

qa.q: A source emits 6.626 J of energy as photons of frequency 1.0 × 10¹⁵ Hz. How many photons is that, in units of 10¹⁹?
qa.e: Energy per photon = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 10¹⁵ = 6.626 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; number = 6.626 ÷ 6.626 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.0 × 10¹⁹.

qa.q: Which statement about Planck's quantum theory is correct?
qa.a: Energy is emitted or absorbed only in discrete packets proportional to frequency
qa.e: Planck proposed E = hν: energy comes in quanta whose size depends on frequency, and E is inversely proportional to wavelength.

qa.q: Photons of red light (700 nm) and violet light (400 nm) are compared. Which is correct?
qa.a: A violet photon carries more energy than a red photon
qa.e: E = hc/λ, so the shorter wavelength of violet light means higher energy per photon.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Electromagnetic waves can travel through vacuum. Reason (R): They consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that need no material medium.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Unlike sound, EM waves are self-sustaining field oscillations, which is why sunlight crosses the vacuum of space.

qa.q: A metal has threshold frequency 7.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. What is its work function in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)?
Photons of energy 5.0 eV fall on a metal whose work function is 2.0 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons, in eV?
A photoelectron (mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) has kinetic energy 4.55 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is its speed in units of 10⁶ m s⁻¹?
In the photoelectric effect, what happens when the intensity of light (above threshold frequency) is increased?
qa.a: More electrons are ejected, with the same maximum kinetic energy
qa.e: Intensity controls the number of photons, hence the number of electrons; the energy of each photon (and so KE) depends only on frequency.

qa.q: Which observation could the wave theory of light NOT explain?
qa.a: Existence of a threshold frequency in the photoelectric effect
qa.e: Wave theory predicts that intense enough light of any frequency should eject electrons; the sharp threshold needs photons of energy hν.

qa.q: Light of frequency 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz strikes a metal with threshold frequency 1.0 × 10¹⁵ Hz. What is the kinetic energy of the electrons in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)?
Which metals are commonly used in photoelectric cells because they emit electrons even with visible light?
qa.a: Caesium and potassium
qa.e: Alkali metals like caesium, rubidium and potassium have low work functions, so even visible light can eject electrons.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Electrons are ejected instantly when light of suitable frequency hits a metal. Reason (R): A single photon transfers all its energy to a single electron in one collision.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since one photon delivers its whole energy at once, there is no need to build up energy over time, so there is no lag.

qa.q: Which series of the hydrogen spectrum lies in the visible region?
qa.a: Balmer
qa.e: The Balmer series (transitions ending at n = 2) falls in the visible region.

qa.q: What is the wavenumber in cm⁻¹ of the line for n₂ = ∞ → n₁ = 1 in hydrogen (the series limit of Lyman)?
What is the wavenumber in cm⁻¹ of the line when an electron falls from n = 4 to n = 2 in hydrogen?
How does an absorption spectrum differ from an emission spectrum of the same element?
qa.a: It shows dark lines at the same wavelengths where the emission spectrum shows bright lines
qa.e: The same energy gaps are involved; in absorption, atoms take those exact wavelengths out of white light, leaving dark lines.

qa.q: Why are line spectra sometimes called the 'fingerprints' of atoms?
qa.a: Each element has its own unique set of lines
qa.e: Each element's electronic energy levels are unique, so its lines identify it, just as fingerprints identify people.

qa.q: In the Paschen series of hydrogen, the electron returns to which level?
qa.e: Paschen lines end at n₁ = 3 and lie in the infrared region.

qa.q: Which observation is the strongest evidence that electrons in atoms have quantised energies?
qa.a: Atoms emit light only at certain fixed wavelengths
qa.e: Discrete lines mean only certain energy differences are allowed, i.e. energy levels are quantised.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Lyman series lies in the ultraviolet region. Reason (R): Lyman transitions end at n = 1, giving the largest energy gaps in hydrogen.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Falling to the lowest level releases the most energy, so the photons have the shortest wavelengths, in the UV.

qa.q: What is the radius of the third Bohr orbit of a hydrogen atom, in pm?
What is the energy of the electron in the second orbit of hydrogen, in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J?
What does the negative sign in the Bohr energy expression signify?
qa.a: The electron is bound and has lower energy than a free electron at rest at infinity
qa.e: A free electron at infinite distance is assigned zero energy; a bound electron has less energy, so its energy is negative.

qa.q: What is the energy of the electron in the first orbit of Li²⁺ (Z = 3), in units of 10⁻¹⁸ J?
Which of these is Bohr's condition for quantised angular momentum?
qa.a: mₑvr = nh/2π
qa.e: Bohr allowed only orbits for which angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of h/2π.

qa.q: What is the radius of the second orbit of He⁺ (Z = 2), in pm?
Which orbit in a hydrogen atom has the lowest (most negative) energy?
qa.e: Eₙ ∝ −1/n², so n = 1 is the most negative and most stable, the ground state.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In Bohr's model, an electron in a stationary orbit does not emit radiation. Reason (R): Energy is emitted only when the electron jumps from a higher to a lower orbit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Bohr's postulates say energy is fixed within an orbit and changes only during a transition, given by ΔE = hν.

qa.q: How much energy (in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J) is emitted when the electron in hydrogen falls from n = 5 to n = 2?
What is the ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state in kJ mol⁻¹ (2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per atom, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)?
What is the wavelength in nm of light emitted when the electron in hydrogen falls from n = 2 to n = 1? (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
How much energy (in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J) must be absorbed to excite a hydrogen electron from n = 1 to n = 3?
qa.e: ΔE = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ (1 − 1/9) = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 8/9 = 1.938 × 10⁻¹⁸ J = 19.38 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Positive, because energy is absorbed.

qa.q: Which phenomenon could Bohr's model NOT explain?
qa.a: Splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field
qa.e: The Zeeman effect needs quantum numbers beyond Bohr's single n. Bohr's model handles hydrogen and hydrogen-like ions well.

qa.q: The sign of ΔE for an electron moving from n = 2 to n = 4 in hydrogen is:
qa.a: Positive, because energy is absorbed
qa.e: Moving to a higher level means going to a less negative energy, so ΔE = Ef − Ei > 0: absorption.

qa.q: Why does Bohr's model fail for the spectrum of a neutral helium atom?
qa.a: It cannot handle atoms with more than one electron
qa.e: Bohr's model treats one electron orbiting a nucleus; electron–electron repulsion in multi-electron atoms is outside it.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Bohr's model explains the spectrum of Li²⁺. Reason (R): Li²⁺ is a hydrogen-like ion with only one electron.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Bohr's theory works for any one-electron species once Z² is included, so it applies to H, He⁺, Li²⁺ and Be³⁺.

qa.q: What is the de Broglie wavelength of a 0.1 kg ball moving at 10 m s⁻¹? Give it in units of 10⁻³⁴ m (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
An electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moves at 1.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. What is its de Broglie wavelength in nm (to two decimal places)?
A particle has a de Broglie wavelength of 0.1 nm. What is its momentum in units of 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹?
Why are wave properties not noticed for a moving car or cricket ball?
qa.a: Their large mass makes the de Broglie wavelength extremely small
qa.e: λ = h/mv; with h so tiny and m large, λ is around 10⁻³⁴ m or less, far beyond detection.

qa.q: Which instrument depends directly on the wave nature of electrons?
qa.a: Electron microscope
qa.e: Electron microscopes use the very short wavelengths of fast electrons to resolve tiny details.

qa.q: Using h/4π = 5.27 × 10⁻³⁵ J s, what is the minimum uncertainty in momentum of an electron located within Δx = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m? Give it in units of 10⁻²⁵ kg m s⁻¹.
If the speed of an electron is made three times larger, its de Broglie wavelength becomes:
qa.a: One-third
qa.e: λ ∝ 1/v, so tripling v makes λ one-third.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The position and momentum of an electron cannot both be known exactly at the same time. Reason (R): Light used to locate an electron changes its momentum by striking it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: To see an electron we need light of wavelength smaller than its size; such energetic photons disturb its momentum, so both cannot be fixed together. This is the textbook explanation of the uncertainty principle.

qa.q: An electron is located within 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m. What is the minimum uncertainty in its velocity in units of 10⁶ m s⁻¹? (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, π = 3.1416)
Why is the concept of a definite orbit for an electron not acceptable?
qa.a: It would require exact position and velocity at the same time, which the uncertainty principle forbids
qa.e: An orbit is a precise path, which means knowing position and momentum together, impossible for an electron.

qa.q: In Schrödinger's equation Ĥψ = Eψ, what does E represent?
qa.a: The total energy of the system
qa.e: E is the total energy (kinetic + potential) of the electron; Ĥ is the Hamiltonian operator.

qa.q: What does solving the Schrödinger equation for the hydrogen atom give?
qa.a: The allowed energy levels and the corresponding wave functions (orbitals)
qa.e: The solutions are quantised energies and wave functions ψ, each characterised by quantum numbers.

qa.q: Which is a reason for the failure of Bohr's model?
qa.a: It ignores the wave nature of the electron
qa.e: Bohr treated the electron purely as a particle in a fixed orbit, ignoring its dual behaviour and the uncertainty principle.

qa.q: For a 40 g golf ball, the uncertainty in position from the uncertainty principle is about 10⁻³³ m. What does this tell us?
qa.a: The uncertainty principle has no practical effect on large objects
qa.e: Such an uncertainty is immeasurably small compared with the ball's size, so classical mechanics works for big objects.

qa.q: An atomic orbital is best described as:
qa.a: A wave function ψ for an electron in an atom
qa.e: In quantum mechanics an orbital is a one-electron wave function; it replaces the idea of a fixed orbit.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The uncertainty principle is significant for electrons but not for cricket balls. Reason (R): The uncertainty in velocity Δv ≥ h/(4πmΔx) is inversely proportional to mass.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A tiny mass gives a large Δv; a large mass makes Δv negligible.

qa.q: For n = 4, what are the possible values of l?
qa.e: l runs from 0 to n − 1, so for n = 4 it is 0, 1, 2, 3 (s, p, d, f).

qa.q: How many orbitals are there in the shell with n = 5?
qa.e: Number of orbitals in a shell = n² = 25.

qa.q: What are the possible mₗ values for a 3d orbital?
qa.e: For d, l = 2, so mₗ = −2, −1, 0, +1, +2: five orientations.

qa.q: What physical meaning does ψ² have?
qa.a: Probability density of finding the electron at a point
qa.e: ψ itself has no physical meaning; ψ² gives the probability per unit volume of finding the electron there.

qa.q: What is the maximum number of electrons that can share the quantum numbers n = 3 and l = 1?
qa.e: n = 3, l = 1 is the 3p subshell: 3 orbitals × 2 electrons = 6.

qa.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an orbital from an orbit?
qa.a: An orbital is a 3-D region of probability holding at most 2 electrons; an orbit is a definite circular path
qa.e: Bohr's orbit is a precise planar path that violates the uncertainty principle; an orbital is a probability region described by ψ.

qa.q: Who proposed the electron spin quantum number?
qa.a: Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit
qa.e: In 1925 George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit proposed that the electron spins, giving mₛ = ±½.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The 2d subshell does not exist. Reason (R): For n = 2, l can only be 0 or 1.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A d subshell needs l = 2, which requires n ≥ 3.

qa.q: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) is NOT possible?
qa.e: For n = 2, l can only be 0 or 1, so l = 2 is impossible.

qa.q: Which set of quantum numbers could describe an electron in a 4f orbital?
qa.e: 4f means n = 4 and l = 3; mₗ = −2 lies within −3 to +3.

qa.q: How many radial nodes does a 3p orbital have?
qa.e: Radial nodes = n − l − 1 = 3 − 1 − 1 = 1.

qa.q: How many angular nodes (nodal planes) does a d orbital have?
qa.e: Angular nodes = l, and l = 2 for d orbitals.

qa.q: Which d orbital has its lobes lying along the x and y axes?
qa.a: dx²−y²
qa.e: dx²−y² points along the axes; dxy, dyz and dxz have lobes between the axes.

qa.q: What is the shape of an s orbital?
qa.a: Spherical
qa.e: s orbitals are spherically symmetric; the probability depends only on distance from the nucleus.

qa.q: What does a boundary surface diagram of an orbital represent?
qa.a: A surface enclosing a region where the probability of finding the electron is high, about 90%
qa.e: It encloses most of the electron density; it is a picture of where the electron is likely to be, not a path.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A 2s orbital has one radial node. Reason (R): Radial nodes = n − l − 1.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: For 2s, n − l − 1 = 2 − 0 − 1 = 1, so there is one spherical node.

qa.q: Which orbital is filled first according to the (n + l) rule?
qa.a: 4s
qa.e: 4s has n + l = 4, lower than 3d (5), 4p (5) and 4d (6).

qa.q: Between 3d and 4p (both n + l = 5), which has lower energy and why?
qa.a: 3d, because it has the lower n
qa.e: When n + l is equal, the orbital with lower n has lower energy.

qa.q: In a hydrogen atom, how do the energies of 3s, 3p and 3d compare?
qa.a: All equal
qa.e: With only one electron there is no shielding, so energy depends only on n; all n = 3 orbitals are degenerate.

qa.q: Why is 2s lower in energy than 2p in a lithium atom?
qa.a: 2s penetrates closer to the nucleus, so it feels a larger effective nuclear charge
qa.e: s electrons penetrate the inner shielding more than p electrons, so they are held more tightly and are lower in energy.

qa.q: What is the maximum number of electrons with n = 3 and mₛ = +½ in an atom?
qa.e: n = 3 has n² = 9 orbitals; each orbital can hold one electron with mₛ = +½, so 9.

qa.q: Which statement is the Pauli exclusion principle?
qa.a: No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers
qa.e: This limits each orbital to 2 electrons of opposite spin. The other options describe Aufbau, Hund's rule and Heisenberg.

qa.q: What is the effective nuclear charge?
qa.a: The net positive charge actually felt by an electron after shielding by other electrons
qa.e: Inner electrons shield outer ones from the full nuclear charge, so Z_eff < Z for outer electrons.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In potassium, the 19th electron enters 4s rather than 3d. Reason (R): The (n + l) value of 4s is lower than that of 3d.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: 4s has n + l = 4 and 3d has 5, so 4s is lower in energy and fills first: K is [Ar]4s¹.

qa.q: What is the electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24)?
qa.a: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹
qa.e: One 4s electron moves to 3d to give a half-filled 3d⁵ subshell, which is extra stable.

qa.q: How many unpaired electrons are in an Fe³⁺ ion (Z of Fe = 26)?
qa.e: Fe = [Ar]3d⁶4s². Fe³⁺ loses two 4s and one 3d electron: [Ar]3d⁵ with 5 unpaired electrons.

qa.q: Which electronic configuration obeys Hund's rule for the 2p electrons of nitrogen?
qa.a: Three 2p orbitals each with one electron, all spins parallel
qa.e: Hund's rule: electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing.

qa.q: What is the configuration of Cu⁺ (Z of Cu = 29)?
qa.a: [Ar] 3d¹⁰
qa.e: Cu = [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹; removing the single 4s electron leaves [Ar]3d¹⁰.

qa.q: Why are half-filled and completely filled subshells extra stable?
qa.a: Symmetrical electron distribution and larger exchange energy
qa.e: Symmetry lowers repulsion effects, and more parallel-spin electrons can exchange positions, giving more exchange energy and stability.

qa.q: How many electrons are in the valence shell of sulphur (Z = 16)?
qa.e: S = [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴; the valence shell (n = 3) holds 2 + 4 = 6 electrons.

qa.q: How many electrons in a ground-state chlorine atom (Z = 17) have l = 1?
qa.e: l = 1 means p electrons: 2p⁶ + 3p⁵ = 11.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Copper has the configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Reason (R): A completely filled d subshell is extra stable.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: One 4s electron shifts to 3d to complete it, gaining extra stability from symmetry and exchange energy.

qa.q: Li (7), Na (23) and K (39) form a Döbereiner triad. What is the mean of the atomic weights of Li and K?
qa.e: (7 + 39)/2 = 23, equal to the atomic weight of sodium.

qa.q: Newlands' law of octaves worked well only up to which element?
qa.a: Calcium
qa.e: Beyond calcium the 'every eighth element' pattern broke down, so the law was not widely accepted.

qa.q: Which scientist plotted atomic volumes against atomic weights and found a periodic pattern?
qa.a: Lothar Meyer
qa.e: Lothar Meyer (1869) showed that physical properties such as atomic volume vary periodically with atomic weight.

qa.q: What was the main limitation of Döbereiner's triads?
qa.a: Only a few such triads could be found among known elements
qa.e: The triad rule fitted only a handful of element groups, so it could not organise all elements.

qa.q: The telluric helix, which arranged elements by atomic weight on a cylinder, was proposed by:
qa.a: Chancourtois
qa.e: French geologist de Chancourtois proposed the cylindrical arrangement in 1862.

qa.q: Why did chemists in the 19th century need to classify elements?
qa.a: The growing number of elements made it hard to study each one separately
qa.e: A classification groups similar elements so that properties can be studied as trends and families.

qa.q: Cl (35.5), Br (80) and I (127) form a triad. How close is Br's atomic weight to the mean of Cl and I?
qa.a: The mean is 81.25, close to 80
qa.e: (35.5 + 127)/2 = 81.25, which is close to 80, so the triad roughly holds.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Newlands compared his arrangement with musical notes. Reason (R): He found that every eighth element resembled the first, like the eighth note of an octave.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The repeat after seven steps reminded Newlands of a musical octave, which gave the law its name.

qa.q: Mendeleev's periodic law states that properties of elements are a periodic function of their:
qa.a: Atomic weights
qa.e: In 1869 Mendeleev based his law on atomic weights; atomic numbers came with Moseley in 1913.

qa.q: Which element did Mendeleev call eka-silicon?
qa.a: Germanium
qa.e: Eka-silicon, the element below silicon, was later discovered as germanium.

qa.q: Mendeleev predicted the formula of the oxide of eka-aluminium as:
qa.a: E₂O₃
qa.e: Like aluminium (Al₂O₃), eka-aluminium was expected to form E₂O₃; gallium forms Ga₂O₃.

qa.q: What is an 'inverted pair' in Mendeleev's table?
qa.a: Two elements placed opposite to their atomic-weight order to keep similar elements together
qa.e: Pairs such as tellurium (128) and iodine (127) were inverted so each sat with its chemical family.

qa.q: Which was a genuine strength of Mendeleev's table?
qa.a: It predicted properties of undiscovered elements
qa.e: His predictions for gallium and germanium were confirmed, showing the power of periodicity.

qa.q: Why could isotopes not be placed properly in Mendeleev's table?
qa.a: They have different atomic weights but identical chemical properties
qa.e: A table ordered by atomic weight should separate isotopes, yet chemically they belong together.

qa.q: Mendeleev predicted the atomic weight of eka-silicon as 72. The measured atomic weight of germanium is 72.6. What is the difference?
qa.e: 72.6 − 72 = 0.6, a remarkably small error for a prediction made before discovery.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table. Reason (R): He believed some elements were yet to be discovered.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: He kept similar elements together, which left blank spaces where undiscovered elements had to fit.

qa.q: What did Moseley's X-ray experiments establish?
qa.a: Atomic number is a more fundamental property than atomic mass
qa.e: √ν of characteristic X-rays plotted against Z gives a straight line, showing that Z governs properties.

qa.q: State the modern periodic law.
qa.a: Physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers
