qa.e: The modern law replaces atomic weight with atomic number.

qa.q: How many groups are there in the long form of the periodic table?
qa.e: IUPAC recommends numbering the groups 1 to 18.

qa.q: How many periods are there in the modern periodic table?
qa.e: There are seven periods, corresponding to n = 1 to 7.

qa.q: Which pair was 'inverted' by atomic weight but is in correct order by atomic number?
qa.a: Co (Z = 27) and Ni (Z = 28)
qa.e: Co (58.9) is heavier than Ni (58.7) but has the smaller Z, so it correctly comes first in the modern table.

qa.q: The lanthanoid series consists of elements with atomic numbers:
qa.e: Lanthanoids are cerium (58) to lutetium (71); 90 to 103 are actinoids.

qa.q: Why are lanthanoids and actinoids placed separately below the main table?
qa.a: To keep the table compact while preserving the similarity of elements in each group
qa.e: Fitting 14 extra elements into periods 6 and 7 would make the table very wide; placing them below keeps it practical.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In the modern periodic table, argon comes before potassium. Reason (R): Argon has a lower atomic number than potassium.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Ar has Z = 18 and K has Z = 19; ordering by Z puts argon first even though it is heavier.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC temporary name of the element with Z = 107?
qa.a: Unnilseptium
qa.e: 1 = un, 0 = nil, 7 = sept, then -ium: unnilseptium (Uns).

qa.q: What is the temporary symbol of the element with Z = 115?
qa.a: Uup
qa.e: 1, 1, 5 → un, un, pent → ununpentium, symbol Uup.

qa.q: The temporary name 'unbinilium' corresponds to which atomic number?
Which root stands for the digit 4 in IUPAC element names?
qa.a: quad
qa.e: IUPAC uses 'quad' (q) for 4, not the Greek 'tetra'.

qa.q: What is the official IUPAC name of element 118?
qa.a: Oganesson
qa.e: Element 118, temporarily ununoctium (Uuo), is now oganesson (Og).

qa.q: What is the IUPAC temporary name for Z = 109?
qa.a: Unnilennium
qa.e: 1 = un, 0 = nil, 9 = enn → unnilennium (Une).

qa.q: Why does IUPAC give temporary names to new elements?
qa.a: To have a neutral name until the discovery is confirmed and a permanent name is approved
qa.e: Systematic names avoid disputes over credit while claims of discovery are verified.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The temporary symbol for Z = 112 is Uub. Reason (R): Symbols are formed from the first letters of the numerical roots.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: un (u), un (u), bi (b) → Uub; the name is ununbium.

qa.q: An element has configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. In which group is it?
qa.e: p-block; group = 10 + (2 + 4) = 16. The element is sulphur.

qa.q: In which period and block is the element with Z = 37?
qa.a: Period 5, s-block
qa.e: Z = 37 is [Kr] 5s¹ (rubidium): highest n = 5, last electron in s.

qa.q: Why does period 4 contain 18 elements?
qa.a: It fills 4s, 3d and 4p orbitals, which hold 2 + 10 + 6 electrons
qa.e: The orbitals filled in period 4 are 4s, 3d and 4p, which together take 18 electrons.

qa.q: What is the group number of an element with configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹?
qa.e: d-block; group = (n−1)d + ns electrons = 10 + 1 = 11. The element is copper.

qa.q: Why do Li, Na and K show similar chemical properties?
qa.a: They all have one electron in their valence s orbital (ns¹)
qa.e: Chemical behaviour depends on valence electrons; all three have ns¹.

qa.q: How many elements are there in the third period?
qa.e: Period 3 fills 3s and 3p only (3d fills in period 4), giving 2 + 6 = 8 elements.

qa.q: Element X has Z = 35. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: It is in period 4, group 17, p-block
qa.e: Z = 35 is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁵ (bromine): period 4, p-block, group 10 + 7 = 17.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Sodium is placed in period 3. Reason (R): Its valence electron is in the shell with n = 3.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Na is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹; the period equals the n of the valence shell.

qa.q: Which property is characteristic of most d-block elements?
qa.a: They form coloured ions and show variable oxidation states
qa.e: Partly filled d orbitals give transition metals coloured ions, variable valence, paramagnetism and catalytic activity.

qa.q: Which group of elements are called chalcogens?
qa.a: Group 16
qa.e: Group 16 (O, S, Se, Te, Po) are the chalcogens; group 17 are halogens.

qa.q: Which of these is a metalloid?
qa.a: Germanium
qa.e: Germanium lies on the metal/non-metal border and shows intermediate properties, which is why it is a semiconductor.

qa.q: What does the term 'transuranium elements' mean?
qa.a: Elements with atomic number greater than 92
qa.e: Elements after uranium (Z = 92) are transuranium; they are mostly synthetic and radioactive.

qa.q: Why do s-block elements rarely occur free in nature?
qa.a: They are highly reactive and readily lose their valence electrons
qa.e: Low ionisation enthalpies make alkali and alkaline earth metals very reactive, so they occur as compounds.

qa.q: Which element is a d-block element but does NOT show typical transition-metal properties?
qa.a: Zinc
qa.e: Zn has a completely filled 3d¹⁰ subshell in its atom and its common ion, so it lacks colour and variable valence.

qa.q: The elements from Z = 90 to Z = 103 are known as:
qa.a: Actinoids
qa.e: Thorium (90) to lawrencium (103) are the actinoids, filling 5f orbitals.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Noble gases are chemically very unreactive. Reason (R): Their valence shells are completely filled (ns² np⁶; He 1s²).
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Closed shells give very high ionisation enthalpies and little tendency to gain electrons, so reactivity is very low.

qa.q: The Cl–Cl bond length in Cl₂ is 198 pm. What is the covalent radius of chlorine in pm?
qa.e: Covalent radius = half the internuclear distance = 198/2 = 99 pm.

qa.q: The distance between neighbouring copper nuclei in copper metal is 256 pm. What is the metallic radius of copper in pm?
qa.e: Metallic radius = 256/2 = 128 pm.

qa.q: Which has the largest radius?
qa.a: K
qa.e: Radius increases down a group (K below Na below Li) and decreases across a period (Mg smaller than Na).

qa.q: Which correctly orders the radii of the isoelectronic ions?
qa.a: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺
qa.e: Same 10 electrons; nuclear charge rises O (8) < F (9) < Na (11) < Mg (12), so size falls in that order.

qa.q: Why is the F⁻ ion (136 pm) much larger than the F atom (64 pm)?
qa.a: The added electron increases repulsion and lowers the effective nuclear charge per electron
qa.e: Ten electrons are held by the same nine protons, so the electron cloud expands.

qa.q: Why does atomic radius decrease from Na to Cl across period 3?
qa.a: Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell
qa.e: Effective nuclear charge rises and shielding by electrons in the same shell is poor, so the electron cloud is pulled inwards.

qa.q: Which pair consists of isoelectronic species?
qa.a: Na⁺ and Ne
qa.e: Na⁺ has 11 − 1 = 10 electrons, the same as Ne.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mg²⁺ is smaller than Na⁺. Reason (R): Mg²⁺ has a higher nuclear charge acting on the same number of electrons.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both have 10 electrons; 12 protons in Mg²⁺ pull them closer than 11 protons in Na⁺.

qa.q: Why do properties such as atomic radius and ionisation enthalpy repeat at regular intervals of atomic number?
qa.a: Valence-shell electronic configurations repeat at regular intervals
qa.e: Elements with the same valence-shell configuration (such as ns¹ or ns² np⁵) recur after 2, 8, 8, 18, 18 and 32 elements, so their properties recur too.

qa.q: Which equation represents the first ionisation enthalpy of sodium?
qa.a: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻
qa.e: Ionisation enthalpy is defined for an isolated gaseous atom losing one electron.

qa.q: Why is the first ionisation enthalpy of nitrogen higher than that of oxygen?
qa.a: N has a stable half-filled 2p³ configuration; O's paired 2p electrons repel each other
qa.e: Removing an electron from O relieves pairing repulsion and leaves a half-filled 2p³; N's half-filled set is extra stable.

qa.q: Why is ΔᵢH₁ of boron lower than that of beryllium?
qa.a: The 2p electron of B is less penetrating and more shielded than the 2s electron of Be
qa.e: B loses a 2p electron, which is shielded by the 2s electrons; Be loses a 2s electron that penetrates closer to the nucleus.

qa.q: An element has ΔᵢH₁ = 520, ΔᵢH₂ = 7297 and ΔᵢH₃ = 11 810 kJ mol⁻¹. In which group is it most likely?
qa.a: Group 1
qa.e: The huge jump after the first electron shows that only one electron lies outside a noble-gas core: an alkali metal (this is lithium).

qa.q: Which element has the lowest first ionisation enthalpy?
qa.a: Cs
qa.e: Ionisation enthalpy decreases down group 1; Cs is the largest atom with the most shielding.

qa.q: Why is ΔᵢH₂ of sodium much larger than its ΔᵢH₁?
qa.a: The second electron must come from the stable noble-gas core of Na⁺ ([Ne])
qa.e: After losing 3s¹, Na⁺ has the neon configuration; removing an electron from the closed 2p⁶ shell needs far more energy.

qa.q: Which period 2 element has the highest first ionisation enthalpy?
qa.a: Neon
qa.e: Noble gases have completely filled shells and the highest ionisation enthalpies in their periods.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ionisation enthalpy decreases down a group. Reason (R): Atomic size and shielding by inner electrons increase down a group.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and better shielded, so less energy is needed to remove it.

qa.q: Which halogen has the most negative electron gain enthalpy?
qa.a: Chlorine
qa.e: Cl (−349 kJ mol⁻¹) beats F (−328) because the extra electron in fluorine's small 2p subshell is strongly repelled.

qa.q: Why do noble gases have positive electron gain enthalpies?
qa.a: The added electron must enter the next, higher shell, which is unfavourable
qa.e: With ns² np⁶ complete, a new electron must go into the (n + 1)s orbital, far from the nucleus, so energy must be supplied.

qa.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?
qa.a: Fluorine
qa.e: Fluorine has the value 4.0; caesium is among the least electronegative.

qa.q: Electronegativity refers to the ability of an atom to:
qa.a: Attract shared electrons towards itself in a compound
qa.e: Electronegativity concerns bonded atoms in a compound; electron gain enthalpy concerns isolated gaseous atoms.

qa.q: Why is the electron gain enthalpy of oxygen less negative than that of sulphur?
qa.a: Oxygen's small size causes strong repulsion between the incoming electron and existing 2p electrons
qa.e: In the compact n = 2 shell, electron–electron repulsion is large; in sulphur's bigger n = 3 shell, the added electron is accommodated more easily.

qa.q: How do electronegativity and metallic character relate across a period?
qa.a: Electronegativity increases and metallic character decreases
qa.e: Moving right, atoms attract electrons more strongly and become less metallic, more non-metallic.

qa.q: Arrange in order of decreasing (most negative first) electron gain enthalpy: O, S, F, Cl.
qa.a: Cl > F > S > O
qa.e: Values: Cl −349, F −328, S −200, O −141 kJ mol⁻¹.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Fluorine has a less negative electron gain enthalpy than chlorine. Reason (R): Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but the reason for A is the strong electron–electron repulsion in fluorine's small 2p subshell, not its electronegativity.

qa.q: What is the oxidation state of oxygen in OF₂?
qa.e: Fluorine is more electronegative and is always −1, so 2(−1) + x = 0 gives x = +2 for oxygen.

qa.q: Which oxide is amphoteric?
qa.a: Al₂O₃
qa.e: Aluminium oxide reacts with acids (forming Al³⁺ salts) and with bases (forming aluminates).

qa.q: Why is the maximum covalency of boron 4 while that of aluminium can be 6?
qa.a: Boron has no d orbitals in its valence shell; aluminium can use 3d orbitals
qa.e: Second-period elements have only 2s and 2p orbitals (four orbitals), limiting covalency to 4.

qa.q: Which pair shows a diagonal relationship?
qa.a: Be and Al
qa.e: Be (group 2, period 2) and Al (group 13, period 3) lie diagonally and have similar properties.

qa.q: Which element forms the most strongly basic oxide in period 3?
qa.a: Sodium
qa.e: Basic character of oxides decreases across the period; Na₂O is the most basic.

qa.q: Arrange in increasing first ionisation enthalpy: Na, Mg, Al, Si.
qa.a: Na < Al < Mg < Si
qa.e: Values (kJ mol⁻¹): Na 496, Al 577, Mg 738, Si 786. Al is lower than Mg because its 3p electron is easier to remove.

qa.q: Arrange in decreasing atomic radius: N, P, O, F.
qa.a: P > N > O > F
qa.e: P is in period 3 (larger); across period 2 radius falls N > O > F.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Second-period elements form strong multiple bonds such as N≡N and C=O. Reason (R): Their small size allows effective sideways (pπ–pπ) overlap of p orbitals.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Small atoms come close enough for their p orbitals to overlap sideways strongly, giving stable π bonds.

qa.q: According to Kössel, a bond between sodium and chlorine forms by:
qa.a: Transfer of an electron from Na to Cl, giving Na⁺ and Cl⁻
qa.e: Electropositive Na loses an electron to become Na⁺ ([Ne]); Cl gains it to become Cl⁻ ([Ar]). Their attraction is the ionic bond.

qa.q: How many electrons are shared between the two nitrogen atoms in N₂?
qa.e: N≡N is a triple bond: three shared pairs = 6 electrons.

qa.q: What is the electrovalence of calcium in CaO?
qa.e: Ca loses two electrons to form Ca²⁺, so its electrovalence is 2.

qa.q: Who coined the term 'covalent bond'?
qa.a: Langmuir
qa.e: Langmuir (1919) refined the Lewis model and introduced the term covalent bond.

qa.q: In the Lewis representation of Cl₂, how many lone pairs does each chlorine atom carry?
qa.e: Each Cl has 7 valence electrons; one is used in the bond pair, leaving 6 electrons = 3 lone pairs.

qa.q: Which statement about the octet rule is correct?
qa.a: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to have eight electrons in their valence shell
qa.e: The rule concerns the valence shell only; hydrogen aims for a duplet, and the rule covers both ionic and covalent bonding.

qa.q: Which molecule contains a double bond?
qa.a: C₂H₄
qa.e: Ethene, H₂C=CH₂, has a C=C double bond. Ethane has single bonds and ethyne a triple bond.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Noble gases rarely form compounds. Reason (R): They already have a stable octet (duplet for He) in their valence shell.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The stability of a complete valence shell is the idea behind the octet rule, and it explains the low reactivity of noble gases.

qa.q: What is the formal charge on the central oxygen atom in O₃?
qa.e: Central O: 6 valence − 2 non-bonding − ½(6 bonding) = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1.

qa.q: How many valence electrons must be shown in the Lewis structure of the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻?
How many electrons surround the central atom in BCl₃?
qa.e: B forms three single bonds (3 pairs) and has no lone pair: 6 electrons, an incomplete octet.

qa.q: Which molecule has an expanded octet around its central atom?
qa.a: SF₆
qa.e: S in SF₆ has six bond pairs = 12 electrons, possible because sulphur can use its 3d orbitals.

qa.q: Which is an odd-electron molecule?
qa.a: NO₂
qa.e: NO₂ has 5 + 12 = 17 valence electrons; an odd total means one atom cannot have an octet.

qa.q: In the best Lewis structure of NH₄⁺, what is the formal charge on nitrogen?
qa.e: N: 5 − 0 lone pair electrons − ½(8) = 5 − 4 = +1. The four H atoms each have FC 0, so the total is +1.

qa.q: Which is NOT a drawback of the octet theory?
qa.a: It explains why atoms such as Na and Cl form ions
qa.e: Explaining ion formation is a success of the octet idea. The other three are genuine drawbacks.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Among possible Lewis structures, the one with the lowest formal charges is usually the most stable. Reason (R): The sum of formal charges in a neutral molecule must be zero.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both statements are true, but R is a bookkeeping rule. A is true because structures with less charge separation have lower energy, not because charges add to zero.

qa.q: Which factor favours the formation of an ionic bond?
qa.a: Low ionisation enthalpy of the metal
qa.e: A metal that loses electrons easily (low ΔᵢH), a non-metal that gains them readily (negative Δ_egH) and a high lattice enthalpy all favour ionic bonding.

qa.q: For sodium, ΔᵢH = 495.8 kJ mol⁻¹, and for chlorine, Δ_egH = −348.7 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the net enthalpy change for Na(g) + Cl(g) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g), in kJ mol⁻¹?
qa.e: 495.8 + (−348.7) = +147.1 kJ mol⁻¹: energy must be supplied, so lattice enthalpy is needed to explain stability.

qa.q: What is lattice enthalpy?
qa.a: Energy required to separate one mole of an ionic solid completely into gaseous ions
qa.e: It measures how strongly ions are held in the crystal; NaCl's value is 788 kJ mol⁻¹.

qa.q: Which compound shows the greatest covalent character?
qa.a: LiI
qa.e: Li⁺ is the smallest cation and I⁻ the largest, most polarisable anion, so LiI is the most covalent.

qa.q: Why is AlCl₃ more covalent than NaCl?
qa.a: Al³⁺ is smaller and more highly charged, so it polarises Cl⁻ more
qa.e: A small cation with high charge has high polarising power, distorting the anion's electron cloud and increasing covalent character.

qa.q: Cu⁺ and Na⁺ have similar sizes and the same charge. Why is CuCl more covalent than NaCl?
qa.a: Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) has poorly shielding d electrons, making it more polarising than Na⁺ (2s² 2p⁶)
qa.e: d electrons shield the nuclear charge less effectively than s and p electrons, so Cu⁺ distorts the anion more.

qa.q: The lattice enthalpy of NaCl is 788 kJ mol⁻¹. Which statement follows?
qa.a: 788 kJ is needed to break one mole of solid NaCl into Na⁺(g) and Cl⁻(g)
qa.e: Lattice enthalpy refers to separating the solid into gaseous ions, not to melting or dissolving.

qa.q: Assertion (A): LiCl is more soluble in organic solvents than NaCl. Reason (R): The small Li⁺ ion polarises Cl⁻ strongly, giving LiCl more covalent character.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: More covalent character makes LiCl behave more like a covalent compound, so it dissolves better in less polar solvents such as ethanol.

qa.q: In H₂O, the first O–H bond needs 502 kJ mol⁻¹ and the second 427 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the average O–H bond enthalpy in kJ mol⁻¹?
How does bond length change as bond order increases between the same two atoms?
qa.a: It decreases
qa.e: More shared electron pairs pull the nuclei closer, so bond length falls.

qa.q: Which species has the same bond order as N₂?
qa.a: CO
qa.e: CO is isoelectronic with N₂ (14 electrons) and also has bond order 3.

qa.q: The van der Waals radius of chlorine (180 pm) is larger than its covalent radius (99 pm) because:
qa.a: It measures half the distance between non-bonded atoms in neighbouring molecules
qa.e: Non-bonded atoms cannot approach as closely as bonded atoms that share electrons.

qa.q: What is the bond angle H–O–H in a water molecule?
qa.e: Two lone pairs on oxygen squeeze the bond pairs closer than the tetrahedral 109.5°, giving 104.5°.

qa.q: Which bond has the highest bond enthalpy?
qa.a: N≡N
qa.e: The triple bond in N₂ (946 kJ mol⁻¹) is far stronger than O=O (498) or H–H (435.8).

qa.q: What is the bond order between carbon and oxygen in CO₂?
qa.e: O=C=O has two double bonds; each C–O link has bond order 2.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Bond enthalpy of N₂ is greater than that of O₂. Reason (R): N₂ has a higher bond order than O₂.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Bond order 3 (N₂) versus 2 (O₂); higher bond order means a stronger bond.

qa.q: What is the bond order of each C–O bond in the carbonate ion?
qa.e: Four bonds (one double + two single) spread over three C–O links: 4/3 ≈ 1.33.

qa.q: What is the bond order of each O–O bond in ozone?
qa.e: One double and one single bond shared over two O–O links: 3/2 = 1.5.

qa.q: What is resonance energy?
qa.a: The difference in energy between the most stable canonical form and the actual resonance hybrid
qa.e: The real hybrid is lower in energy than even the most stable canonical form; the difference measures the extra stability.

qa.q: Which statement about canonical structures is correct?
qa.a: They have no real existence; the molecule is the hybrid
qa.e: Canonical forms are only a way of describing delocalised electrons; atoms do not move between them.

qa.q: The C–O bond length in CO₂ (115 pm) lies between the C=O (121 pm) and C≡O (110 pm) lengths. This is explained by:
qa.a: Resonance among O=C=O, ⁻O–C≡O⁺ and ⁺O≡C–O⁻
qa.e: Contributions from triple-bonded forms shorten the bond below a pure double bond.

qa.q: In ozone, the single O–O bond length is 148 pm and the double O=O is 121 pm. The actual O–O bond length (128 pm) is:
qa.a: Between the two, showing partial double-bond character
qa.e: The hybrid has bonds intermediate between single and double, confirming resonance.

qa.q: How many canonical structures are usually drawn for the carbonate ion?
qa.e: The C=O double bond can be placed on any of the three oxygen atoms.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Benzene's six C–C bonds are all of equal length. Reason (R): Benzene is a resonance hybrid of two Kekulé structures.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Delocalisation makes every C–C bond intermediate (139 pm) between C–C and C=C.

qa.q: Which molecule has zero dipole moment?
qa.a: BF₃
qa.e: BF₃ is trigonal planar; three equal B–F bond dipoles at 120° cancel.

qa.q: Why does NH₃ have a larger dipole moment than NF₃?
qa.a: In NH₃ the lone pair moment adds to the bond moments; in NF₃ it opposes them
qa.e: In NH₃ the N–H bond dipoles point towards N, the same direction as the lone pair. In NF₃ the N–F dipoles point away from N, opposing the lone pair.

qa.q: A molecule AB₂ has a dipole moment of 1.85 D. What can you conclude about its shape?
qa.a: It is bent, not linear
qa.e: A linear AB₂ would cancel its bond dipoles; a non-zero μ shows the molecule is bent (as in H₂O).

qa.q: Two charges of magnitude 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C are separated by 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. What is the dipole moment in units of 10⁻²⁹ C m?
Which bond is the most polar?
qa.a: H–F
qa.e: The electronegativity difference between H and F is the largest, so the bond is most polar.

qa.q: CCl₄ contains four polar C–Cl bonds. Why is it a non-polar molecule?
qa.a: Its tetrahedral symmetry makes the four bond dipoles cancel
qa.e: Four equal dipoles arranged tetrahedrally add to zero.

qa.q: Which molecule has a non-zero dipole moment?
qa.a: CHCl₃
qa.e: In CHCl₃ one C–H bond replaces a C–Cl bond, breaking the symmetry so the dipoles no longer cancel.

qa.q: Assertion (A): BeF₂ has zero dipole moment. Reason (R): Be–F bonds are non-polar.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true because BeF₂ is linear and the two equal bond dipoles cancel. R is false: Be–F bonds are strongly polar.

qa.q: What is the shape of SF₄?
qa.a: See-saw
qa.e: S: 6 + 4 = 10 electrons = 5 pairs (4 bond, 1 lone) → AB₄E → see-saw.

qa.q: How many lone pairs are on the central atom of XeF₄?
qa.e: Xe: 8 + 4 = 12 electrons = 6 pairs; 4 are bond pairs, so 2 lone pairs (square planar).

qa.q: Why is the bond angle in NH₃ (107°) smaller than in CH₄ (109.5°)?
qa.a: The lone pair on N repels the bond pairs more strongly than bond pairs repel each other
qa.e: lp–bp repulsion > bp–bp repulsion, so the N–H bonds are pushed closer.

qa.q: Which correctly orders electron-pair repulsions?
qa.a: lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp
qa.e: Lone pairs are attached to only one nucleus and occupy more space, so they repel most.

qa.q: What is the shape of the SO₂ molecule?
qa.a: Bent
qa.e: S has 3 electron domains (2 bond regions + 1 lone pair) → AB₂E → bent.

qa.q: In ClF₃, where are the two lone pairs placed in the trigonal bipyramidal arrangement?
qa.a: Both in equatorial positions
qa.e: Equatorial positions have fewer 90° neighbours, minimising lone-pair repulsion; this makes the molecule T-shaped.

qa.q: Which pair of species have the same shape?
qa.a: CH₄ and NH₄⁺
qa.e: Both have four bond pairs and no lone pair on the central atom: tetrahedral.

qa.q: Assertion (A): XeF₄ is square planar. Reason (R): Its two lone pairs occupy opposite (trans) positions of an octahedron.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Six pairs give an octahedral arrangement; placing the two lone pairs opposite each other minimises lp–lp repulsion and leaves the four F atoms in a square plane.

qa.q: What is the H–H bond length, at which the potential energy of the two-atom system is minimum?
qa.a: 74 pm
qa.e: At 74 pm attraction and repulsion balance and the energy is lowest.

qa.q: According to valence bond theory, a covalent bond forms when:
qa.a: Half-filled orbitals of two atoms overlap and their electrons pair with opposite spins
qa.e: Overlap of half-filled orbitals lets the two electrons occupy the shared region with paired spins.

qa.q: Which type of overlap does NOT result in bond formation?
qa.a: Negative overlap (orbitals of opposite phase)
qa.e: Opposite phases cancel electron density between nuclei, so no bond forms.

qa.q: Why could simple valence bond theory not explain the shape of CH₄?
qa.a: Pure p orbitals are at 90°, but CH₄ has four identical bonds at 109.5°
qa.e: Using one 2s and three 2p orbitals directly would give unequal bonds and 90° angles; hybridisation solves this.

qa.q: A π bond is formed by:
qa.a: Sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals
qa.e: π bonds have electron density above and below the internuclear axis from lateral p–p overlap.

qa.q: Why does potential energy decrease as two hydrogen atoms first approach each other?
qa.a: New attractive forces between each nucleus and both electrons exceed the new repulsive forces
qa.e: At moderate distances, nucleus–electron attractions dominate over nucleus–nucleus and electron–electron repulsions.

qa.q: What type of overlap forms the bond in HF?
qa.a: s–p head-on, giving a σ bond
qa.e: H uses 1s and F uses a half-filled 2p orbital along the bond axis.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Energy is released when an H–H bond forms. Reason (R): The system reaches a minimum of potential energy at the bond length.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Going from separated atoms (zero) to the minimum (−435.8 kJ mol⁻¹) releases that energy.

qa.q: How many σ bonds are there in ethene, C₂H₄?
qa.e: Four C–H σ bonds + one C–C σ bond (the C=C also has one π) = 5σ.

qa.q: How many σ and π bonds are in ethyne, C₂H₂?
qa.a: 3σ and 2π
qa.e: Two C–H σ bonds + C≡C (1σ + 2π) = 3σ, 2π.

qa.q: How many σ bonds are in benzene, C₆H₆?
qa.e: Six C–C σ bonds in the ring and six C–H σ bonds = 12σ (plus 3π).

qa.q: Why is a σ bond stronger than a π bond?
qa.a: Head-on overlap is greater than sideways overlap
qa.e: The extent of orbital overlap decides bond strength; axial overlap is larger.

qa.q: Which is a condition for hybridisation?
qa.a: The orbitals mixing must have almost equal energy
qa.e: Hybridisation involves valence orbitals of nearly equal energy on the same atom.

qa.q: How many σ and π bonds are in CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂ (buta-1,3-diene)?
qa.a: 9σ and 2π
qa.e: Six C–H σ + three C–C σ = 9σ; two C=C each add one π = 2π.

qa.q: When one s and two p orbitals hybridise, how many hybrid orbitals form?
qa.e: The number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed: 1 + 2 = 3 sp² orbitals.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rotation about a C=C double bond is restricted. Reason (R): Rotation would break the sideways overlap of the π bond.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The π bond needs parallel p orbitals; twisting destroys the overlap, so rotation does not occur freely.

qa.q: What is the hybridisation of oxygen in H₂O?
qa.a: sp³
qa.e: O has 2 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs = 4 electron domains → sp³; the shape is bent with angle 104.5°.

qa.q: What is the percentage s character in an sp² hybrid orbital (to two decimal places)?
qa.e: One s out of three mixed orbitals: 1/3 × 100 = 33.3%.

qa.q: Why are the axial P–Cl bonds in PCl₅ slightly longer than the equatorial ones?
qa.a: Axial bond pairs experience more repulsion from the equatorial bond pairs
qa.e: Each axial bond pair is at 90° to three equatorial pairs, so it is repelled more and is pushed slightly farther out.

qa.q: What are the hybridisation and geometry of SF₆?
qa.a: sp³d², octahedral
qa.e: Six S–F bond pairs and no lone pair need six hybrid orbitals: sp³d², octahedral.

qa.q: The carbon atoms in ethyne are sp hybridised. What is the H–C–C bond angle?
qa.e: Two sp orbitals point in opposite directions, so ethyne is linear.

qa.q: Which molecule has an sp²-hybridised central atom?
qa.a: BF₃
qa.e: B in BF₃ has three bond pairs and no lone pair → sp², trigonal planar.

qa.q: In ethene, which orbitals form the C=C π bond?
qa.a: Unhybridised 2p orbitals on each carbon
qa.e: Each carbon keeps one unhybridised 2p orbital perpendicular to the molecular plane; these overlap sideways to form the π bond.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The C≡C bond (120 pm) is shorter than the C=C bond (134 pm). Reason (R): sp orbitals have more s character than sp² orbitals and hold electrons closer to the nucleus.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Higher s character makes hybrid orbitals smaller and more compact, so bonds formed by sp carbon are shorter (together with the higher bond order).

qa.q: How many molecular orbitals form when four atomic orbitals combine?
qa.e: The number of MOs always equals the number of atomic orbitals combined.

qa.q: Which statement about an antibonding molecular orbital is correct?
qa.a: It has a node between the nuclei and higher energy than the parent atomic orbitals
qa.e: Subtracting wave functions cancels density between nuclei, creating a node and raising the energy.

qa.q: Which pair of atomic orbitals CANNOT combine if z is the molecular axis?
qa.a: 2pz and 2px
qa.e: 2pz and 2px have different symmetry about the z-axis, so their net overlap is zero.

qa.q: A bonding molecular orbital is formed by:
qa.a: Addition of atomic wave functions, ψ_A + ψ_B
qa.e: Constructive interference increases electron density between the nuclei.

qa.q: Which is a salient feature of molecular orbital theory?
qa.a: A molecular orbital is influenced by two or more nuclei
qa.e: MOs are polycentric; electrons in them belong to the molecule as a whole.

qa.q: Why can the 1s orbital of one atom not combine effectively with the 2s orbital of an identical neighbouring atom?
qa.a: Their energies are too different
qa.e: Only atomic orbitals of comparable energy combine to an appreciable extent.

qa.q: Which molecular orbital is formed from sideways combination of 2px orbitals?
qa.a: π2px
qa.e: With z as the bond axis, 2px orbitals overlap sideways to give π2px (bonding) and π*2px (antibonding).

qa.q: Assertion (A): Electrons in bonding MOs stabilise a molecule. Reason (R): Bonding MOs have higher energy than the atomic orbitals from which they form.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: bonding MOs are lower in energy than the parent atomic orbitals, which is why they stabilise the molecule.

qa.q: What is the bond order of F₂ (18 electrons) from MO theory?
qa.e: F₂: N_b = 10, N_a = 8 (σ*1s², σ*2s², π*2p⁴); bond order = ½(10 − 8) = 1.

qa.q: Why does Be₂ not exist?
qa.a: Its bond order is zero
qa.e: Be₂ (8 electrons): σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s²; N_b = N_a = 4, so bond order = 0.

qa.q: In which of these is σ2pz LOWER in energy than π2px and π2py?
qa.a: O₂
qa.e: For O₂ and F₂ there is little s–p mixing, so σ2pz lies below the π2p orbitals; for B₂, C₂ and N₂ the order is reversed.

qa.q: A species has bond order 2.5. Compared with a related species of bond order 2, its bond is:
qa.a: Shorter and stronger
qa.e: Higher bond order gives higher bond enthalpy and shorter bond length.

qa.q: B₂ has the configuration σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² π2px¹ π2py¹. What is its magnetic nature?
qa.a: Paramagnetic
qa.e: By Hund's rule the two π electrons are unpaired, so B₂ is paramagnetic (bond order 1).

qa.q: What is the bond order of H₂⁺ (one electron in σ1s)?
qa.e: N_b = 1, N_a = 0 → ½(1 − 0) = 0.5; H₂⁺ exists but is weaker than H₂.

qa.q: A molecule has all its MO electrons paired. It will be:
qa.a: Diamagnetic
qa.e: Diamagnetism arises when there are no unpaired electrons.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The bond in C₂ consists of two π bonds and no σ bond (in simple MO terms). Reason (R): In C₂ the four electrons beyond σ*2s fill the two π2p orbitals, which lie below σ2pz.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: C₂: σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s² σ*2s² (π2px² = π2py²). Bond order 2 comes from two π pairs; σ2pz is empty.

qa.q: How many unpaired electrons does an O₂ molecule have according to MO theory?
qa.e: The last two electrons occupy π*2px and π*2py singly (Hund's rule).

qa.q: What is the bond order of O₂⁺?
qa.e: O₂⁺ has 15 electrons: removing one π* electron from O₂ gives N_b = 10, N_a = 5 → 2.5.

qa.q: Which oxygen species has the longest O–O bond?
qa.a: O₂²⁻
qa.e: Peroxide has the lowest bond order (1), so its bond is the longest.

qa.q: Which correctly orders stability?
qa.a: O₂⁺ > O₂ > O₂⁻ > O₂²⁻
qa.e: Bond orders 2.5 > 2 > 1.5 > 1; higher bond order means greater stability.

qa.q: Which species is diamagnetic?
qa.a: O₂²⁻
qa.e: In peroxide both π* orbitals are completely filled, so all electrons are paired.

qa.q: What is the bond order of Li₂?
qa.e: Li₂ (6 electrons): σ1s² σ*1s² σ2s²; N_b = 4, N_a = 2; ½(4 − 2) = 1.

qa.q: Which species has the higher bond dissociation enthalpy, N₂ or N₂⁺?
qa.a: N₂, because its bond order (3) exceeds that of N₂⁺ (2.5)
qa.e: Removing an electron from N₂ takes it from the bonding σ2pz orbital, lowering bond order to 2.5.

qa.q: Assertion (A): O₂ is paramagnetic. Reason (R): The Lewis structure of O₂ shows all electrons paired.
qa.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but R does not explain A; the paramagnetism comes from two unpaired π* electrons predicted by MO theory, which the Lewis structure misses.

qa.q: Hydrogen bonding is significant only when hydrogen is bonded to:
qa.a: F, O or N
qa.e: Only these small, highly electronegative atoms make H strongly δ⁺ and also carry lone pairs to accept H-bonds.

qa.q: Why does water have a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulphide?
qa.a: Water molecules form extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonds
qa.e: Extra energy is needed to break hydrogen bonds before water can boil; H₂S does not H-bond significantly.

qa.q: Which compound shows intramolecular hydrogen bonding?
qa.a: o-Nitrophenol
qa.e: The –OH and –NO₂ groups are adjacent in o-nitrophenol, so they H-bond within the molecule.

qa.q: Why is o-nitrophenol more volatile than p-nitrophenol?
qa.a: Intramolecular H-bonding in o-nitrophenol reduces association between molecules
qa.e: In the ortho isomer the H-bond is used up inside the molecule; para molecules associate through intermolecular H-bonds and boil higher.

qa.q: Why does ice float on water?
qa.a: Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open cage-like structure that is less dense than liquid water
qa.e: The open H-bonded lattice of ice takes up more volume than the same mass of liquid water.

qa.q: Which is the correct representation of hydrogen bonding in HF?
qa.a: H–F···H–F···H–F
qa.e: The δ⁺ H of one molecule is attracted to the F of the next; covalent bonds are solid lines and H-bonds dotted.

qa.q: The hydrogen bond is best described as:
qa.a: A weak, mainly electrostatic attraction between a δ⁺ hydrogen and a lone pair on F, O or N
qa.e: It is far weaker than covalent bonds but stronger than ordinary van der Waals attractions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ethanol is miscible with water but ethane is not. Reason (R): Ethanol can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The –OH of ethanol H-bonds with water; non-polar ethane cannot.

qa.q: Which is an example of an isolated system?
qa.a: Hot coffee in a sealed, perfectly insulated thermos flask
qa.e: An isolated system exchanges neither energy nor matter; the ideal sealed thermos approximates this.

qa.q: A closed system can exchange with its surroundings:
qa.a: Energy but not matter
qa.e: The walls of a closed system stop matter but allow heat and work to pass.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a state function?
qa.a: Work
qa.e: Work depends on the path taken; U, H and V depend only on the state.

qa.q: Which set of variables is commonly used to describe the state of a gas?
qa.a: p, V, T and n
qa.e: Macroscopic properties p, V, T and n define the state; q and w are path quantities.

qa.q: A gas goes from state A to state B by two different routes. Which quantity has the same value for both routes?
qa.a: ΔU
qa.e: ΔU is the change in a state function, so it depends only on A and B. q and w individually depend on the path, though q + w is the same.

qa.q: The system together with its surroundings is called:
qa.a: The universe
qa.e: System + surroundings = universe (in thermodynamic language).

qa.q: Why is a living animal an open system?
qa.a: It exchanges both matter (food, air, wastes) and energy (heat) with its surroundings
qa.e: Eating, breathing and giving off heat involve both matter and energy transfer.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The change in altitude when trekking from a base camp to a summit is like a state function. Reason (R): It depends only on the starting and ending points, not on the route.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Height gained depends only on the two points, just as ΔU or ΔH depends only on initial and final states; the distance walked, like work, depends on the route.

qa.q: A gas absorbs 650 J of heat and does 280 J of work. What is ΔU in J?
In an adiabatic process, 120 J of work is done on a system. What is ΔU in J?
qa.e: Adiabatic: q = 0, so ΔU = w = +120 J (work done on the system is positive).

qa.q: Which mathematical statement is the first law of thermodynamics?
qa.a: ΔU = q + w
qa.e: The first law relates change in internal energy to heat and work exchanged.

qa.q: A system releases 250 J of heat and 100 J of work is done on it. What is ΔU in J?
Why is internal energy called a state function?
qa.a: Its change depends only on initial and final states
qa.e: Joule showed that the same adiabatic work produces the same change of state, so ΔU is path-independent.

qa.q: In which situation is ΔU = q?
qa.a: When no work is done (e.g. heating at constant volume with no other work)
qa.e: With w = 0, the first law reduces to ΔU = q.

qa.q: Which statement follows from the first law?
qa.a: Energy of an isolated system remains constant
qa.e: The first law is the law of conservation of energy.

qa.q: Assertion (A): When a gas is compressed in an insulated cylinder, its temperature rises. Reason (R): Work done on the gas increases its internal energy because q = 0.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Adiabatic: ΔU = w > 0, and higher internal energy of an ideal gas shows up as higher temperature, as when a bicycle pump warms up.

qa.q: A gas expands from 2 L to 10 L against a constant external pressure of 1 atm. What is w in L atm?
Taking 1 L atm = 101.3 J, express −8 L atm in joules.
1 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K expands reversibly and isothermally to 10 times its volume. What is w in J (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
Why does a reversible expansion give the maximum work?
qa.a: The external pressure is always only infinitesimally less than the gas pressure
qa.e: The gas pushes against the largest possible opposing pressure at every stage, so it does the most work.

qa.q: 2 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K are compressed reversibly and isothermally from 10 L to 1 L. What is w in J (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
qa.e: w = −2.303 × 2 × 8.314 × 300 × log(1/10) = +11488.29 J. Compression means work is done on the gas, so w is positive.

qa.q: What is the work done when a gas expands freely into a vacuum?
qa.a: Zero
qa.e: There is no opposing external pressure, so w = −p_ex ΔV = 0.

qa.q: In which case is the work done BY the gas greater for the same expansion from V₁ to V₂ at constant T?
qa.a: Reversible expansion
qa.e: Reversible expansion gives the maximum magnitude of work; irreversible steps against lower pressure give less, and free expansion gives none.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Work is not a state function. Reason (R): The work done in expanding a gas from V₁ to V₂ depends on how the expansion is carried out.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Free, irreversible and reversible routes between the same states give different work, so work depends on path.

qa.q: For the isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, which is always true?
qa.a: ΔU = 0
qa.e: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature; with T constant, ΔU = 0.

qa.q: An ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly, doing 3.2 kJ of work. How much heat (in kJ) does it absorb?
1 mol of an ideal gas expands isothermally from 5 L to 15 L against a constant pressure of 2 atm. What is q in L atm?
For free expansion of an ideal gas, which set is correct?
qa.e: No external pressure (w = 0); an ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, so no heat is needed (q = 0) and ΔU = 0.

qa.q: In an adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas, the temperature:
qa.a: Falls, because ΔU = w is negative
qa.e: With q = 0, work done by the gas comes from its internal energy, so U and T fall.

qa.q: 1 mol of an ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally at 300 K from 2 L to 20 L. What is q in J (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
A gas is compressed adiabatically, with 500 J of work done on it. What is ΔU in J?
qa.e: q = 0, so ΔU = w = +500 J; the gas warms up.

qa.q: Assertion (A): For an isothermal process of an ideal gas, heat absorbed equals work done by the gas. Reason (R): ΔU = 0 for such a process, so q = −w.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: All heat absorbed is converted into work done by the gas, because internal energy cannot change at constant T.

qa.q: For which reaction is ΔH equal to ΔU?
qa.a: H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)
qa.e: Δn_g = 2 − 2 = 0, so Δn_g RT = 0 and ΔH = ΔU.

qa.q: ΔH for combustion of methane, CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), is −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. What is ΔU in kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
At constant pressure, the heat absorbed by a system equals:
qa.a: ΔH
qa.e: Since H = U + pV, at constant p the heat exchanged is q_p = ΔH.

qa.q: The enthalpy of vaporisation of water at 373 K is 40.79 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔU of vaporisation in kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
What is Δn_g for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g)?
qa.e: Gaseous products 2 − gaseous reactants 3 = −1.

qa.q: A reaction has ΔH = −50 kJ. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: It is exothermic: heat is released at constant pressure
qa.e: Negative ΔH means the system releases heat to the surroundings.

qa.q: For the decomposition CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) at 1000 K, by how much does ΔH exceed ΔU, in kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
Assertion (A): For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔH is more negative than ΔU. Reason (R): Δn_g for this reaction is negative.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Δn_g = −2, so ΔH = ΔU − 2RT, making ΔH more negative than ΔU.

qa.q: Which is an intensive property?
qa.a: Density
qa.e: Density (mass/volume) is the same for a drop and a bucket of the same liquid.

qa.q: How much heat in J is needed to raise the temperature of 60 g of iron by 20 K (c = 0.45 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)?
For an ideal gas, C_v = 12.47 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is C_p in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
Why is C_p greater than C_v for a gas?
qa.a: At constant pressure, part of the heat supplied does work of expansion
qa.e: At constant volume all heat raises internal energy; at constant pressure extra heat is needed for expansion work.

qa.q: The ratio of two extensive properties is:
qa.a: An intensive property
qa.e: Doubling the amount doubles both, so their ratio stays the same: e.g. density, molar volume.

qa.q: A 500 J heat input raises the temperature of a metal block by 10 K. What is the heat capacity of the block in J K⁻¹?
What is the molar heat capacity of water in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, given c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and M = 18 g mol⁻¹?
Assertion (A): Heat capacity is an extensive property. Reason (R): A larger amount of a substance needs more heat for the same rise in temperature.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: C scales with the amount of substance, which is what makes it extensive; specific and molar heat capacities are intensive.

qa.q: A bomb calorimeter measures which quantity directly?
qa.a: ΔU
qa.e: Reaction occurs at constant volume, so no pV work: q_v = ΔU.

qa.q: A reaction in a bomb calorimeter (C_cal = 10.0 kJ K⁻¹) raises the temperature by 2.5 K. How much heat in kJ is released by the reaction?
qa.e: q = C_cal ΔT = 10.0 × 2.5 = 25 kJ absorbed by the calorimeter, so 25 kJ released.

qa.q: 50 mL of 1.0 M HCl and 50 mL of 1.0 M NaOH are mixed in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature rises by 6.8 K. Taking mass of solution 100 g and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, what is ΔH of neutralisation in kJ per mole of water formed?
Why is the heat measured in a coffee-cup calorimeter equal to ΔH?
qa.a: The reaction occurs at constant (atmospheric) pressure
qa.e: Heat exchanged at constant pressure is q_p = ΔH.

qa.q: In a calorimeter experiment the water temperature falls. What does this indicate about the reaction?
qa.a: It is endothermic
qa.e: The reaction absorbed heat from the water, so ΔH (or ΔU) is positive.

qa.q: 2 g of a fuel burns in a bomb calorimeter of heat capacity 15 kJ K⁻¹; the temperature rises by 4 K. What is the heat released per gram, in kJ g⁻¹?
qa.e: Total q = 15 × 4 = 60 kJ for 2 g, so 30 kJ g⁻¹.

qa.q: Why must a bomb calorimeter be made of strong steel?
qa.a: Combustion in pure oxygen at constant volume produces high pressure
qa.e: The sealed vessel must withstand the pressure generated by rapid combustion, which is also why it is used only with proper safety precautions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Heat measured in a bomb calorimeter for a reaction involving gases may differ from its ΔH. Reason (R): A bomb calorimeter measures ΔU, and ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: When Δn_g ≠ 0, ΔH and ΔU differ by Δn_g RT, so the bomb value must be corrected to get ΔH.

qa.q: What does the standard state of a substance mean?
qa.a: The pure substance at 1 bar and a specified temperature
qa.e: Standard state refers to the pure form at 1 bar; the temperature is specified, usually 298 K.

qa.q: Δ_fusH of ice is 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ and Δ_vapH of water is 45.07 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273 K. What is Δ_subH of ice at 273 K in kJ mol⁻¹?
qa.e: Δ_subH = Δ_fusH + Δ_vapH = 6.01 + 45.07 = 51.08 kJ mol⁻¹.

qa.q: For 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), Δ_rH° = −571.6 kJ mol⁻¹. What is Δ_rH° for H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) in kJ mol⁻¹?
qa.e: Halving the equation halves Δ_rH: −571.6/2 = −285.8.

qa.q: Why must physical states be written in a thermochemical equation?
qa.a: The enthalpy change depends on the states of reactants and products
qa.e: Forming H₂O(l) releases more heat than forming H₂O(g), because condensation releases extra enthalpy.

qa.q: How much heat in kJ is needed to melt 36 g of ice at 273 K (Δ_fusH = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹, H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)?
If the reaction A → B has Δ_rH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹, then for B → A, Δ_rH is:
qa.a: −40 kJ mol⁻¹
qa.e: Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of its enthalpy change.

qa.q: Which equation correctly expresses the standard reaction enthalpy?
qa.a: Δ_rH° = Σ aᵢ H°(products) − Σ bᵢ H°(reactants)
qa.e: Products minus reactants, each weighted by its stoichiometric coefficient.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Burning 2 mol of methane releases twice the heat of burning 1 mol. Reason (R): Enthalpy change is an extensive property.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: ΔH scales with the amount reacting; doubling the coefficients doubles ΔH.

qa.q: Calculate Δ_cH° of methane: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), given Δ_fH° (kJ mol⁻¹): CH₄ = −74.8, CO₂ = −393.5, H₂O(l) = −285.8.
Which equation represents the standard enthalpy of formation of water?
qa.a: H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l)
qa.e: Formation means one mole of compound from elements in their reference states (H₂ and O₂ gases, not atoms).

qa.q: What is Δ_fH° of O₂(g) at 298 K?
qa.e: O₂(g) is the reference state of oxygen, so its standard enthalpy of formation is zero.

qa.q: Given S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g), ΔH = −297 kJ and 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −198 kJ, find ΔH for S(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) → SO₃(g), in kJ.
qa.e: Take the first equation as is (−297) and half the second (−99): −297 + (−99) = −396 kJ.

qa.q: Hess's law is a consequence of the fact that:
qa.a: Enthalpy is a state function
qa.e: Since ΔH depends only on initial and final states, any route gives the same total.

qa.q: Given Δ_fH° (kJ mol⁻¹): NH₃(g) = −46.1. What is Δ_rH° for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), in kJ mol⁻¹?
qa.e: 2 × (−46.1) − 0 = −92.2 kJ mol⁻¹, since N₂ and H₂ are elements in their reference states.

qa.q: C(graphite) → C(diamond) has Δ_rH° = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹. What is Δ_fH° of diamond in kJ mol⁻¹?
qa.e: Graphite is the reference state (Δ_fH° = 0), so Δ_fH°(diamond) = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The enthalpy change for C → CO₂ is the same whether carbon burns directly or first to CO and then to CO₂. Reason (R): Hess's law says the total enthalpy change is independent of the path.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: −110.5 + (−283.0) = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹, the same as direct combustion.

qa.q: The enthalpy of atomisation of CH₄ is 1665 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the mean C–H bond enthalpy in kJ mol⁻¹?
qa.e: Four C–H bonds break: 1665/4 = 416.25 kJ mol⁻¹ (about 416).

qa.q: Using bond enthalpies H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242 and H–Cl = 431 kJ mol⁻¹, estimate Δ_rH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, in kJ.
The standard enthalpy of combustion of glucose is −2802 kJ mol⁻¹. How much heat is released when 45 g of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) is burnt, in kJ?
For a metal like sodium, the enthalpy of atomisation is the same as its:
qa.a: Enthalpy of sublimation
qa.e: Na(s) → Na(g) gives separate gaseous atoms directly; this is sublimation.

qa.q: Why are reaction enthalpies from mean bond enthalpies only approximate?
qa.a: Mean bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds and do not match each molecule exactly
qa.e: A C–H bond in CH₄ is not identical to one in C₂H₆; averages introduce small errors.

qa.q: Which bond-enthalpy expression is correct for a gas-phase reaction?
qa.a: Δ_rH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed)
qa.e: Breaking bonds costs energy (positive); forming bonds releases it (negative).

qa.q: Using C–H = 414, Cl–Cl = 243, C–Cl = 330 and H–Cl = 431 kJ mol⁻¹, estimate Δ_rH for CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, in kJ.
qa.e: Only one C–H and one Cl–Cl break (414 + 243 = 657); one C–Cl and one H–Cl form (330 + 431 = 761). Δ_rH = 657 − 761 = −104 kJ.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Combustion reactions are exothermic. Reason (R): In combustion, the bonds formed in CO₂ and H₂O are stronger overall than the bonds broken in the fuel and oxygen.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: More energy is released by forming strong C=O and O–H bonds than is needed to break C–H, C–C and O=O bonds.

qa.q: Using: Δ_subH(Na) = 108.4, Δ_iH(Na) = 496, ½Δ_bondH(Cl₂) = 121, Δ_egH(Cl) = −348.6 and Δ_fH°(NaCl) = −411.2 kJ mol⁻¹, find the lattice enthalpy of NaCl in kJ mol⁻¹.
The lattice enthalpy of a salt is +700 kJ mol⁻¹ and its hydration enthalpy is −720 kJ mol⁻¹. What is its enthalpy of solution in kJ mol⁻¹?
qa.e: Δ_solH = 700 + (−720) = −20 kJ mol⁻¹: it dissolves exothermically.

qa.q: What does lattice enthalpy represent?
qa.a: Energy to separate one mole of an ionic solid into gaseous ions
qa.e: It is defined for complete separation into gaseous ions, a positive quantity.

qa.q: Which law makes the Born–Haber cycle possible?
qa.a: Hess's law
qa.e: The sum of enthalpy changes round a closed cycle must equal the direct formation enthalpy.

qa.q: HCl(g) in 10 mol H₂O: ΔH = −69.01 kJ mol⁻¹; in 40 mol H₂O: −72.79 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the enthalpy of dilution from 10 to 40 mol of water per mole of HCl, in kJ?
A salt has a lattice enthalpy much larger than the magnitude of its hydration enthalpy. It is expected to be:
qa.a: Poorly soluble, or soluble with absorption of heat
qa.e: If breaking the lattice costs far more than hydration returns, Δ_solH is strongly positive and dissolution is unfavourable.

qa.q: In the Born–Haber cycle for NaCl, which step is exothermic?
qa.a: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g)
qa.e: Chlorine releases 348.6 kJ mol⁻¹ when it gains an electron; the other three steps absorb energy.

qa.q: Assertion (A): NaCl dissolves in water although its lattice enthalpy is +788 kJ mol⁻¹. Reason (R): The hydration enthalpy of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (−784 kJ mol⁻¹) almost balances the lattice enthalpy, and the entropy increase on dissolving helps.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Δ_solH is only +4 kJ mol⁻¹, and the increase in disorder when ions spread through water makes dissolution spontaneous.

qa.q: What is the entropy change in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ when 1 mol of water vaporises at 373 K (Δ_vapH = 40.79 kJ mol⁻¹)? Give the answer to two decimal places.
Which process is endothermic yet spontaneous at room temperature?
qa.a: Dissolution of ammonium chloride in water
qa.e: NH₄Cl absorbs heat as it dissolves (the solution cools) but dissolves on its own because entropy increases.

qa.q: Which has the highest entropy per mole at the same temperature?
qa.a: H₂O(g)
qa.e: Gas molecules move freely and randomly, so the gas has the greatest disorder.

qa.q: For which reaction does the entropy of the system decrease?
qa.a: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)
qa.e: 4 mol of gas become 2 mol of gas, so disorder falls.

qa.q: A process has ΔS_system = −20 J K⁻¹ and ΔS_surroundings = +50 J K⁻¹. What is ΔS_total in J K⁻¹, and is it spontaneous?
qa.a: 30, spontaneous
qa.e: ΔS_total = −20 + 50 = +30 J K⁻¹ > 0, so the process is spontaneous even though the system's entropy falls.

qa.q: The same 1000 J of heat is transferred reversibly at 250 K and at 500 K. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: The entropy change is larger at 250 K (4 J K⁻¹) than at 500 K (2 J K⁻¹)
qa.e: ΔS = q/T: 1000/250 = 4 and 1000/500 = 2 J K⁻¹. Heat added to a colder system causes more disorder.

qa.q: What is the entropy change in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ when 1 mol of ice melts at 273 K (Δ_fusH = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹)? Give two decimal places.
Assertion (A): Decrease in enthalpy alone cannot decide spontaneity. Reason (R): Some endothermic processes, such as evaporation of water, are spontaneous.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Endothermic spontaneous processes show that entropy also matters, so ΔH alone is not enough.

qa.q: For a reaction at 298 K, ΔH = −10 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −50 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG in kJ mol⁻¹?
qa.e: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −10 − 298 × (−0.050) = −10 + 14.9 = +4.9 kJ mol⁻¹; non-spontaneous at 298 K.

qa.q: At what temperature (in K) does a reaction with ΔH = +179.1 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +160.2 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ reach ΔG = 0? Give the answer to two decimal places.
qa.e: T = ΔH/ΔS = 179 100/160.2 = 1117.98 K. Above this temperature, CaCO₃ decomposition becomes spontaneous.

qa.q: A reaction has ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0. It is:
qa.a: Spontaneous at all temperatures
qa.e: Both terms in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS are negative, so ΔG < 0 at every temperature.

qa.q: A reaction with ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0 is spontaneous:
qa.a: Only at low temperatures
qa.e: At low T, ΔH dominates and ΔG < 0; at high T, the positive −TΔS term wins and ΔG > 0.

qa.q: What does ΔG = 0 indicate for a process at constant T and p?
qa.a: The system is at equilibrium
qa.e: Neither direction is favoured; forward and reverse tendencies balance.

qa.q: For a reaction, ΔH = +40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG at 300 K, in kJ mol⁻¹?
qa.e: ΔG = 40 − 300 × 0.100 = 40 − 30 = +10 kJ mol⁻¹, non-spontaneous at 300 K (it becomes spontaneous above 400 K).

qa.q: Which expression defines Gibbs energy?
qa.a: G = H − TS
qa.e: G = H − TS; at constant T this gives ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Decomposition of CaCO₃ is spontaneous only at high temperature. Reason (R): It is endothermic with a positive entropy change.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: For ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG becomes negative only when TΔS exceeds ΔH, i.e. at high T.

qa.q: What is Δ_rG° in kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K for a reaction with K = 10 (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)? Give two decimal places.
A reaction at 298 K has Δ_rG° = −11.41 kJ mol⁻¹. What is log K (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
If Δ_rG° for a reaction is positive, then the equilibrium constant K is:
qa.a: Less than 1
qa.e: −RT ln K > 0 means ln K < 0, so K < 1: reactants are favoured.

qa.q: Which statement is the third law of thermodynamics?
qa.a: Entropy of a perfectly crystalline substance approaches zero as T approaches 0 K
qa.e: The third law fixes a zero of entropy for perfect crystals at absolute zero.

qa.q: The second law of thermodynamics can be stated as:
qa.a: In a spontaneous process the entropy of the universe increases
qa.e: ΔS_universe > 0 for spontaneous processes.

qa.q: At equilibrium, which is true?
qa.a: Δ_rG = 0
qa.e: Δ_rG (not Δ_rG°) is zero at equilibrium; Δ_rG° is a fixed value related to K.

qa.q: A reaction has K = 1 at 298 K. What is its Δ_rG° in kJ mol⁻¹?
Assertion (A): Reactions with large negative Δ_rG° go almost to completion. Reason (R): A large negative Δ_rG° corresponds to a very large equilibrium constant.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: K = 10^(−Δ_rG°/2.303RT); a large negative Δ_rG° makes K huge, so products dominate at equilibrium.

qa.q: Which statement about a solid–liquid equilibrium such as ice ⇌ water at 273 K is correct?
qa.a: The rate of melting equals the rate of freezing
qa.e: At the melting point, molecules move between ice and water at equal rates, so the amounts stay the same.

qa.q: Why does a soda bottle fizz when opened?
qa.a: Lower CO₂ pressure above the liquid reduces CO₂ solubility (Henry's law)
qa.e: Gas solubility is proportional to its partial pressure; releasing pressure lets dissolved CO₂ escape.

qa.q: The normal boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapour pressure equals:
qa.a: 1.013 bar (1 atm)
qa.e: At 1.013 bar, vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure and bubbles form throughout the liquid.

qa.q: Which substance can set up a solid–vapour equilibrium in a closed vessel?
qa.a: Camphor
qa.e: Camphor sublimes, so its solid and vapour can coexist in equilibrium.

qa.q: In a saturated solution of sugar in contact with undissolved sugar, which is true?
qa.a: Sugar dissolves and crystallises at equal rates
qa.e: It is a dynamic equilibrium: dissolution and crystallisation balance, so concentration stays constant.

qa.q: Why do we say equilibrium can be set up only in a closed system?
qa.a: Matter must not escape, otherwise the reverse process cannot keep pace
qa.e: If vapour or gas escapes, the reverse process (e.g. condensation) cannot balance the forward process.

qa.q: Which property becomes constant when the liquid ⇌ vapour equilibrium is reached at a fixed temperature?
qa.a: Vapour pressure
qa.e: The equilibrium is characterised by a constant vapour pressure at a given temperature.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Fish find less dissolved oxygen in warm water. Reason (R): The solubility of gases in liquids decreases with increase in temperature.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Gases dissolve less in warmer water, which is why warm ponds can starve fish of oxygen.

qa.q: Which correctly describes chemical equilibrium?
qa.a: Rates of forward and backward reactions are equal
qa.e: Equilibrium is reached when the two opposing rates match, keeping concentrations constant (not equal).

qa.q: What does the deuterium-labelled ammonia experiment demonstrate?
qa.a: Chemical equilibrium is dynamic
qa.e: Mixed species like NH₂D appear only if forward and backward reactions continue at equilibrium.

qa.q: Who proposed the law of mass action?
qa.a: Guldberg and Waage
qa.e: Norwegian chemists Guldberg and Waage stated it in 1864.

qa.q: What is the Kc expression for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)?
qa.a: [NO₂]² / ([NO]²[O₂])
qa.e: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient (not multiplied by it).

qa.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) at equilibrium, [H₂] = [I₂] = 0.1 M and [HI] = 0.7 M. What is Kc?
1 mol each of H₂ and I₂ are heated in a closed vessel. Which statement about equilibrium is correct?
qa.a: The same equilibrium would be reached by heating the equivalent amount of HI (2 mol) at the same temperature
qa.e: Equilibrium is reachable from either direction and its composition depends only on conditions, not on the starting side.

qa.q: According to the law of mass action, the rate of A + B → products is proportional to:
qa.e: Rate is proportional to the product of active masses (molar concentrations) of the reactants.

qa.q: Assertion (A): At equilibrium, the concentrations of all species remain constant. Reason (R): At equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions occur at equal rates.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Each species is formed and used up at the same rate, so its concentration does not change.

qa.q: For a reaction, Kc = 2.5 × 10⁻². What is Kc for the reverse reaction?
At equilibrium, [N₂] = 0.1 M, [H₂] = 0.2 M and [NH₃] = 0.2 M for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. What is Kc (in mol⁻² L²)?
For A ⇌ B, K₁ = 2 and for B ⇌ C, K₂ = 3. What is K for A ⇌ C?
qa.e: Adding equations multiplies their equilibrium constants: 2 × 3 = 6.

qa.q: For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, Kc = 100. What is Kc for SO₂ + ½O₂ ⇌ SO₃?
qa.e: Halving the equation gives K' = √K = √100 = 10.

qa.q: 0.5 mol PCl₅, 0.2 mol PCl₃ and 0.2 mol Cl₂ are at equilibrium in a 2 L flask: PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂. What is Kc in mol L⁻¹?
qa.e: Concentrations: PCl₅ 0.25 M, PCl₃ 0.1 M, Cl₂ 0.1 M; Kc = (0.1 × 0.1)/0.25 = 0.04.

qa.q: Which equilibrium is homogeneous?
qa.a: CH₃COOC₂H₅(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COOH(aq) + C₂H₅OH(aq) in one liquid phase
qa.e: Ester hydrolysis in solution has all species in one liquid phase; the others mix solids with gases or liquids.

qa.q: If Kc for a reaction is K, what is Kc when the equation is multiplied by 3?
qa.a: K³
qa.e: Each concentration term is cubed, so the whole constant is raised to the third power.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The value of Kc depends on how the balanced equation is written. Reason (R): Coefficients appear as powers of concentrations in the Kc expression.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Doubling coefficients squares every term, so K changes to K²; the equilibrium itself is the same.

qa.q: For which reaction is Kp = Kc?
qa.a: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
qa.e: Δn = 2 − 2 = 0, so (RT)⁰ = 1 and Kp = Kc.

qa.q: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) at 500 K, Kc = 0.04 mol L⁻¹. What is Kp in bar (R = 0.0831 bar L mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)?
What is the equilibrium constant expression for CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)?
qa.a: Kp = p(CO₂)
qa.e: Pure solids have constant activity and are omitted, leaving only the CO₂ pressure.

qa.q: What are the units of Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
qa.a: mol⁻² L²
qa.e: Kc = [NH₃]²/[N₂][H₂]³ has units (mol L⁻¹)^(2 − 4) = (mol L⁻¹)⁻² = mol⁻² L².

qa.q: Why are pure solids and liquids omitted from equilibrium constant expressions?
qa.a: Their concentrations (molar densities) are constant at a given temperature
qa.e: The amount per unit volume of a pure solid or liquid does not change, so it is absorbed into K.

qa.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), Kp = Kc(RT)^x. What is x?
In the equilibrium H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂O(g) at 30 °C, Kp equals:
qa.a: The vapour pressure of water at 30 °C
qa.e: The liquid is omitted, so Kp = p(H₂O), which is the equilibrium vapour pressure.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Adding more CaCO₃(s) to the CaCO₃ ⇌ CaO + CO₂ equilibrium does not change the CO₂ pressure. Reason (R): Pure solids do not appear in the equilibrium constant expression.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Kp = p(CO₂) depends only on temperature, so the amount of solid present does not affect it.

qa.q: For a reaction, Kc = 2.0. At some instant Qc = 0.5. What will happen?
qa.a: The reaction proceeds forward
qa.e: Q < K, so more products must form to reach equilibrium.

qa.q: For 2A ⇌ B, Kc = 4. If [A] = 0.5 M and [B] = 2.0 M at a moment, what is Qc?
qa.e: Qc = [B]/[A]² = 2.0/0.25 = 8. Since Q > K, the reaction goes backward.

qa.q: A reaction has Kc = 4.8 × 10⁻³¹ at 298 K. What does this tell you?
qa.a: Hardly any products form; reactants predominate
qa.e: A tiny K means the equilibrium lies far to the left (this is N₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2NO at room temperature).

qa.q: 1.0 mol each of H₂ and I₂ are heated in a 1 L flask. Kc = 64 for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI. What is the equilibrium [HI] in mol L⁻¹?
qa.e: With x = 0.8 from 2x/(1 − x) = 8, [HI] = 2x = 1.6 M.

qa.q: In the same experiment (Kc = 64, 1.0 mol each of H₂ and I₂ in 1 L), what is the equilibrium [H₂] in mol L⁻¹?
Which value of K indicates that both reactants and products are present in appreciable amounts?
qa.e: K between 10⁻³ and 10³ means neither side overwhelmingly dominates.

qa.q: For N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), Kc = 0.01 at a high temperature. At some moment [N₂] = [O₂] = 1.0 M and [NO] = 0.2 M. What is Qc and the direction of change?
qa.a: Qc = 0.04; backward
qa.e: Qc = (0.2)²/(1.0 × 1.0) = 0.04 > Kc = 0.01, so NO decomposes (backward reaction) until Q = K.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A reaction with Q > K moves in the backward direction. Reason (R): When Q > K, the product concentrations are higher than at equilibrium relative to reactants.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Too much product (relative to equilibrium) means products must convert back into reactants to lower Q to K.

qa.q: ΔG° for a reaction at 300 K is −5744.1 J mol⁻¹. What is K (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
What is ΔG° in kJ mol⁻¹ at 300 K for a reaction with K = 1000 (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)? Give two decimal places.
Which relation holds at equilibrium?
qa.a: ΔG° = −RT ln K
qa.e: Setting ΔG = 0 and Q = K in ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q gives ΔG° = −RT ln K.

qa.q: For a reaction at some instant, Q = 5 while K = 50. Which is true?
qa.a: ΔG < 0 and the forward reaction is spontaneous
qa.e: ΔG = RT ln(Q/K); since Q/K < 1, ln is negative and ΔG < 0.

qa.q: A reaction has ΔG° = +10 kJ mol⁻¹. What can you say about K?
qa.e: Positive ΔG° makes ln K negative, so K lies between 0 and 1.

qa.q: What is log K at 298 K if ΔG° = −11.41 kJ mol⁻¹ (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)?
Why does ΔG° = 0 correspond to K = 1?
qa.a: Because −RT ln K = 0 only when ln K = 0, i.e. K = 1
qa.e: ln 1 = 0, so ΔG° = −RT ln 1 = 0.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A reaction with a very large K has a large negative ΔG°. Reason (R): ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Large K makes log K large and positive, so −2.303 RT log K is large and negative.

qa.q: State Le Chatelier's principle.
qa.a: A system at equilibrium responds to a change by shifting so as to counteract the change
qa.e: The system partially undoes the imposed change by shifting the equilibrium position.

qa.q: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), what is the effect of adding more Cl₂ at constant volume?
qa.a: Equilibrium shifts backward, forming more PCl₅
qa.e: Adding a product makes Q > K, so the reverse reaction consumes some of the added Cl₂.

qa.q: Why does the red colour of [Fe(SCN)]²⁺ fade when oxalic acid is added?
qa.a: Oxalic acid binds Fe³⁺, removing a reactant and shifting equilibrium backward
qa.e: Removing Fe³⁺ lowers its concentration, so the complex dissociates to replace it.

qa.q: What is the effect of increasing pressure on H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)?
qa.a: No shift in equilibrium position
qa.e: Both sides have 2 mol of gas, so changing pressure does not favour either side.

qa.q: For CO(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ CH₄(g) + H₂O(g), reducing the volume of the container will:
qa.a: Increase the amount of CH₄ and H₂O
qa.e: Reducing volume raises pressure; the side with fewer gas moles (2 versus 4) is favoured.

qa.q: When a product is removed from an equilibrium mixture, what happens to K?
qa.a: K stays the same; the equilibrium shifts forward
qa.e: Only temperature changes K; removing product lowers Q, so the reaction moves forward to restore Q = K.

qa.q: In the industrial manufacture of SO₃ (2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃), why is a high pressure helpful?
qa.a: The product side has fewer gas moles (2 versus 3)
qa.e: Increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer moles of gas, increasing SO₃ yield.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Increasing pressure on N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) increases the amount of N₂O₄. Reason (R): The reverse reaction reduces the total number of gas molecules.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: 2 mol NO₂ form 1 mol N₂O₄, lowering the pressure, which partly counteracts the imposed increase.

qa.q: What is the effect of adding an inert gas to an equilibrium mixture at constant volume?
qa.a: No effect on the equilibrium position
qa.e: At constant volume, partial pressures (and molar concentrations) of the reacting gases are unchanged.

qa.q: For an endothermic reaction, increasing the temperature:
qa.a: Increases K and shifts equilibrium forward
qa.e: Adding heat favours the direction that absorbs heat, the forward endothermic direction.

qa.q: Why does a tube of NO₂/N₂O₄ turn darker brown when placed in hot water?
qa.a: The forward reaction N₂O₄ → 2NO₂ is endothermic and is favoured by heating
qa.e: Heating shifts the equilibrium towards brown NO₂ because that direction absorbs heat.

qa.q: What is the role of iron in the Haber process?
qa.a: It is a catalyst that helps equilibrium be reached faster
qa.e: A catalyst only changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached, not the yield at equilibrium.

qa.q: Which is the only factor that changes the value of the equilibrium constant of a given reaction?
qa.a: Temperature
qa.e: K depends only on temperature; other changes alter Q and the position, not K.

qa.q: Why is the Haber process run at about 500 °C even though lower temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield?
qa.a: At low temperature the reaction is too slow; 500 °C is a compromise between rate and yield
qa.e: The forward reaction is exothermic, so high T lowers K, but rate matters for production; a catalyst and high pressure compensate.

qa.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0. Which change increases the equilibrium amount of SO₃?
qa.a: Lowering the temperature
qa.e: Lowering T favours the exothermic forward reaction. Catalysts and inert gas at constant volume do not shift equilibrium.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant. Reason (R): A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and backward reactions by the same amount.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both rates increase by the same factor, so their ratio, which is K, stays the same.

qa.q: What is the conjugate base of H₂SO₄?
qa.a: HSO₄⁻
qa.e: Removing one H⁺ from H₂SO₄ gives HSO₄⁻.

qa.q: What is the conjugate acid of NH₃?
qa.a: NH₄⁺
qa.e: Adding one H⁺ to NH₃ gives NH₄⁺.

qa.q: In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, which species acts as the Brønsted acid on the left side?
qa.a: H₂O
qa.e: Water donates a proton to ammonia, so water is the acid here.

qa.q: Which is a Lewis acid but not a Brønsted acid?
qa.a: BF₃
qa.e: BF₃ has no proton to donate, but its electron-deficient boron accepts an electron pair.

qa.q: Why does H⁺ exist as H₃O⁺ in water?
qa.a: A bare proton is very reactive and bonds to a lone pair on a water molecule
qa.e: A proton has an enormous charge density, so it attaches to the oxygen lone pair of water.

qa.q: Which species can act both as a Brønsted acid and a Brønsted base?
qa.a: HCO₃⁻
qa.e: HCO₃⁻ can lose a proton (→ CO₃²⁻) or gain one (→ H₂CO₃), so it is amphoteric.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of the Arrhenius concept?
qa.a: It applies only to aqueous solutions and cannot explain the basicity of NH₃
qa.e: Arrhenius needs OH⁻ in the formula and water as solvent; NH₃'s basic nature is better explained by Brønsted–Lowry.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The conjugate base of a strong acid is a weak base. Reason (R): A strong acid gives up its proton readily, so its conjugate base has little tendency to take it back.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: HCl is strong, so Cl⁻ barely accepts protons; it is a very weak base.

qa.q: Which substance is a weak electrolyte in water?
qa.a: Acetic acid
qa.e: Acetic acid ionises only partly, so its few ions are in equilibrium with un-ionised molecules. NaCl, HCl and NaOH ionise almost completely (strong electrolytes).

qa.q: What is the pH of a 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M HNO₃ solution at 298 K?
qa.e: HNO₃ is a strong acid, so [H₃O⁺] = 10⁻⁴ M and pH = 4.

qa.q: What is [OH⁻] in mol L⁻¹ in a solution where [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M at 298 K? Give the answer in units of 10⁻⁹.
What is the pH of 0.01 M NaOH at 298 K?
The pH of 10⁻⁸ M HCl is closest to:
qa.e: Water itself supplies about 10⁻⁷ M H₃O⁺, which is larger than 10⁻⁸ M; total [H₃O⁺] ≈ 1.05 × 10⁻⁷ M gives pH ≈ 6.98. An acid can never give a pH above 7.

qa.q: At 298 K, a solution has pOH = 3.2. What is its pH?
qa.e: pH = 14 − pOH = 14 − 3.2 = 10.8, a basic solution.

qa.q: How many times more H₃O⁺ does a solution of pH 3 contain compared with one of pH 6?
qa.e: Each pH unit is a factor of 10, so a difference of 3 units is 10³ = 1000.

qa.q: What is the value of Kw at 298 K?
Assertion (A): The pH of pure water at 333 K is less than 7, yet the water is neutral. Reason (R): Kw increases with temperature, but [H₃O⁺] still equals [OH⁻].
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Ionisation of water is endothermic, so Kw rises with T and [H₃O⁺] exceeds 10⁻⁷ M; since [OH⁻] rises equally, water stays neutral.

qa.q: In HCl + NH₃ → NH₄⁺ + Cl⁻, why does the proton transfer go almost completely to the right?
qa.a: The proton moves from the stronger acid (HCl) to the stronger base (NH₃), giving the weaker acid NH₄⁺ and the weaker base Cl⁻
qa.e: Proton transfer goes mainly from the stronger acid to the stronger base. HCl is much stronger than NH₄⁺, and NH₃ is a much stronger base than Cl⁻.

qa.q: What is the pH of 0.1 M HA (Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵)?
What is the degree of ionisation α of 0.1 M HA (Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵)?
The Kb of NH₃ is 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ (rounded). What is the Ka of NH₄⁺ at 298 K, in units of 10⁻⁹?
qa.e: Ka = Kw/Kb = 10⁻¹⁴/10⁻⁵ = 10⁻⁹.

qa.q: A weak base has pKb = 4.75. What is the pKa of its conjugate acid at 298 K?
What is the pH of 0.01 M of a weak base with Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ at 298 K?
Which acid is the strongest? (pKa values given)
qa.a: HA, pKa = 3.2
qa.e: Lowest pKa means highest Ka, so HA is the strongest.

qa.q: When a weak acid solution is diluted ten-fold, its degree of ionisation becomes about:
qa.a: √10 ≈ 3.16 times larger
qa.e: α = √(Ka/c); dividing c by 10 multiplies α by √10.

qa.q: Assertion (A): 0.1 M acetic acid has a higher pH than 0.1 M HCl. Reason (R): Acetic acid is only partially ionised, so it produces fewer H₃O⁺ ions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Lower [H₃O⁺] from a weak acid means a higher pH (about 2.9 versus 1).

qa.q: Why is HI a stronger acid than HF in water?
qa.a: The H–I bond is much weaker than the H–F bond
qa.e: Down group 17, atom size increases and the H–A bond weakens, so H⁺ is released more easily.

qa.q: Which correctly orders acid strength across period 2?
qa.a: CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF
qa.e: Across a period, the electronegativity of A rises, making the H–A bond more polar and H⁺ easier to lose.

qa.q: What is the effect of adding sodium acetate to a solution of acetic acid?
qa.a: Ionisation of acetic acid is suppressed and pH increases
qa.e: Extra acetate (a common ion) shifts CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ to the left, lowering [H₃O⁺].

qa.q: An aqueous solution of sodium acetate is:
qa.a: Basic
qa.e: CH₃COO⁻ hydrolyses: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻, raising pH above 7.

qa.q: For the salt of a weak acid (pKa = 4.8) and weak base (pKb = 4.4), what is the pH of its aqueous solution?
For H₃PO₄, which is correct about its successive ionisation constants?
qa.a: Ka₁ > Ka₂ > Ka₃
qa.e: Each proton is removed from an increasingly negative species, which is progressively harder.

qa.q: Why is an aqueous solution of NH₄Cl acidic?
qa.a: NH₄⁺ hydrolyses: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺
qa.e: NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of the weak base NH₃ and donates protons to water; Cl⁻ (from a strong acid) does not hydrolyse.

qa.q: Assertion (A): An aqueous solution of KCN is basic. Reason (R): CN⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid HCN and hydrolyses to give OH⁻.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: CN⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCN + OH⁻ produces hydroxide ions, making the solution basic.

qa.q: Which pair forms an acidic buffer?
qa.a: CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa
qa.e: A weak acid with its conjugate base (as a salt) resists pH change; HCl/NaCl involves a strong acid, which cannot buffer.

qa.q: A buffer contains equal concentrations of a weak acid (pKa = 4.76) and its sodium salt. What is its pH?
qa.e: log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa = 4.76.

qa.q: What is the pH of a buffer that is 0.2 M in NH₄OH and 0.2 M in NH₄Cl (pKb = 4.75, 298 K)?
A buffer is 1.0 M in HA (pKa = 5.0) and 0.1 M in NaA. What is its pH?
How does an acetate buffer resist a fall in pH when a little HCl is added?
qa.a: CH₃COO⁻ ions combine with the added H⁺ to form weakly ionised CH₃COOH
qa.e: The conjugate base mops up added H⁺, so [H₃O⁺] barely changes.

qa.q: To prepare a buffer of pH about 9, which pair is most suitable?
qa.a: NH₄OH and NH₄Cl (pKa of NH₄⁺ ≈ 9.25)
qa.e: A buffer works best when the target pH is close to the pKa of the weak acid involved.

qa.q: A buffer has pKa = 6.8 and [salt]/[acid] = 10. What is its pH?
Assertion (A): A mixture of HCl and NaCl is not a buffer. Reason (R): HCl is a strong acid and Cl⁻ is too weak a base to absorb added H⁺.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Buffers need a weak acid–conjugate base pair that can neutralise both added acid and base.

qa.q: The solubility of AgCl in water is 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹. What is its Ksp, in units of 10⁻¹⁰?
The molar solubility of CaF₂ is 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. What is its Ksp in units of 10⁻¹¹?
Ksp of a salt MX is 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁰. What is its molar solubility in units of 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹?
What is the solubility of AgCl (Ksp = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰) in 0.1 M NaCl, in units of 10⁻⁹ mol L⁻¹?
qa.e: [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.1 M from NaCl, so s = Ksp/[Cl⁻] = 10⁻¹⁰/0.1 = 10⁻⁹ M, ten thousand times less than in pure water.

qa.q: Equal volumes of 2 × 10⁻⁴ M BaCl₂ and 2 × 10⁻⁴ M Na₂SO₄ are mixed. Ksp(BaSO₄) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰. Will BaSO₄ precipitate?
qa.a: Yes, because Q_sp = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ exceeds Ksp
