qa.e: After mixing, each concentration halves to 1 × 10⁻⁴ M; Q_sp = (10⁻⁴)(10⁻⁴) = 10⁻⁸ > 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰, so precipitation occurs.

qa.q: Which expression gives Ksp of Ag₂CrO₄ in terms of its molar solubility s?
qa.a: 4s³
qa.e: Ag₂CrO₄ ⇌ 2Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻; Ksp = (2s)²(s) = 4s³.

qa.q: Why does passing HCl gas through a saturated solution of impure NaCl give pure NaCl crystals?
qa.a: The common Cl⁻ ion raises the ionic product above Ksp, so NaCl precipitates while impurities stay dissolved
qa.e: Extra Cl⁻ makes [Na⁺][Cl⁻] exceed NaCl's Ksp, forcing pure NaCl out; impurities are present in small amounts and remain dissolved.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The solubility of BaSO₄ is lower in a solution of Na₂SO₄ than in pure water. Reason (R): SO₄²⁻ is a common ion that shifts BaSO₄(s) ⇌ Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ to the left.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: With [SO₄²⁻] increased, less Ba²⁺ can stay in solution while Ksp stays the same.

qa.q: A salt dissolves to the extent of 0.004 mol L⁻¹ in water at 298 K. How is it classified?
qa.a: Sparingly soluble
qa.e: Below 0.01 M a salt is sparingly soluble; 0.01 to 0.1 M is slightly soluble; above 0.1 M is soluble.

qa.q: In 2FeCl₃ + H₂ → 2FeCl₂ + 2HCl, FeCl₃ is:
qa.a: Reduced, because it loses an electronegative element (Cl)
qa.e: Removal of an electronegative element is reduction in the classical sense.

qa.q: In ZnO + C → Zn + CO, which is the reducing agent?
qa.a: C
qa.e: Carbon removes oxygen from ZnO (reducing it) and is itself oxidised to CO.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of oxidation by removal of hydrogen?
qa.a: 2H₂S + O₂ → 2S + 2H₂O (for H₂S)
qa.e: H₂S loses its hydrogen to form sulphur, so it is oxidised.

qa.q: An oxidising agent is a substance that:
qa.a: Gets reduced while oxidising another substance
qa.e: The oxidant takes oxygen-removing or electron-accepting role and is itself reduced.

qa.q: In 2HgCl₂ + SnCl₂ → Hg₂Cl₂ + SnCl₄, what happens to SnCl₂?
qa.a: It is oxidised by gaining an electronegative element (Cl)
qa.e: SnCl₂ becomes SnCl₄ by adding chlorine, an electronegative element, which is oxidation.

qa.q: Why are oxidation and reduction called complementary processes?
qa.a: One cannot occur without the other in a reaction
qa.e: Whatever is lost by one substance (oxygen, electrons) must be gained by another, so they always occur together.

qa.q: In Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, the oxidising agent is:
qa.a: Fe₂O₃
qa.e: Fe₂O₃ gives oxygen to CO (oxidising it) and is itself reduced to Fe.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The reaction 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO is a redox reaction. Reason (R): Magnesium is oxidised and oxygen is reduced in the same reaction.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Mg gains oxygen (oxidation) while O₂ is converted into oxide ions (reduction), so both processes occur together.

qa.q: In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, which half reaction represents oxidation?
qa.a: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻
qa.e: Sodium loses an electron: that is oxidation.

qa.q: What do you observe when a zinc rod is dipped in copper sulphate solution for some time?
qa.a: The blue colour fades and reddish copper deposits on the zinc
qa.e: Zn reduces Cu²⁺ (blue) to Cu metal and itself becomes colourless Zn²⁺.

qa.q: Why does no reaction occur when a copper rod is placed in zinc sulphate solution?
qa.a: Copper has a lower tendency than zinc to release electrons
qa.e: Cu cannot reduce Zn²⁺ because zinc holds its place higher in the activity series.

qa.q: How many electrons are transferred in Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s)?
qa.e: One Cu atom loses 2 electrons, which are taken by two Ag⁺ ions (one each).

qa.q: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, the oxidising agent is:
qa.a: Cu²⁺
qa.e: Cu²⁺ accepts electrons from Zn, so it is the oxidising agent and is itself reduced.

qa.q: Which pair of observations correctly places Zn, Cu and Ag in the activity series?
qa.a: Zn reduces Cu²⁺; Cu reduces Ag⁺
qa.e: These competitive reactions show the order of electron-releasing tendency: Zn > Cu > Ag.

qa.q: Which mnemonic correctly sums up the electronic definitions?
qa.a: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain
qa.e: Oxidation = loss of electrons; reduction = gain of electrons.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, zinc is the reducing agent. Reason (R): Zinc loses electrons to Cu²⁺.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A substance that donates electrons reduces another species and is itself oxidised.

qa.q: What is the oxidation number of Mn in KMnO₄?
What is the average oxidation number of Fe in Fe₃O₄?
qa.e: 3x + 4(−2) = 0 → x = +8/3. Fe₃O₄ contains Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ in a 1 : 2 ratio, giving the average.

qa.q: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in OF₂?
qa.e: F is always −1; 2(−1) + x = 0 → x = +2.

qa.q: What is the oxidation number of S in the S₂O₃²⁻ (thiosulphate) ion, taken as an average?
In the reaction 2KI + Cl₂ → 2KCl + I₂, which element undergoes an increase in oxidation number?
qa.a: Iodine, from −1 to 0
qa.e: Iodide (−1) becomes I₂ (0): oxidation. Chlorine goes 0 → −1: reduction.

qa.q: What is the Stock name of CuO?
qa.a: Copper(II) oxide
qa.e: O is −2, so Cu is +2: copper(II) oxide.

qa.q: What is the oxidation number of N in NH₄⁺?
Assertion (A): In S₄O₆²⁻, the average oxidation number of sulphur is +2.5. Reason (R): All four sulphur atoms in S₄O₆²⁻ have exactly the same oxidation state.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: 4x − 12 = −2 gives x = +2.5 (A true). Structurally, two S atoms are +5 and two are 0, so R is false; +2.5 is just an average.

qa.q: Which decomposition reaction is NOT a redox reaction?
qa.a: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)
qa.e: In CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, Ca stays +2, C stays +4 and O stays −2.

qa.q: In P₄ + 3OH⁻ + 3H₂O → PH₃ + 3H₂PO₂⁻, phosphorus changes from 0 to:
qa.a: −3 and +1
qa.e: In PH₃, P = −3; in H₂PO₂⁻: 2(+1) + x + 2(−2) = −1 → x = +1. P is both reduced and oxidised.

qa.q: Which halogen is the strongest oxidising agent?
qa.a: F₂
qa.e: Oxidising power decreases down group 17: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

qa.q: What happens when chlorine water is added to potassium iodide solution?
qa.a: I₂ is liberated (brown colour)
qa.e: Cl₂ + 2KI → 2KCl + I₂; chlorine oxidises iodide to iodine.

qa.q: Cr₂O₃ + 2Al → Al₂O₃ + 2Cr is an example of:
qa.a: Metal displacement reaction
qa.e: Aluminium displaces chromium from its oxide; Al is oxidised (0 → +3) and Cr is reduced (+3 → 0).

qa.q: Which species cannot undergo disproportionation?
qa.a: ClO₄⁻
qa.e: In ClO₄⁻, Cl is +7, its maximum; it can only be reduced, not oxidised, so it cannot disproportionate.

qa.q: In 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, how many electrons are transferred per molecule of O₂ formed?
qa.e: Two O atoms go from −1 to 0 (losing 2 electrons in total) as one O₂ forms; another two O atoms gain those 2 electrons going to −2.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Br₂ can displace I₂ from KI solution but not Cl₂ from KCl solution. Reason (R): The oxidising power of halogens decreases in the order Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A halogen can oxidise only the halide ions of halogens below it in the group.

qa.q: How many electrons are gained per MnO₄⁻ ion when it is reduced to Mn²⁺ in acidic medium?
qa.e: Mn changes from +7 to +2: a gain of 5 electrons.

qa.q: In the balanced equation MnO₄⁻ + xFe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + xFe³⁺ + 4H₂O, what is x?
qa.e: MnO₄⁻ gains 5 e⁻; each Fe²⁺ loses 1 e⁻, so 5 Fe²⁺ are needed.

qa.q: How many H⁺ ions appear in the balanced equation 2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + yH⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O?
qa.e: 8H₂O contain 16 H, so 16H⁺ are needed. Charge check: −2 − 10 + 16 = +4 = 2 × (+2) ✓.

qa.q: In basic medium, after balancing as in acid, how are H⁺ ions removed?
qa.a: Add an equal number of OH⁻ to both sides and combine H⁺ + OH⁻ into H₂O
qa.e: Adding OH⁻ to both sides keeps the equation balanced while converting H⁺ into water.

qa.q: Which is the correctly balanced reduction half-reaction for dichromate in acid?
qa.a: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O
qa.e: Atoms: 2 Cr, 7 O, 14 H each side; charge: −2 + 14 − 6 = +6 = 2 × (+3).

qa.q: In 2MnO₄⁻ + I⁻ + H₂O → 2MnO₂ + IO₃⁻ + 2OH⁻ (basic medium), what is the change in ON of iodine?
qa.a: From −1 to +5
qa.e: I⁻ is −1; in IO₃⁻, x + 3(−2) = −1 → x = +5. Iodine loses 6 electrons, matching 2 × 3 gained by two MnO₄⁻.

qa.q: In the oxidation number method, what must be made equal before adding H₂O and H⁺?
qa.a: Total increase in ON and total decrease in ON
qa.e: Electrons lost must equal electrons gained, which means total ON increase = total ON decrease.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A correctly balanced redox equation must be balanced for both atoms and charge. Reason (R): Electrons lost in oxidation must equal electrons gained in reduction.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since electrons are neither created nor destroyed, matching electron transfer ensures charge balance as well as atom balance.

qa.q: Why is no external indicator needed in titrations with KMnO₄ in acidic medium?
qa.a: MnO₄⁻ is intensely coloured while Mn²⁺ is nearly colourless, so excess KMnO₄ shows pink
qa.e: Once all reductant is used, the next drop of purple MnO₄⁻ is not decolourised, giving a pink end point.

qa.q: 20.0 mL of 0.02 M KMnO₄ oxidises Fe²⁺ completely in acid (MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O). How many moles of Fe²⁺ reacted, in units of 10⁻³ mol?
In the same titration, the Fe²⁺ sample had a volume of 25.0 mL. What is [Fe²⁺] in mol L⁻¹?
In iodometric titration, what is the role of starch?
qa.a: It forms a blue complex with iodine; the colour disappears at the end point
qa.e: Starch is a sensitive indicator for iodine; when all I₂ has reacted with thiosulphate, the blue colour vanishes.

qa.q: How many moles of thiosulphate react with one mole of iodine?
qa.e: I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻.

qa.q: Which indicator is used in titrations of Fe²⁺ with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇?
qa.a: Diphenylamine
qa.e: The Cr₂O₇²⁻ → Cr³⁺ colour change (orange to green) is not sharp, so diphenylamine, a redox indicator, is used.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of the oxidation number concept?
qa.a: It treats bonds as fully ionic, so average values like +2.5 for S in S₄O₆²⁻ do not show the actual states
qa.e: ON is a bookkeeping device; averages can hide the fact that atoms of the same element are in different states.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In the reaction 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂ + I₂, iodide acts as a reducing agent. Reason (R): Iodide ions are oxidised from −1 to 0.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Two I⁻ lose electrons to form I₂ while Cu²⁺ is reduced to Cu⁺ (in Cu₂I₂).

qa.q: What is E°cell in volts for a cell made from Zn²⁺/Zn (E° = −0.76 V) and Ag⁺/Ag (E° = +0.80 V)?
qa.e: Silver is the cathode: E°cell = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V.

qa.q: What is the function of the salt bridge in a Daniell cell?
qa.a: It completes the circuit and keeps the two solutions electrically neutral
qa.e: Ions migrate through the salt bridge to balance charge as Zn²⁺ forms and Cu²⁺ is removed.

qa.q: In a Daniell cell, electrons flow through the external wire from:
qa.a: Zinc to copper
qa.e: Zinc is oxidised and releases electrons at the anode; they travel to the copper cathode where Cu²⁺ is reduced.

qa.q: Which is the strongest oxidising agent?
qa.e: The most positive reduction potential means the greatest tendency to gain electrons.

qa.q: What is the standard electrode potential of the standard hydrogen electrode?
qa.e: SHE is assigned 0.00 V at all temperatures by convention; it is the reference for all other E° values.

qa.q: Can a copper vessel be used to store a 1 M AgNO₃ solution? (E°: Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V, Ag⁺/Ag = +0.80 V)
qa.a: No, copper will reduce Ag⁺ and dissolve as Cu²⁺
qa.e: Ag⁺ has the higher E°, so it is reduced by Cu; E°cell = 0.80 − 0.34 = +0.46 V is positive, so the reaction is spontaneous.

qa.q: Which conditions define the standard electrode potential?
qa.a: 1 M ion concentration, gases at 1 bar, 298 K
qa.e: Standard conditions for electrode potentials are unit concentration (1 M), 1 bar pressure for gases and 298 K.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Zinc can displace hydrogen from dilute acids but copper cannot. Reason (R): E° of Zn²⁺/Zn is negative while E° of Cu²⁺/Cu is positive relative to the SHE.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Metals with E° below 0 are better reducing agents than H₂ and can reduce H⁺ to H₂; copper (+0.34 V) cannot.

qa.q: Who first synthesised an organic compound (urea) from an inorganic one?
qa.a: Friedrich Wöhler
qa.e: Wöhler (1828) heated ammonium cyanate to get urea.

qa.q: What is the hybridisation of carbon in CH₃–CH₃?
qa.a: sp³
qa.e: Each carbon forms four σ bonds (tetrahedral), so it is sp³.

qa.q: What is the percentage s character in the hybrid orbitals of the carbon atoms of ethyne?
qa.e: Ethyne carbons are sp hybridised: one s and one p, so 50% s character.

qa.q: Which carbon is the most electronegative?
qa.a: sp-hybridised carbon
qa.e: Greater s character keeps electrons closer to the nucleus, so sp carbon attracts electrons most.

qa.q: Why does a π bond make a molecule reactive?
qa.a: Its electrons are spread above and below the bond axis and easily available to attacking reagents
qa.e: Loosely held π electrons attract electrophiles, so double and triple bonds are reaction sites.

qa.q: In H₂C=O (methanal), what is the hybridisation of carbon?
qa.a: sp²
qa.e: Carbon has three σ bonds (two C–H, one C–O) and one π bond: sp², trigonal planar.

qa.q: Arrange C–H bond lengths in ethane, ethene and ethyne from longest to shortest.
qa.a: Ethane > ethene > ethyne
qa.e: As s character increases (sp³ → sp² → sp), the carbon's orbital is smaller, making the C–H bond shorter.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Free rotation is not possible about the C=C bond in ethene. Reason (R): Rotation would break the sideways overlap of p orbitals that forms the π bond.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The π bond requires parallel p orbitals; twisting breaks it, which needs a lot of energy.

qa.q: How many hydrogen atoms are on the carbon at a corner of a bond-line structure that joins two other carbons by single bonds?
qa.e: That carbon has two C–C bonds; it needs two more bonds, supplied by two H atoms.

qa.q: What is the condensed formula of the alkane whose bond-line formula is a zig-zag of five line segments?
qa.a: CH₃(CH₂)₄CH₃
qa.e: Five segments join six carbons: CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃, hexane.

qa.q: In a wedge–dash drawing, a normal (plain) line represents a bond that is:
qa.a: In the plane of the paper
qa.e: Plain lines lie in the plane; wedges come out of it and dashes go behind it.

qa.q: What is the molecular formula of cyclohexane, drawn as a hexagon in bond-line notation?
qa.a: C₆H₁₂
qa.e: Each of the six corners is a CH₂ group (two C–C bonds + two H), giving C₆H₁₂.

qa.q: Which is the condensed formula of 2-methylpropane?
qa.a: (CH₃)₃CH
qa.e: A central CH bonded to three CH₃ groups: (CH₃)₃CH, C₄H₁₀.

qa.q: A bond-line structure shows a four-carbon zig-zag with –OH on the second carbon. What is the compound?
qa.a: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, butan-2-ol
qa.e: Four carbons with OH on C2: butan-2-ol.

qa.q: How many carbon atoms are present in a bond-line formula drawn as a zig-zag of three segments with a branch line from the second corner?
qa.e: Three segments give four main-chain carbons; the branch adds one more carbon at its end: 5 carbons (2-methylbutane).

qa.q: Assertion (A): Bond-line formulas are convenient for large organic molecules. Reason (R): They omit carbon and hydrogen symbols but keep heteroatoms and the bonding pattern.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Removing routine C and H labels reduces clutter while all structural information remains recoverable.

qa.q: By what mass do successive members of a homologous series differ?
qa.e: They differ by one –CH₂– unit: 12 + 2 = 14 u.

qa.q: Which is a heterocyclic compound?
qa.a: Pyridine
qa.e: Pyridine has a nitrogen atom in its ring; the others have only carbon in their rings.

qa.q: What does the word root 'pent' signify in an IUPAC name?
qa.a: Five carbon atoms in the parent chain
qa.e: Word roots show chain length: pent = 5 carbons.

qa.q: Formic acid gets its common name from:
qa.a: Red ants (Latin formica)
qa.e: It was first obtained by distilling red ants.

qa.q: Which compound is alicyclic?
qa.a: Cyclopentane
qa.e: Cyclopentane is a ring of carbons without aromatic character.

qa.q: In the IUPAC name 'butan-2-one', the secondary suffix '-one' indicates:
qa.a: A ketone group
qa.e: '-one' is the suffix for a ketone (>C=O) group; here it is on C2 of a four-carbon chain.

qa.q: Which statement about members of a homologous series is correct?
qa.a: They have the same functional group and similar chemical properties
qa.e: Chemical properties are similar; physical properties change gradually with chain length.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Methanol, ethanol and propan-1-ol belong to the same homologous series. Reason (R): They have the same –OH functional group and differ by CH₂ units.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Same functional group plus a regular CH₂ difference defines a homologous series.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
qa.a: 2-Methylbutane
qa.e: Longest chain has 4 carbons with a methyl on C2 (numbering from the nearer end).

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₄C?
qa.a: 2,2-Dimethylpropane
qa.e: The longest chain is three carbons with two methyls on C2.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH(C₂H₅)CH₂CH₂CH₃?
qa.a: 4-Ethyl-3-methylheptane
qa.e: Longest chain: 7 carbons (heptane). Numbering gives methyl on C3 and ethyl on C4 (locants 3,4 versus 4,5). Alphabetical order: ethyl before methyl.

qa.q: The IUPAC name of the tert-butyl group is:
qa.a: 1,1-Dimethylethyl
qa.e: –C(CH₃)₃: an ethyl group whose C1 carries two extra methyls.

qa.q: Which name follows the lowest locant rule correctly?
qa.a: 2,3,5-Trimethylhexane
qa.e: For this hexane, numbering from one end gives 2,3,5 and from the other 2,4,5; at the first point of difference 3 < 4, so 2,3,5 is correct.

qa.q: How many carbon atoms are present in 3-ethyl-2-methylpentane?
qa.e: Pentane (5) + ethyl (2) + methyl (1) = 8 carbons (C₈H₁₈).

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of the cyclic compound with a methyl and an ethyl group on adjacent ring carbons of cyclohexane?
qa.a: 1-Ethyl-2-methylcyclohexane
qa.e: Both substituents get locants 1 and 2 either way; ethyl comes first alphabetically, so it receives the lower number.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In alphabetising substituents, 'di' in dimethyl is ignored. Reason (R): Multiplying prefixes like di and tri only show how many identical groups are present.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Dimethyl is alphabetised under 'm'; e.g. 4-ethyl-2,2-dimethylhexane, with ethyl before dimethyl.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO?
qa.a: Butanal
qa.e: Four carbons including the CHO carbon (C1), aldehyde suffix '-al'.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃COCH₂CH₃?
qa.a: Butan-2-one
qa.e: Four-carbon chain; C=O at C2 from the nearer end.

qa.q: In a compound containing both –OH and –CHO groups, which becomes the suffix?
qa.a: –CHO (as -al)
qa.e: Aldehyde outranks alcohol, so –CHO is the suffix and –OH becomes 'hydroxy': e.g. 3-hydroxypropanal.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of HOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOH?
qa.a: Butanedioic acid
qa.e: Four carbons including both COOH carbons, with two acid groups: butanedioic acid (succinic acid).

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of a benzene ring carrying a methyl group and a nitro group on adjacent carbons (CH₃ on C1)?
qa.a: 1-Methyl-2-nitrobenzene
qa.e: Locants 1,2 either way; alphabetical order gives methyl the lower number: 1-methyl-2-nitrobenzene (o-nitrotoluene).

qa.q: Which prefix denotes a –CN group when it is not the principal group?
qa.a: Cyano
qa.e: As a substituent, –CN is 'cyano'; as the principal group it is the suffix '-nitrile'.

qa.q: 1,3-Dichlorobenzene is also called:
qa.a: m-Dichlorobenzene
qa.e: 1,3 relationship = meta (m-).

qa.q: Assertion (A): CH₂=CH–CH₂–OH is named prop-2-en-1-ol. Reason (R): The –OH group gets priority for the lowest locant over the double bond.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Numbering from the CH₂OH end gives OH locant 1 and the double bond starts at C2. The principal group is numbered first.

qa.q: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are examples of:
qa.a: Chain isomers
qa.e: They have the same formula, C₅H₁₂, but different carbon skeletons.

qa.q: Which pair are functional group isomers?
qa.a: Ethanol and methoxymethane
qa.e: Both are C₂H₆O but one is an alcohol and the other an ether.

qa.q: How many structural isomers are possible for C₅H₁₂?
qa.e: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.

qa.q: Metamerism is shown by compounds that:
qa.a: Have different alkyl groups on either side of the same functional group
qa.e: Ethers, ketones, amines and esters show metamerism when alkyl groups around the functional group change.

qa.q: But-1-ene and but-2-ene are:
qa.a: Position isomers
qa.e: Same chain and functional group (C=C) but the double bond is in a different position.

qa.q: Why does but-2-ene show geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism but but-1-ene does not?
qa.a: In but-2-ene each double-bonded carbon has two different groups; in but-1-ene one carbon has two identical H atoms
qa.e: Cis–trans isomers need restricted rotation plus two different groups on each carbon of the double bond.

qa.q: Which pair are metamers?
qa.a: CH₃–O–CH₂CH₂CH₃ and CH₃CH₂–O–CH₂CH₃
qa.e: Methoxypropane and ethoxyethane (both C₄H₁₀O ethers) have different alkyl groups on either side of the –O– group.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Propanal and propanone are isomers. Reason (R): Both have the molecular formula C₃H₆O.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Same molecular formula with different structures (aldehyde vs ketone) makes them functional group isomers.

qa.q: What is the hybridisation and shape of a methyl carbocation, CH₃⁺?
qa.a: sp², trigonal planar
qa.e: Carbon uses three sp² orbitals for C–H bonds and has an empty p orbital.

qa.q: Which carbocation is the most stable?
qa.a: (CH₃)₃C⁺
qa.e: The tertiary cation has three electron-releasing methyl groups (and nine hyperconjugating C–H bonds).

qa.q: Homolytic cleavage of a covalent bond produces:
qa.a: Free radicals
qa.e: Each fragment keeps one electron, giving neutral species with unpaired electrons.

qa.q: How many electrons are in the valence shell of the positively charged carbon in a carbocation?
qa.e: It forms three bonds (six electrons) and has an empty orbital, so it is electron deficient.

qa.q: Heterolysis of CH₃–Br in which bromine keeps the bonding pair gives:
qa.a: CH₃⁺ and Br⁻
qa.e: Bromine is more electronegative and takes both electrons, leaving the carbon positive.

qa.q: Which correctly orders alkyl free radicals by stability?
qa.a: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl
qa.e: Like carbocations, radicals are stabilised by more alkyl groups (hyperconjugation).

qa.q: What is the shape of a carbanion such as CH₃⁻?
qa.a: Pyramidal (sp³)
qa.e: Carbon has three bond pairs and one lone pair, like the nitrogen in NH₃.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Tertiary carbocations are more stable than primary carbocations. Reason (R): Alkyl groups release electrons and disperse the positive charge.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: More alkyl groups mean more +I and hyperconjugation, spreading the charge and lowering energy.

qa.q: Which species is a nucleophile?
qa.a: NH₃
qa.e: NH₃ has a lone pair it can donate; the others are electron deficient.

qa.q: Which species is an electrophile?
qa.a: AlCl₃
qa.e: Al in AlCl₃ has only six valence electrons and accepts an electron pair.

qa.q: What does a full-headed curved arrow represent in a mechanism?
qa.a: Movement of an electron pair
qa.e: Full-headed arrows track pairs; half-headed (fish-hook) arrows track single electrons.

qa.q: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃–CH₃ (Ni catalyst) is an example of:
qa.a: Addition reaction
qa.e: Two H atoms add across the double bond.

qa.q: In CH₃Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CN + Br⁻, the curved arrow should start from:
qa.a: The lone pair on the carbon of CN⁻ and point to the carbon of CH₃Br
qa.e: Arrows start at an electron source (the nucleophile's lone pair) and end at the electron-poor atom; a second arrow moves the C–Br pair onto Br.

qa.q: Why is the carbonyl carbon in >C=O an electrophilic centre?
qa.a: Oxygen is more electronegative and pulls electron density away, leaving carbon partially positive
qa.e: Polarisation C^δ⁺=O^δ⁻ makes the carbon attractive to nucleophiles.

qa.q: CH₃CH₂Br + KOH (alcoholic) → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O is a/an:
qa.a: Elimination reaction
qa.e: H and Br are removed from adjacent carbons to form a C=C double bond.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Water can act as a nucleophile. Reason (R): The oxygen atom in water has lone pairs of electrons.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Any species with an available lone pair can donate it to an electrophile.

qa.q: Which group shows a +I effect?
qa.a: –CH₃
qa.e: Alkyl groups release electron density through σ bonds; the others withdraw it.

qa.q: Why is chloroacetic acid stronger than acetic acid?
qa.a: The −I effect of Cl stabilises the carboxylate anion
qa.e: Withdrawing electron density spreads the negative charge of ClCH₂COO⁻, making ionisation easier.

qa.q: Which acid is stronger, HCOOH or CH₃COOH, and why?
qa.a: HCOOH, because CH₃ (+I) destabilises the acetate ion
qa.e: Electron release by CH₃ intensifies the negative charge on CH₃COO⁻, so acetic acid is weaker.

qa.q: The inductive effect becomes negligible after about how many bonds from the group causing it?
qa.e: Inductive polarisation fades quickly along a chain and is very small beyond about three bonds.

qa.q: Which statement about the electromeric effect is correct?
qa.a: It is temporary and occurs only in the presence of an attacking reagent
qa.e: It is a complete shift of a π electron pair caused by an approaching reagent and disappears when the reagent is removed.

qa.q: When H⁺ attacks ethene, the π electrons shift towards the carbon to which H⁺ attaches. This is:
qa.a: +E effect
qa.e: In the +E effect, the π pair moves to the atom that bonds with the attacking reagent.

qa.q: Which is the strongest acid?
qa.a: F₃CCOOH
qa.e: Three highly electronegative F atoms give the strongest −I effect and the most stable anion.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The inductive effect is a permanent effect. Reason (R): It arises from the difference in electronegativity of atoms joined by σ bonds and is present even without any reagent.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Bond polarity is a fixed property of the molecule, so the inductive effect is always there.

qa.q: How many α-hydrogens does the tert-butyl carbocation have?
qa.e: Three CH₃ groups are attached to C⁺, each with 3 H: 9 α-H for hyperconjugation.

qa.q: Which group shows a −R effect?
qa.a: –NO₂
qa.e: The nitro group pulls π electrons from a conjugated system towards itself.

qa.q: Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?
qa.a: The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance; ethoxide is not
qa.e: The negative charge on phenoxide is delocalised over the benzene ring, stabilising it.

qa.q: Which is NOT a rule for writing resonance structures?
qa.a: Atoms may change positions between structures
qa.e: Moving atoms would give a different compound (an isomer), not a resonance structure.

qa.q: Hyperconjugation involves delocalisation of:
qa.a: σ electrons of a C–H bond adjacent to an unsaturated or electron-deficient carbon
qa.e: σ(C–H) electrons overlap with an adjacent empty p orbital or π system ('no-bond resonance').

qa.q: Which alkene is the most stable according to hyperconjugation?
qa.a: (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂
qa.e: 2,3-Dimethylbut-2-ene has 12 α-hydrogens, the most hyperconjugative structures.

qa.q: Arrange in increasing acid strength: ethanol, phenol, p-nitrophenol.
qa.a: Ethanol < phenol < p-nitrophenol
qa.e: Phenoxide is resonance stabilised; a para-NO₂ group (−R and −I) stabilises it further.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In chlorobenzene, Cl shows a +R effect. Reason (R): A lone pair on chlorine can be delocalised into the benzene ring.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Donation of a lone pair into the ring is a +R (mesomeric) effect, though Cl also has a −I effect.

qa.q: A spot travels 2.4 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm. What is its Rf value?
qa.e: Rf = 2.4/8.0 = 0.3. Rf is always less than 1.

qa.q: Which method is used to purify glycerol, which decomposes at its boiling point?
qa.a: Distillation under reduced pressure
qa.e: Lowering the pressure lowers the boiling point, so glycerol distils without decomposing.

qa.q: Why does a steam-volatile liquid distil below its normal boiling point in steam distillation?
qa.a: The mixture boils when the sum of the vapour pressures of the liquid and water equals atmospheric pressure
qa.e: Because each component contributes vapour pressure, their sum reaches 1 atm at a lower temperature than either alone.

qa.q: Which pair is best separated by fractional distillation?
qa.a: Two miscible liquids with close boiling points
qa.e: A fractionating column allows repeated vaporisation–condensation, separating liquids whose boiling points are close.

qa.q: In paper chromatography, what acts as the stationary phase?
qa.a: Water held in the cellulose of the paper
qa.e: Paper chromatography is partition chromatography; water trapped in paper fibres is stationary.

qa.q: What is the role of activated charcoal during crystallisation?
qa.a: It adsorbs coloured impurities
qa.e: Activated charcoal has a huge surface area that adsorbs coloured impurities, which are then filtered off.

qa.q: How can colourless compounds be located on a TLC plate?
qa.a: Under ultraviolet light or by exposing the plate to iodine vapour
qa.e: Many organic compounds fluoresce or show dark spots under UV, and iodine vapour stains them brown.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Aniline can be purified by steam distillation. Reason (R): Aniline is steam-volatile and immiscible with water.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both conditions are required for steam distillation, and aniline meets both.

qa.q: Which mixture can be separated by sublimation?
qa.a: Naphthalene and common salt
qa.e: Naphthalene changes directly from solid to vapour on heating and re-forms as solid on a cool surface, while common salt stays behind.

qa.q: In differential extraction, an aqueous solution of an organic compound is shaken with an immiscible organic solvent in a separating funnel. Where does most of the compound end up?
qa.a: In the layer of the solvent in which it is more soluble
qa.e: The compound distributes itself between the two immiscible liquids and moves mostly into the solvent in which it is more soluble; the layers are then run off separately.

qa.q: In Lassaigne's test for nitrogen, the Prussian blue colour is due to:
qa.a: Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃
qa.e: Cyanide from NaCN forms hexacyanidoferrate(II), which combines with Fe³⁺ to give Prussian blue.

qa.q: Why is the sodium fusion extract boiled with HNO₃ before testing for halogens with AgNO₃?
qa.a: To decompose NaCN and Na₂S, which would otherwise precipitate with Ag⁺
qa.e: Ag⁺ would also precipitate AgCN or Ag₂S; boiling with acid expels HCN and H₂S first.

qa.q: Which observation confirms bromine in an organic compound?
qa.a: Pale yellow precipitate with AgNO₃, sparingly soluble in ammonia
qa.e: AgBr is pale yellow and only sparingly soluble in NH₃; AgCl is white and soluble; AgI is yellow and insoluble.

qa.q: How is hydrogen detected when an organic compound is heated with CuO?
qa.a: Water formed turns anhydrous copper sulphate blue
qa.e: Hydrogen is oxidised to water, which hydrates white anhydrous CuSO₄ to blue.

qa.q: A violet colour with sodium nitroprusside indicates the presence of:
qa.a: Sulphur
qa.e: Sulphide ions from Na₂S react with sodium nitroprusside to give a violet colour.

qa.q: Why must organic compounds be fused with sodium before testing for N, S and halogens?
qa.a: To convert covalently bonded elements into ionic forms (NaCN, Na₂S, NaX) that give ionic tests
qa.e: Ionic tests need ions in solution; fusion with sodium breaks covalent bonds and forms soluble sodium salts.

qa.q: Which reagent is used to test for phosphorus after oxidising it to phosphate?
qa.a: Ammonium molybdate with nitric acid
qa.e: Phosphate forms a yellow precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate with ammonium molybdate in HNO₃.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Lassaigne's test for nitrogen is not shown by hydrazine (NH₂NH₂). Reason (R): Hydrazine has no carbon, so NaCN cannot form during fusion.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The test depends on forming cyanide, which needs both carbon and nitrogen.

qa.q: 0.25 g of an organic compound gave 0.33 g of CO₂ on combustion. What is the percentage of carbon, to two decimal places?
In the Dumas method, 0.3 g of a compound gave 44.8 mL of N₂ at STP. What is the percentage of nitrogen, to two decimal places?
In Kjeldahl's method, the ammonia from 0.40 g of a compound neutralised 12.5 mL of 0.5 M H₂SO₄. What is the percentage of nitrogen?
In Liebig's method, which substance absorbs the water formed?
qa.a: Anhydrous calcium chloride
qa.e: Anhydrous CaCl₂ absorbs water; KOH (in a U-tube) absorbs CO₂.

qa.q: Why can Kjeldahl's method not be used for nitrobenzene?
qa.a: The nitrogen of the nitro group is not converted into ammonium sulphate
qa.e: Nitro, azo and ring nitrogen are not fully converted to (NH₄)₂SO₄ under Kjeldahl digestion.

qa.q: 0.45 g of an organic compound gave 0.27 g of water on combustion. What is the percentage of hydrogen, to two decimal places?
In the Dumas method, why is the gas collected over KOH solution?
qa.a: KOH absorbs CO₂, leaving pure nitrogen to be measured
qa.e: The CO₂ used to sweep the apparatus and formed by combustion is absorbed, so the gas volume is nitrogen only.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In Liebig's method, the percentage of carbon is calculated as (12/44) × (mass of CO₂/mass of compound) × 100. Reason (R): 44 g of CO₂ contains 12 g of carbon.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The fraction of carbon in CO₂ is 12/44, which converts CO₂ mass to carbon mass.

qa.q: 0.2 g of a compound gave 0.287 g of AgCl in the Carius method. What is the percentage of chlorine?
0.16 g of a compound gave 0.233 g of BaSO₄. What is the percentage of sulphur?
0.2 g of a compound gave 0.111 g of Mg₂P₂O₇ (M = 222). What is the percentage of phosphorus?
In the Carius method for halogens, the compound is heated with:
qa.a: Fuming HNO₃ and AgNO₃ in a sealed tube
qa.e: Fuming nitric acid destroys the organic matter and converts halogen to halide, precipitated as AgX by silver nitrate.

qa.q: A compound contains 40% C and 6.7% H, and no other element besides oxygen. What is %O?
In the direct estimation of oxygen, CO is converted to CO₂ by passing it over:
qa.a: I₂O₅
qa.e: I₂O₅ + 5CO → I₂ + 5CO₂; the CO₂ formed is measured to find oxygen.

qa.q: Which factor converts a mass of AgBr into a mass of bromine (Ag = 108, Br = 80)?
qa.e: Molar mass AgBr = 188; the bromine fraction is 80/188.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In the Carius method, the sealed tube must be cooled before opening. Reason (R): The tube contains gases under high pressure after heating.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Heating fuming HNO₃ with organic matter produces gases; opening a hot tube could burst it, so it is cooled and opened behind a screen.

qa.q: What is the general formula of alkanes?
qa.a: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
qa.e: Each alkane is saturated; e.g. butane, C₄H₁₀, has 2 × 4 + 2 = 10 hydrogens.

qa.q: How many hydrogen atoms are present in an alkane with 10 carbon atoms?
qa.e: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 10 gives H = 22 (decane, C₁₀H₂₂).

qa.q: In 2,2,4-trimethylpentane, how many primary carbon atoms are there?
qa.e: Three CH₃ on C2 (counting C1), the CH₃ on C4 and C5: five methyl carbons, each bonded to one carbon.

qa.q: A tertiary carbon atom is bonded to how many other carbon atoms?
qa.e: Primary 1, secondary 2, tertiary 3, quaternary 4.

qa.q: Which is the main component of CNG?
qa.a: Methane
qa.e: Compressed natural gas is mainly methane; LPG is mainly butane and propane.

qa.q: Which hydrocarbon is unsaturated?
qa.a: Propene
qa.e: Propene has a C=C double bond; the others contain only single bonds.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₂CH–CH(CH₃)₂?
qa.a: 2,3-Dimethylbutane
qa.e: Longest chain has 4 carbons with methyls on C2 and C3.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Butane and 2-methylpropane are isomers. Reason (R): Both have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀ but different carbon skeletons.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Same formula and different chains make them chain isomers.

qa.q: Which alkane is formed by heating sodium propanoate with soda lime?
qa.a: Ethane
qa.e: Decarboxylation removes one carbon: CH₃CH₂COONa → CH₃CH₃.

qa.q: What is the product of the Wurtz reaction of ethyl bromide with sodium in dry ether?
qa.a: Butane
qa.e: 2C₂H₅Br + 2Na → C₂H₅–C₂H₅ + 2NaBr; the product has 4 carbons.

qa.q: Why is the Wurtz reaction not suitable for preparing an alkane with an odd number of carbons, such as propane?
qa.a: A mixture of two different alkyl halides gives a mixture of three alkanes that is hard to separate
qa.e: CH₃Br + C₂H₅Br with Na gives ethane, propane and butane together.

qa.q: In Kolbe's electrolysis of sodium ethanoate, which alkane is formed and at which electrode?
qa.a: Ethane at the anode
qa.e: Acetate ions are oxidised at the anode to CH₃• radicals, which combine to form ethane; H₂ forms at the cathode.

qa.q: Which reagent reduces CH₃CH₂Cl to ethane?
qa.a: Zn and dilute HCl
qa.e: Zn/HCl provides hydrogen that replaces chlorine. Na in ether would give butane (Wurtz).

qa.q: How many moles of H₂ are needed to convert 1 mol of ethyne fully into ethane?
qa.e: CH≡CH + 2H₂ → CH₃CH₃: each π bond takes one H₂.

qa.q: Which method gives an alkane with one carbon fewer than the starting compound?
qa.a: Decarboxylation with soda lime
qa.e: Soda lime removes –COONa as Na₂CO₃, shortening the chain by one carbon.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Methane cannot be prepared by Kolbe's electrolysis. Reason (R): Kolbe's electrolysis joins two alkyl groups, so the product has at least two carbons.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Even the smallest carboxylate (acetate) gives ethane, so methane is impossible by this method.

qa.q: Why does pentane boil at a higher temperature than 2,2-dimethylpropane?
qa.a: Pentane has a larger surface area and stronger van der Waals forces
qa.e: Both are C₅H₁₂; the straight chain has more contact area, so intermolecular forces are stronger.

qa.q: Which step is a termination step in the chlorination of methane?
qa.a: •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl
qa.e: Two radicals combine and no new radical is formed, so the chain stops.

qa.q: Why is iodination of alkanes carried out with an oxidising agent such as HIO₃?
qa.a: The reaction is reversible; the oxidising agent removes HI formed
qa.e: HI reduces the iodoalkane back to the alkane; oxidising it to I₂ drives the reaction forward.

qa.q: What is the product when methane and oxygen are passed over heated Mo₂O₃?
qa.a: Methanal (HCHO)
qa.e: Controlled oxidation over molybdenum oxide gives methanal: CH₄ + O₂ → HCHO + H₂O.

qa.q: n-Hexane heated at 773 K and 10–20 atm over Cr₂O₃ on alumina gives:
qa.a: Benzene
qa.e: This is aromatisation (dehydrogenation and cyclisation) of n-hexane to benzene.

qa.q: Which reaction gives CO and H₂ (synthesis gas)?
qa.a: CH₄ + H₂O over Ni at 1273 K
qa.e: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂ is the steam reforming of methane.

qa.q: Arrange in order of ease of free-radical substitution of hydrogen: 1° H, 2° H, 3° H.
qa.e: The radicals formed are stabilised in the order 3° > 2° > 1°, so 3° hydrogens are replaced most easily.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Chlorination of methane does not occur in the dark at room temperature. Reason (R): Light is needed to split Cl₂ into chlorine free radicals.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Without the initiation step (homolysis of Cl–Cl by hν or heat), the chain reaction cannot start.

qa.q: Which conformation of ethane is the most stable?
qa.a: Staggered
qa.e: Staggered keeps C–H bond pairs on adjacent carbons farthest apart, minimising torsional strain.

qa.q: The energy difference between eclipsed and staggered ethane is about:
qa.a: 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹
qa.e: The barrier is small, about 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹, so rotation is nearly free at room temperature.

qa.q: What is torsional strain?
qa.a: Repulsion between electron clouds of C–H bonds on adjacent carbons when they are eclipsed
qa.e: It is greatest in the eclipsed form and least in the staggered form.

qa.q: Why can the conformations of ethane not be isolated at room temperature?
qa.a: The energy barrier to rotation is very small, so they interconvert rapidly
qa.e: About 12.5 kJ mol⁻¹ is easily supplied by thermal energy at room temperature.

qa.q: In a Newman projection of ethane, the front carbon is represented by:
qa.a: A point where three C–H bonds meet
qa.e: The front carbon is a dot with three bonds; the back carbon is a circle with three bonds coming from its edge.

qa.q: What is the dihedral angle between C–H bonds on adjacent carbons in the eclipsed conformation?
qa.e: In the eclipsed form, the back C–H bonds lie exactly behind the front ones.

qa.q: Conformations differ from each other in:
qa.a: The spatial arrangement of atoms produced by rotation about a single bond
qa.e: Conformers have the same bonding; they differ only by rotation about a σ bond.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rotation about the C–C bond in ethane is almost free. Reason (R): The C–C bond in ethane is a σ bond, symmetrical about the bond axis.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Rotation does not reduce σ overlap; only a small torsional barrier opposes it.

qa.q: Which alkene shows geometrical isomerism?
qa.a: But-2-ene
qa.e: In but-2-ene each double-bonded carbon has H and CH₃, two different groups.

qa.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)=CH₂?
qa.a: 2-Methylbut-1-ene
qa.e: Longest chain containing C=C has 4 carbons; numbering from the =CH₂ end puts the double bond at C1 and methyl at C2.

qa.q: Which isomer of but-2-ene has zero dipole moment?
qa.a: trans-But-2-ene
qa.e: In the trans form, the two C–CH₃ bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.

qa.q: How many σ and π bonds are in ethene?
qa.a: 5σ and 1π
qa.e: Four C–H σ bonds + one C–C σ bond, plus one π bond in C=C.

qa.q: Why is the C=C bond enthalpy (681 kJ mol⁻¹) less than twice the C–C bond enthalpy (348 kJ mol⁻¹)?
qa.a: The π bond formed by sideways overlap is weaker than a σ bond
qa.e: Sideways overlap is less effective than head-on overlap, so the π component adds less than a full σ bond.

qa.q: How many structural isomers (ignoring geometrical isomers) are possible for alkenes of formula C₄H₈?
qa.e: But-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene.

qa.q: Which property is usually higher for the trans isomer of an alkene than for its cis isomer?
qa.a: Melting point
qa.e: The more symmetrical trans form packs better in the crystal lattice, so it melts at a higher temperature.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Propene does not show geometrical isomerism. Reason (R): One carbon of its double bond carries two identical hydrogen atoms.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: For cis–trans isomers, each double-bonded carbon must carry two different groups; =CH₂ fails this.

qa.q: Which reagent converts but-2-yne into trans-but-2-ene?
qa.a: Sodium in liquid ammonia
qa.e: Na/liquid NH₃ gives anti addition of hydrogen, forming the trans alkene.

qa.q: What is the major product when 2-bromopropane is heated with alcoholic KOH?
qa.a: Propene
qa.e: Alcoholic KOH eliminates HBr from adjacent carbons: CH₃CHBrCH₃ → CH₃CH=CH₂.

qa.q: 1,2-Dibromoethane reacts with zinc dust to give:
qa.a: Ethene
qa.e: Zn removes both bromine atoms from adjacent carbons (dehalogenation): CH₂Br–CH₂Br + Zn → CH₂=CH₂ + ZnBr₂.

qa.q: What is the role of concentrated H₂SO₄ when ethanol is heated with it to form ethene?
qa.a: Dehydrating agent (acid catalyst) removing water
qa.e: It protonates –OH and helps remove a water molecule, forming the C=C bond.

qa.q: Which is the composition of Lindlar's catalyst?
qa.a: Palladium on charcoal partially deactivated by sulphur compounds or quinoline
qa.e: The poisoned Pd catalyst stops hydrogenation at the alkene stage.

qa.q: Which alkene has the highest boiling point?
qa.a: Hex-1-ene
qa.e: Boiling point rises with chain length because van der Waals forces increase.

qa.q: Dehydrohalogenation and acidic dehydration of alcohols are both examples of:
qa.a: β-Elimination reactions
qa.e: In both, atoms are removed from two adjacent carbons to create a double bond.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Hydrogenation of an alkyne over Lindlar's catalyst stops at the alkene. Reason (R): The partially poisoned catalyst is not active enough to hydrogenate the alkene further.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Deactivated Pd reduces the more reactive triple bond but not the resulting double bond.

qa.q: What is the major product when HBr adds to propene in the absence of peroxide?
qa.a: 2-Bromopropane
qa.e: Markovnikov's rule: Br attaches to the double-bond carbon with fewer H (C2), through the more stable 2° carbocation.

qa.q: In the presence of benzoyl peroxide, HBr adds to propene to give:
qa.a: 1-Bromopropane
qa.e: The peroxide effect gives anti-Markovnikov addition by a free-radical mechanism.

qa.q: Why is no peroxide effect observed with HCl?
qa.a: The H–Cl bond is too strong to be broken homolytically by the radicals formed
qa.e: With bond enthalpy 430.5 kJ mol⁻¹, H–Cl is not cleaved by the free radicals, so the chain cannot start.

qa.q: Which observation confirms unsaturation in an organic compound?
qa.a: Reddish-orange bromine in CCl₄ is decolourised
qa.e: Br₂ adds across C=C or C≡C bonds, so its colour disappears.

qa.q: In the electrophilic addition of HBr to propene, why does the secondary carbocation form rather than the primary one?
qa.a: The secondary carbocation is more stable (hyperconjugation and +I effect of two alkyl groups)
qa.e: The more stable intermediate forms faster, which leads to the Markovnikov product.

qa.q: Arrange hydrogen halides in order of reactivity towards alkenes.
qa.a: HI > HBr > HCl
qa.e: Weaker H–X bonds (HI weakest) give H⁺ more readily.

qa.q: What is the major product when HBr adds to 2-methylpropene without peroxide?
qa.a: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane
qa.e: H⁺ adds to =CH₂ forming the tertiary carbocation; Br⁻ attaches to it.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr takes place in the presence of peroxides. Reason (R): Peroxides change the mechanism from ionic to free-radical, and Br• adds to give the more stable radical.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Br• adds to the less substituted carbon so that the more stable radical forms; H is then taken from HBr.

qa.q: What are the products of ozonolysis of propene?
qa.a: Ethanal and methanal
qa.e: CH₃CH=CH₂ splits at C=C: CH₃CH=O and O=CH₂.

qa.q: An alkene gives only ethanal on ozonolysis. What is it?
qa.a: But-2-ene
qa.e: CH₃CH=CHCH₃ splits into two identical CH₃CHO fragments.

qa.q: What is Baeyer's reagent and what does it show?
qa.a: Cold dilute aqueous KMnO₄; its purple colour fades with unsaturated compounds
qa.e: Alkenes reduce cold dilute KMnO₄ while forming glycols, so the purple colour disappears.

qa.q: Acid-catalysed hydration of propene gives mainly:
qa.a: Propan-2-ol
qa.e: Markovnikov addition: H goes to =CH₂, OH to the middle carbon via the 2° carbocation.

qa.q: What is formed when but-2-ene is oxidised by hot acidic KMnO₄?
qa.a: Two molecules of ethanoic acid
qa.e: Vigorous oxidation cleaves C=C; each CH₃CH= fragment becomes CH₃COOH.

qa.q: Which polymer is formed from propene?
qa.a: Polypropene
qa.e: Propene molecules link through their double bonds to form polypropene.

qa.q: Ozonolysis of an alkene gives CH₃COCH₃ and HCHO. The alkene is:
qa.a: 2-Methylpropene
qa.e: Joining (CH₃)₂C= and =CH₂ gives (CH₃)₂C=CH₂.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ozonolysis is used to locate the position of a double bond. Reason (R): The double bond is cleaved and each of its carbons becomes a carbonyl carbon.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Identifying the carbonyl fragments tells exactly which carbons were joined by C=C.

qa.q: What is the general formula of alkynes?
qa.a: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂
qa.e: Each triple bond removes four H atoms compared with the alkane: e.g. ethyne C₂H₂.

qa.q: How many σ and π bonds are there in the C≡C bond of ethyne?
qa.a: 1σ and 2π
qa.e: One sp–sp σ bond plus two π bonds from sideways overlap of two pairs of p orbitals.

qa.q: What gas is produced when water is added to calcium carbide?
qa.a: Ethyne
qa.e: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂.

qa.q: Why is the hydrogen of ethyne acidic?
qa.a: The sp carbon has 50% s character and holds the C–H electrons closely, stabilising the acetylide ion
qa.e: High s character makes the carbon electronegative, so H⁺ can be removed to give HC≡C⁻.

qa.q: Which alkyne does NOT react with sodium metal?
qa.a: But-2-yne
qa.e: But-2-yne has no hydrogen on a triple-bonded carbon.

qa.q: What is the H–C–C bond angle in ethyne?
qa.e: sp hybridisation gives a linear molecule.

qa.q: How many structural isomers are possible for alkynes of formula C₅H₈?
qa.e: Pent-1-yne, pent-2-yne and 3-methylbut-1-yne.

qa.q: Assertion (A): 1,2-Dibromoethane can be converted to ethyne. Reason (R): Two successive dehydrohalogenations (alcoholic KOH, then NaNH₂) remove two molecules of HBr.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: BrCH₂CH₂Br → CH₂=CHBr → HC≡CH.

qa.q: What is the product of acid-catalysed hydration of ethyne in the presence of Hg²⁺?
qa.a: Ethanal
qa.e: The enol CH₂=CHOH formed first rearranges into the more stable aldehyde CH₃CHO.

qa.q: Hydration of propyne (Hg²⁺/H⁺) gives:
qa.a: Propanone
qa.e: Markovnikov addition places OH on the middle carbon; the enol tautomerises to the ketone CH₃COCH₃.

qa.q: What is the product when excess HBr adds to ethyne?
qa.a: 1,1-Dibromoethane
qa.e: In the second step, Br⁻ adds to the carbon that already has Br (Markovnikov), giving CH₃CHBr₂.

qa.q: How many molecules of ethyne combine to form one molecule of benzene in cyclic polymerisation?
qa.e: 3C₂H₂ → C₆H₆: six carbons and six hydrogens.

qa.q: Under what conditions is ethyne converted into benzene?
qa.a: Passing through a red-hot iron tube at 873 K
qa.e: Cyclic trimerisation occurs on a hot iron surface at about 873 K.

qa.q: Why do alkynes decolourise more bromine per mole than alkenes?
qa.a: A triple bond has two π bonds, so it can add two molecules of Br₂
qa.e: Each π bond takes one Br₂; C≡C takes two, C=C takes one.

qa.q: Polyacetylene is notable because it:
qa.a: Conducts electricity
qa.e: Its long chain of alternating double bonds lets it conduct electricity when suitably treated.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Hydration of ethyne gives ethanal and not vinyl alcohol. Reason (R): Vinyl alcohol (CH₂=CHOH) is an unstable enol that rearranges to the more stable carbonyl compound.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Enols with –OH on a C=C carbon tautomerise to aldehydes or ketones.

qa.q: What is the length of each C–C bond in benzene?
qa.a: 139 pm
qa.e: All bonds are identical and intermediate between single (154 pm) and double (133 pm) bonds, because of resonance.

qa.q: According to Hückel's rule, how many π electrons does an aromatic ring with n = 2 contain?
qa.e: 4n + 2 = 4(2) + 2 = 10 (as in naphthalene).

qa.q: Which compound is NOT aromatic?
qa.a: Cyclooctatetraene
qa.e: Cyclooctatetraene has 8 π electrons (not 4n + 2) and is non-planar (tub-shaped).

qa.q: What is the hybridisation of each carbon in benzene?
qa.a: sp²
qa.e: Each carbon forms three σ bonds (two C–C, one C–H) at 120° and keeps one p orbital for the π cloud.

qa.q: How many aromatic isomers have the formula C₈H₁₀?
qa.e: Ethylbenzene and o-, m- and p-xylene (dimethylbenzenes).

qa.q: Benzene can be prepared from phenol by:
qa.a: Passing phenol vapour over heated zinc dust
qa.e: Zinc dust removes oxygen: C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO.

qa.q: Why does benzene burn with a sooty flame?
qa.a: It has a high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, so combustion in air is incomplete
qa.e: Aromatic compounds like C₆H₆ (C : H = 1 : 1) leave unburnt carbon as soot.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Benzene does not decolourise bromine water easily, unlike ethene. Reason (R): Benzene's delocalised π electrons give it extra stability, so it prefers substitution to addition.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Addition would destroy the stable aromatic system, so benzene resists it under ordinary conditions.

qa.q: What is the electrophile in the nitration of benzene?
qa.a: NO₂⁺
qa.e: Sulphuric acid protonates nitric acid, which loses water to form the nitronium ion NO₂⁺.

qa.q: What is the role of anhydrous AlCl₃ in Friedel–Crafts reactions?
qa.a: A Lewis acid that generates the electrophile (R⁺ or RCO⁺)
qa.e: AlCl₃ accepts Cl⁻ from RCl or RCOCl, producing the carbocation or acylium ion.

qa.q: Benzene reacts with CH₃COCl in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃ to give:
qa.a: Acetophenone (C₆H₅COCH₃)
qa.e: Friedel–Crafts acylation attaches the CH₃CO group to the ring.

qa.q: In the arenium ion (σ-complex) formed during electrophilic substitution, the carbon attacked by the electrophile is:
qa.a: sp³ hybridised
qa.e: It now has four σ bonds (to H, E and two ring carbons), so aromaticity is temporarily lost.

qa.q: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition with electrophiles?
qa.a: Loss of H⁺ restores the stable aromatic system, whereas addition would destroy it
qa.e: Keeping the delocalised 6π system is energetically favourable, so the arenium ion loses H⁺ instead of adding a nucleophile.

qa.q: What is the product when benzene is heated with fuming sulphuric acid?
qa.a: Benzenesulphonic acid
qa.e: SO₃ is the electrophile; the product is C₆H₅SO₃H.

qa.q: In the chlorination of benzene with Cl₂/FeCl₃, which species removes the proton in the last step?
qa.a: [FeCl₄]⁻
qa.e: [FeCl₄]⁻ takes H⁺ from the arenium ion, forming HCl and regenerating FeCl₃.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Anhydrous conditions are needed for Friedel–Crafts reactions. Reason (R): Water reacts with AlCl₃ and destroys its ability to act as a Lewis acid.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: AlCl₃ is hydrolysed by water, so it can no longer generate the electrophile.

qa.q: Which group is a meta director?
qa.a: –NO₂
qa.e: –NO₂ withdraws electrons (−R, −I), leaving meta positions relatively electron-richer.

qa.q: Why is chlorine an ortho/para director even though it deactivates the benzene ring?
qa.a: Its +R effect increases electron density at ortho and para positions, while its −I effect lowers overall reactivity
qa.e: Inductive withdrawal outweighs resonance donation in reactivity, but resonance decides where the electrophile attacks.

qa.q: What is formed when benzene reacts with chlorine in the presence of UV light at about 500 K?
qa.a: Benzene hexachloride (C₆H₆Cl₆)
qa.e: UV light promotes free-radical addition of three Cl₂ molecules to give 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane.

qa.q: Nitration of chlorobenzene gives mainly:
qa.a: o- and p-chloronitrobenzene
qa.e: Cl directs ortho and para; p-isomer usually predominates for steric reasons.

qa.q: To prepare m-chloronitrobenzene from benzene, which sequence is correct?
qa.a: Nitration first, then chlorination
qa.e: –NO₂ directs the incoming Cl to the meta position; chlorinating first would give o/p products.

qa.q: Arrange in increasing reactivity towards electrophilic substitution: benzene, phenol, nitrobenzene.
qa.a: Nitrobenzene < benzene < phenol
qa.e: –NO₂ deactivates, –OH activates, benzene is in between.

qa.q: How many moles of H₂ are needed to convert 1 mol of benzene completely into cyclohexane?
qa.e: C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂ (Ni, high temperature and pressure).

qa.q: Assertion (A): –OCH₃ is an ortho/para-directing activating group. Reason (R): The lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the ring (+R), raising electron density at ortho and para positions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The +R effect of the methoxy group outweighs its −I effect, activating the ring at o and p positions.

qa.q: Which is a carcinogenic polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbon?
qa.a: 3,4-Benzopyrene
qa.e: Benzopyrene, with five fused rings, is a well-known carcinogen formed by incomplete combustion.

qa.q: Polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons are mainly formed by:
qa.a: Incomplete combustion of organic matter like tobacco, coal and petroleum
qa.e: Partial burning gives fused-ring aromatic compounds in soot and smoke.

qa.q: How can benzene be converted into acetophenone?
qa.a: CH₃COCl with anhydrous AlCl₃
qa.e: Friedel–Crafts acylation introduces the COCH₃ group.

qa.q: Which reagent converts propene into propan-2-ol?
qa.a: H₂O in the presence of an acid catalyst
qa.e: Acid-catalysed hydration follows Markovnikov's rule, placing –OH on C2.

qa.q: Starting from sodium propanoate, which method gives ethane?
qa.a: Heating with soda lime
qa.e: Decarboxylation removes one carbon (3 → 2). Kolbe electrolysis of sodium propanoate would give butane.

qa.q: How would you convert benzene into p-nitrotoluene?
qa.a: Friedel–Crafts methylation first, then nitration
qa.e: –CH₃ directs the incoming NO₂ to ortho/para; nitrobenzene would direct methyl to meta (and resists Friedel–Crafts).

qa.q: How do PAHs such as benzopyrene cause cancer?
qa.a: After metabolic activation they damage DNA
qa.e: Body enzymes convert them into reactive species that bind DNA and cause mutations.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ethyne can be converted into benzene in one step. Reason (R): Three ethyne molecules undergo cyclic polymerisation in a red-hot iron tube at 873 K.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: 3HC≡CH → C₆H₆ in one step under these conditions.
